Several years ago, friendly Reader, we published a sufficiently sizeable volume by various authors treating chemistry <note>original Greek: "περὶ χημείας" (peri chēmeias). # PREFACE

*...to shed light <note>original: "lucem dare". The printer is continuing the metaphor of "bringing to light" (publishing) previously hidden or obscure knowledge.</note>: so that men, eager for this most excellent and most useful art <note term="Art">In the Renaissance, an "Art" (Ars) was a systematic body of knowledge or a craft—in this case, alchemy—used to perfect or imitate Nature.</note>, might be able to use and enjoy it. But someone will say that by these editions of mine, I bring more harm to the public good than benefit, since the art is vain and no science at all; they claim it deals not with entirely certain things, but with the uncertain and the rarely occurring—indeed, most rare, or perhaps never—and that it merely discusses the opinions of many men. For no one, they say, in our own or in the previous century, has actually achieved what the writers of this art so magnificently and in so many ways promise. Since, therefore, it lacks its intended goal, and yet all things are done for the sake of a goal, it follows that it is neither an art nor a science, and that those who engage in these matters, or who believe lazy impostors <note>The "impostor" or "fraudulent alchemist" was a common character in 16th-century literature; the printer is acknowledging the bad reputation alchemy often had due to con artists.</note>, are ridiculous and foolish. # PROPOSITIONS OR
## MAXIMS OF THE [GREAT] ART
### Chemical.

### PROPOSITION I.

Everything pure and clean extracted from its ore <note>original: "minera"</note>, from stones, and then from foreign matters, without any preparation, which does not melt like wax <note>original: "funditur vt cera"</note>, is unsuitable for this work. From this it is concluded that all metals are excluded, and all species of Marcasite <term>Marcasite: iron pyrites or other metallic ores that resemble precious metals but were considered "immature"</term>, glass, crystal, coral, and all pearls which do not liquefy in fire.

### *Proposition II.*

Every sublimable substance <term>sublimable: a substance that can be turned into vapor by heat and then solidified again</term> that adheres to the sides of the vessel, preventing the viewing of the foreign matter within the vessel, is removed from and unsuitable for this business. For this reason, all four principal spirits are especially excluded, namely: quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and every kind of tutty <term>tutty: a substance, often zinc oxide, collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term> and magnesia <note>original: "magnesiæ"; in this context, likely a reference to various dark minerals or ores used in the alchemical process rather than the modern chemical</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the fundamental "propositions" of the chemical art, establishing criteria for selecting materials by excluding substances that do not melt like wax or those that obscure the vessel during sublimation.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, chemical propositions, metallurgy, marcasite, four spirits, quicksilver, arsenic, sulfur, tutty, magnesia</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the list of alchemical "Propositions" or fundamental rules for the Great Work, specifically focusing on the exclusion of organic materials and the required speed of transformation for the active chemical principle.</meta>

### Proposition III.

Every mineral that is not of the earth <note>original: "cuius non sit terra"</note> is foreign and hostile to this work. By this rule, all things originating from animals are excluded, such as hair, blood, flesh, dung, eggs, and the like; and also all animals themselves, such as turtles, beetles <note>original: "caragdi"; likely referring to scarabs or specific insects</note>, moles, frogs, bees, and similar creatures.

### Proposition IIII.

Any animate thing proceeding from inanimate things is unsuitable for this greater art. By this proposition, all "superfluities" of animals are especially excluded, as well as all vegetable matter and anything derived from them—for instance: wine, burning water <term>burning water: "aqua ardens," an early term for distilled alcohol or aqua vitae</term>, oil, honey, urine, sperm, and things of this nature.

### Proposition V.

<margin>3 11</margin>
Everything which cannot be blackened, whitened, and reddened <note>These colors—black, white, and red—represent the three primary stages of the alchemical transformation: Nigredo, Albedo, and Rubedo.</note> by fire within one hour of a natural day <term>natural day: a full twenty-four hour period</term>, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the masculine principle <term>masculine principle: the active, "sulfurous" agent in the chemical marriage, believed to provide the form and seed for the Stone</term>.

<summary>This page continues the foundational rules of alchemy by strictly forbidding the use of organic animal or plant matter in the "Great Work." It also establishes a time-based trial by fire to identify the "masculine" or active mineral component of the process.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, organic exclusion, aqua ardens, masculine principle, color stages, nigredo, albedo, rubedo, natural day</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the numbered list of alchemical "Propositions" or axioms. While the previous page excluded organic materials and defined the masculine principle, this page defines the feminine principle, the necessity of duality (the chemical marriage), and the requirement for procedural simplicity.</meta>

### *Proposition VI.*

Everything that lacks red smoke <note>original: "fumo rubeo"</note>, when enclosed in a small vessel over a proper fire, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the feminine principle <term>feminine principle: the passive, "mercurial" component of the alchemical process, intended to be fertilized by the masculine "sulfur"</term>. By the two aforementioned maxims <note>referring to Propositions V and VI</note>, alum and salts are excluded, as well as every kind of borax <note>original: "baurachiorum"</note> and vitriol <note>original: "gignarum"; likely referring to various metallic sulfates or salts</note>, and all liquids proceeding from them.

### *Proposition VII.*

No thing of a single number <note>meaning a single, solitary substance</note> can complete a work of a higher order. From this it is most clearly drawn that the Philosophers' Stone <term>Philosophers' Stone: the legendary alchemical substance capable of perfecting base metals and human health</term> is made from two things: namely, the male and the female, or the red and the white <note>These colors refer to the active sulfur and the passive mercury respectively</note>.

### *Proposition VIII.*

Whatever cannot be completed in a single vessel and in a single number is unsuitable for this work. And from this, a plurality of vessels is especially excluded <note>The author advocates for the "Single Vessel" theory, where the entire transformation occurs within one sealed container, often called the Hermetic Vase</note>.

### *Proposition IX.*

Whatever within the space of one hundred days

It also emphasizes that the entire process should ideally occur within a single vessel.</summary>

## Proposition X.

Everything that, in the first six days, when melted over a proper fire in the physical vessel <term>physical vessel: the "vas philosophicum" or Hermetic egg, a specially prepared glass container used to hold the alchemical matter</term> within its necessary furnace, does not appear saffron-yellow <note>original: "croceum"</note>; and in the next six days, red <note>original: "rubeum"</note>; and in the subsequent days, white with a perfect whiteness; and in the concluding thirty days, most intensely red with a perfect redness <note>original: "rubedine perfecta"</note>—this thing is not intended for this work. From this is especially drawn the method of operation: namely, that the physical stone must be placed in a glass vessel closed inviolably <note>meaning hermetically sealed, so no spirits or vapors can escape</note> in a physical furnace, and it must be melted over a slow fire, and in that melting it must be held at a uniform fire for the space

of eighteen days: in the first six days the medicine <term>medicine: another name for the Philosophers' Stone, referring to its power to "heal" or perfect base metals</term> will be saffron-yellow <note>original: "crocea"</note>, in the other six days it will be red, and in the other six it will be black, and afterward red with a most intense redness. You shall maintain this for thirty days, during which you must nourish the said stone with two lights <note>referring to lamps or wicks used as heat sources</note>—not very thick ones—day and night for the space of the said thirty days. 

When these are finished, a saffron color will appear, which will cover all the red like a cloud. And that saffron color will cease within the space of 8 days. Afterward, a perfect and clear whiteness will appear, like the star of Diana <note>The "Star of Diana" refers to the Moon, representing the White Work (Albedo) which produces silver</note>; and it will be a perfect medicine for Silver <note>original: "Luna"</note> upon Mercury, and upon imperfect bodies <term>imperfect bodies: base metals, such as lead or tin, which the alchemist seeks to transmute into noble metals</term> to infinity. 

Furthermore, by adding one light, it must be nourished for the space of thirty days with three lights, and then a most ruddy medicine will appear in the manner of scarlet <note>original: "Scarlati"</note>, and it will be a perfect medicine for the Red <note>The "Red Work" (Rubedo) which produces gold</note> upon Mercury, and upon imperfect bodies forever and to infinity, with Christ favoring; thanks be to God.

## Proposition XI.

Every medicine <term>medicine: the alchemical agent or Philosophers' Stone, so-called because it "heals" base metals into gold</term> which cannot multiply itself to infinity is not part of the intent of the "Great Work" <note>original: "operis maioris ordinis," referring to the highest level of alchemical achievement</note> of the higher order. From this it is most clearly deduced that the multiplication <note>The ability of the Stone to increase its own quantity or potency</note> of this work is one part of the aforementioned medicine: for the Redness <note>The final stage of the process, called the Rubedo</note>, the previously mentioned vessel must be set with twelve parts [of the substance] over a fire of three lights <note>referring to three lamps or wicks used as a specific heat source</note> for fifteen days, and it will reach the final redness. It will then be an Elixir <term>Elixir: a liquid or powder capable of transmuting metals</term> for perfect red, and in this way you can multiply it infinitely.

## Proposition XII.

Whatever exceeds the value of one ounce of pure gold is not part of the intent of the higher order. And from this it is most clearly deduced that those things which compose the physical stone <term>physical stone: the Philosophers' Stone in its tangible form</term>, if they exceed one ounce of pure gold, they are not of the intent of the higher order. And from this it most especially follows that 15 grains of ferment <term>ferment: a small amount of precious metal added to the alchemical "medicine" to act as a catalyst or "seed" for the final transformation</term> are suitable for the work of the higher order, since they are purchased at a low price <note>A core alchemical belief was that the "Prima Materia" or starting material for the Stone was something common and inexpensive, not gold itself</note>.

<summary>This page defines the "Great Work" of the higher order by two criteria: the resulting medicine must be infinitely capable of multiplying itself, and the starting materials must not be expensive or exceed the value of an ounce of gold.</summary>
<keywords>Multiplication, Great Work, Elixir, Rubedo, Redness, Physical Stone, Ferment, Alchemy, Economics of Alchemy</keywords>

### Proposition XIII.
### & final.

Only that which is composed of **incombustible oil** <term>incombustible oil: a symbolic alchemical term for the "fixed sulfur" or the "soul" of a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate even under extreme heat</term> and of **fusible salt** <term>fusible salt: a purified mineral "body" that melts easily, representing the union of the volatile and the fixed principles</term> is favorable to this art. From this it is most especially concluded that the **Physical Stone** <term>Physical Stone: the tangible, completed Philosophers' Stone in its final state, capable of performing transmutations</term> is composed of incombustible oil and fusible salt.

->Thanks be to God, amen.<-

### T V R B A

...cooks, and the goal is reached. Truly the stars and heavenly bodies, since they are fiery, are by nature suited for the work of cooking and warming <note>original Latin: *coctionis & fomenti*; in alchemy, these terms describe the gentle, sustained heat required for spiritual and physical maturation</note>. So that they might endure and perform their duty rightly, God established the air between them and the earth, and between the things to be warmed and cooked. This air contains the stars and prevents them—especially the flame of the Sun, for I say nothing of the others—from burning up all existing things. And if the air did not breathe into the spirits by which creatures are generated, the Sun would destroy all existing things with its heat. 

But also the water would destroy all things with its coldness and moisture, unless the air intervened. Therefore, since air is hot and moist <note>Though the text says *calidus & siccus* (hot and dry), the traditional Aristotelian quality of air is hot and moist. Eximidius's argument here emphasizes air as the bridge between fire and water.</note>, it thus harmonizes the heat of the celestial fire and stars with the watery coldness, so that an enduring friendship remains between them. From this harmony proceeds the warming and the benefit of decoction <term>decoction: the alchemical process of heating a substance in a closed vessel to bring it to maturity or "ripeness"</term> for all existing things.

**The ASSEMBLY says:** You have described fire well; continue, therefore.

<margin>2</margin>
**HE says:** I magnify and honor the air, because by it the work is improved, as it thickens and thins, and as it is heated and cooled. Its thickness occurs when things are distinguished in the heavens due to the rising of the sun. Its thinness occurs when the air is thinned and heated by the second Sun <note>original: *ex altero Sole*; this may refer to the "philosophical sun" or the internal heat of the alchemical vessel, as opposed to the literal sun in the sky</note>. When that air is thinned, the Sun becomes near: and by its nearness, heat reaches man and all creatures.

### PHILOSOPHY

...thickens the air. <margin>3</margin> But know, Assembly, that the density <note>original: *spissitudo*; in this context, it refers to the physical weight, solidity, or "coarseness" of an element</note> of the four beginnings rests in the earth alone. This is because the density of fire falls into the air, while the density of air—along with that which is gathered from the density of fire—falls into the water. The density of water also, combined with what is joined from the density of fire and air, rests in the earth. Thus, the density of these four elements rests in the earth, and in the earth they are joined together. The earth itself is therefore denser than all the other elements, as is clearly apparent and can be seen. Fire, however, is thinner <note>original: *rarior*; refers to the "subtlety" or lack of physical weight in an element</note> than the rest; and just as the earth, being denser, is lower, so fire is higher and more noble. Air is less thin than fire, and water is again less thin than air. For everything cold and moist possesses less thinness than that which is hot and moist. Furthermore, earth is of less thinness than water because it is cold and dry; and everything cold and dry is less thin than that which is cold and moist.

<margin>4</margin> **PYTHAGORAS** said: O sons of learning, you have well arranged the descriptions of these natures from which God created all things. Therefore, proceed.

To this **LUCAS** said: I declare to you that from these four natures, God created all things, and all created things return to them. In these they are generated, and in these they die in their own time, just as God has ordained.

**LOCASTES** said: Know that the creation of the world was created from two dense things and two thin things

<margin>9</margin> **PYTHAGORAS** said: I declare that God existed before all things. When He was alone, He created four things, simple in number, which are the four elements. These are of the same essence—that is, the same matter—yet of different forms; these are the simple qualities which are converted into one another. From these elements, once they were created, He thereafter created all things, both of the sublime and the lower realms. This was because it was necessary for creatures to be drawn from a certain root, from which they might multiply to inhabit the world. Therefore, before all things, God created the four elements, from which He later created whatever He willed—namely, various natures, some of which He created from a single element.

The **ASSEMBLY** <note>original: *Turba*; refers to the gathering of philosophers listening to the discourse</note> asked: What are those things, Master, which the sublime God created from only one?

And **HE** <note>Pythagoras</note> replied: They are the angels, whom God created from fire.

And the **ASSEMBLY** asked: What things are created from two?

And **HE** replied: From two were created the Sun, the Moon, and the stars—namely, from air and fire. Therefore, angels are more radiant than the Sun, the Moon, and the stars, because they were created from one single thing, which is the fourth <note>likely referring to fire, the highest and most "subtle" of the four elements in this hierarchical system</note> and the thinnest <note>original: *rarissimum*</note> of all. However, the Sun, Moon, and stars were created from a composition of fire and air.

The **Assembly** asked: And from where does the creation of heaven come?

And **He** <note>Pythagoras</note> replied: God created the heaven from water and air; thus, the heaven too is composed of two elements—one being the thinner <note>original: *rariorum*; meaning less dense or more subtle</note>, namely air, and the other being the denser, namely water.

And they said: Master, continue your discourse and explain those things made of three.

And **He** replied: From three elements God created the winged creatures, the beasts, and the plants—specifically from air, water, and earth.

The **ASSEMBLY** then said: Distinguish between these, Master.

And **He** said: Some were created from air and earth; others, however, from fire, air, and earth. Of the latter, the winged creatures and all things possessing breath <note>original: *spiritum*; refers to the "breath of life" or vital spirit</note> are an example; while of the former, plants are the example. Indeed, all beasts are made from earth, air, and fire; whereas plants are made from water, <margin>x</margin> earth, and air, and they have nothing in common with fire.

And they asked: Shall we then say that fire is present even in plants?

And **He** replied: You would be speaking the truth: for due to the heat of the air hidden within them—just as I have indicated that a thin fire exists within the air—fire is present in them because fire is in the air, and air is in the plants. However, speaking of elemental fire <term>elemental fire: the pure, primary form of the element fire, as opposed to mere heat</term> in itself, it is not present except in those things possessing breath and a soul. But from all four elements, man was create—

...creatures emerge, which are most precious. Of those elements that join together, two are visible and tangible, while two are neither visible nor tangible. Because if those which are visible and tangible are joined, undoubtedly the others that are contained within the first two are also mixed in. For air, participating in fire, also has something in common with water; similarly, it was said above that the earth embraces all these within itself. If you mix our copper <note>original: *æs*; in this context, it refers to the solid "earthy" base of the alchemical work, not necessarily common metal</note>, which is "earth," with water, you will achieve a great thing. For when our copper is placed in seawater and cooked, the earth reveals itself by drinking the water and embracing the other two elements within itself. This is signified by the progress of the work—namely, by the grinding and the coagulation of the stone <term>stone: *lapis*, the "Philosopher's Stone" or the completed alchemical substance</term>—and immediately from these, coins <note>original: *nummos*; likely referring to the small, transformed disks or the valuable resulting substance</note> are made. <margin>11</margin>
**Aristenes** said: The key to this work is the **art of coins** <note>original: *numorum ars*; an alchemical metaphor for the transformation and "minting" of base metals into precious ones</note>. Take, therefore, the body that has been shown to you and shape it into thin plates; then place them in the water of our sea, which, while it is being managed, is called **Permanent Water** <term>Permanent Water: *Aqua permanens*, a central alchemical term for a solvent that does not wet the hands and dissolves metals into their primary matter</term>. Afterward, place it over a gentle fire until the plates are broken down and become water. Then join it to the **Ethelia** <term>Ethelia: a technical term for the hidden spirit or vaporous essence of a substance, often associated with the process of sublimation</term>, and roast them together over a slow fire until it becomes a thickened broth. Turn this into its own **Ethelia** until it is coagulated and becomes a varied coin.

# PHILOSOPHERS

->a 5<-

...to know what it is that putrefies and renews a thing, and of what flavor it is, and what is its distance and proximity, and how friendship is made after enmity, and how corruption and generation <note>original: *corruptio & generatio*; the cycle of breaking down a substance and rebirthing it in a perfected state</note> occur, and how those natures embrace each other, and how they become harmonious in a slow fire: with these things noted and perceived, apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of these stated qualities, do not approach the work, since everything is harmful, and a misfortune and sorrow. Now understand the words of the Sages, and retain this brief saying: namely, that **Nature rejoices in nature**, and **Nature contains nature**, and **Nature conquers and overcomes nature**. <note>original: *Natura natura lætatur, & naturam continet, & natura naturam vincit & superat*; a foundational axiom of alchemy attributed to Pseudo-Democritus, suggesting that only substances of a similar essence can transform one another.</note>

In these words the whole work is encompassed. Dismiss therefore superfluous speeches, and take **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury</note>, and congeal it in the body of **magnesia** <term>magnesia: in alchemy, this rarely refers to magnesium oxide; it is a cryptic term for the "crude matter" or "mother" of the stone</term>, and of **sulfur that is not burned**, and turn it into a white nature. And if you place it upon our copper, it will become white. And if you wish to make it red, it will become red. And if you cook it further, it will become gold. I say also, that it turns the sea itself into red, and into **gold-glue** <term>auricollam: also known as chrysocolla, a substance used in the soldering of gold, here representing a transformative agent</term>: and likewise it turns gold into red fire, because **Nature rejoices in nature**. Cook it therefore in moisture, until the hidden nature appears: and when you see this, soak it seven times with **permanent water** <note>original: *aqua permanente*; a stable, non-wetting alchemical solvent, often identified with philosophical mercury</note>, by cooking...

<summary>Parmenides explains the fundamental alchemical axiom that Nature acts upon its own kind and provides a sequence for transforming mercury and magnesia into white and red stages, eventually reaching gold. He emphasizes that the operator must understand the natural sympathies and "friendships" between elements before beginning the work.</summary>

->## PHILOSOPHY ##<-

...know ye, that the body cannot dye <note>original: "tingere"; to tint, color, or transform the internal nature of a metal</note> itself, unless the hidden spirit is extracted from its belly, and it becomes body, soul, and spirit (which is the spiritual tincture). The dense is joined to the moist, because sulphurs are contained by sulphurs, and by right of nature, nature rejoices when its own nature approaches. <note>This is a famous alchemical axiom: "Nature rejoices in nature, nature conquers nature, nature rules nature."</note>

Then follows the perfect color, similar to a common coin, and it is the **Elixir** <note>original: "Yxir"; a corruption of the Arabic "al-iksir"</note> composed of the moist and the dry, a tincture that dyes unchangeably. # TURBA

<note>Space for decorative initial 'A' left blank</note> [A]ttend, children of the doctrine, to how painters are unable to paint with their colors until they turn them into ashes and pulverize them. Similarly, philosophers are often unable to prepare medicines for their sick unless the ingredients are crushed and pulverized. For if you manage this ash subtly, many things will proceed from it, because copper <term>copper: the Latin "aes" refers to copper, bronze, or brass, but in alchemy, it represents the base "body" of the work</term>, like a human being, possesses both a body and a spirit. <note>The following section is underlined in the original manuscript</note>A human’s breathing comes from the air; likewise, copper receives life through inspired moisture, and it is multiplied and increased just like all other things.<note>End of underlining</note> And for this reason, the philosophers said that copper becomes better when it is burned than it was before. Furthermore, this copper of ours becomes water when it is first cooked; then, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened <note>original: "inspissatur"</note>, until it becomes a stone surpassing every metal. After this, it is broken, soaked, and roasted with a more intense fire until it is colored and becomes like "burnt blood"; then place your coins <note>original: "nummos," likely referring to pieces of base metal</note> within it, and it dyes them into gold. For just as seed <note>original: "sperma," here meaning the generative principle or biological seed</note> is not produced from blood unless it is cooked diligently in the liver <note>original: "epate"</note>, so our work is by no means a tincture <term>tincture: a substance capable of "staining" or transforming the properties of another material, specifically into gold</term> unless it is cooked diligently until it becomes a powder, and thus through putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the stage of "rotting" or breakdown (often associated with the color black) necessary for spiritual rebirth of the matter</term> that very seed is made spiritual in its effect. For only then will the color you have sought be found, and not otherwise.

For in the belly of Corsufle the true nature is hidden, and this true nature is that **tingeing spirit** <term>spiritus tingens: the volatile essence or "soul" capable of transforming and coloring base metals</term> which it obtained from the nummous <note>original: "nummosa," likely meaning coin-like or shimmering with a metallic luster</note> and flashing **permanent water** <term>aqua permanens: the "eternal water" or universal solvent, a central mystery of the Great Work</term>. It is extracted in this way: grind the Corsufle and apply water seven times, until it drinks all the moisture and receives the power that stands against the fight of the fire, and then it is called "rust." Therefore, rot it diligently until it becomes a spiritual powder in the color of dried blood, a color which the power of the fire introduces until it is clothed in an unchangeable color.

The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. That which we seek is sold publicly at the lowest price, and if it were known, merchants would not sell even a tiny bit of it. Therefore, they become permanent.

### PHILOSOPHY

Therefore, he will be long-suffering, and will freely enjoy the virtue of patience, walking in the righteous path of this art <note>In alchemy, the "Art" refers to the Great Work or *Magnum Opus*, the process of transforming base matter into the Philosopher's Stone</note>. But he who thinks he can gather fruit from our books more quickly is mistaken; indeed, it would have been better for him never to have looked at them at all. For our books seem to do a great injury to those who read our writings only once, twice, or thrice; such people find their understanding and all their study frustrated, and (what is worst of all) they lose the wealth, labor, and time they have spent on this art. 

Nevertheless, he who bends his back to the reading of our books and devotes himself to them studiously, applying and sharpening his memory and mind—and is not entangled in vain thoughts, but prays to God, as Solomon did, for the granting of wisdom rather than for riches—he shall reign as a king in our kingdom without end, until he dies.

However, they likewise become **non-fleeing** <note>original: *non fugientes*; referring to "fixed" substances that are stable and remain solid under the heat of the fire</note> because, through the intervention of fire, they embrace and contain each other.

Therefore, take those things which do not flee and join them; wash the body with what is bodiless, and with that which lacks a body, make the body solid, until you turn it into a body with non-fleeing bodies. Turn earth into water, water into fire, and fire into air; hide the fire in the innermost parts of the water, and the earth in the belly of the air. Mix the hot with the moist, and the dry with the cold; because **Nature overcomes nature**; and then **Nature rejoices in nature** <note>original: *Natura naturam superat... Natura naturæ congaudet*; these are foundational axioms in alchemy, traditionally attributed to the philosopher Bolos of Mendes/Pseudo-Democritus</note>; so—

**BELUS** said: Many things have been discussed concerning composition; however, composition and contraction are one and the same thing. ...**greatest** <note>original: *maximum*. This completes the sentence from the previous page: "This is the greatest secret..."</note>: because only **sulfur** <term>Sulfur: In alchemy, the active, combustible, and masculine principle, often associated with the power to "color" or "fix" a substance</term> whitens copper. It must also be made known to you, investigators of this art, that that sulfur could not whiten the copper until it has been whitened in the prior work: for it is the habit of this sulfur to **flee** <note>Alchemists used "fleeing" to describe substances that were volatile and would evaporate or sublimate when heated</note>. This happens as soon as the quicksilver and the copper itself are joined. For then they often mutually dissolve and conceive, and do not allow flight, but both become quicksilver. And so this, which at first was neither copper nor quicksilver, is nevertheless made so by the mixing of quicksilver: which, namely, being added to the quicksilver, contains the first quicksilver, whose habit was to flee. Wherefore the philosophers said: **Sulfurs are contained by sulfurs.** 

Furthermore, know that sulfurs **dye** <note>original: *tingunt*. To "dye" meant to permanently change the color and nature of a metal, essentially transmuting it</note>, and then they undoubtedly flee, unless they have been joined to quicksilver of their own kind. Therefore, do not think that which dyes and then flees is the **coin** <note>original: *nummum*. # THE PRINTER
## To the Reader.

It seemed good to us, honest Reader, that we should look to your benefit by including another copy of the *Turba* <note>original: "Turbae". This refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among ancient sages.</note> that we had in our possession. We have added this not so much because of a different arrangement of the text, but rather for the variety of the philosophical maxims and names. For it happens that in the other volume, the same concept is expressed with a different meaning, in different words, and attributed to a different author; we provide this so that in a matter of such great importance <note>Refers to the "Great Work" of alchemy—the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, you might not go astray, but may follow whichever version appeals to you more in your own operations. Farewell; and if you find anything of use here, you should credit that most distinguished and excellent Physician, Master William Rascalon of Worms <note>original: "Guilielmo Rascalono Vormatiensi". William Rascalon was a 16th-century physician from Worms, Germany, known for his interest in Paracelsian medicine and his collection of alchemical manuscripts.</note>, through whose generosity we obtained these copies.

<summary>In this preface, the printer explains that they are providing a second version of the "Turba Philosophorum" to help the reader. By comparing different wordings and attributions, the alchemist can better understand the difficult instructions for the "Great Work."</summary>

<keywords>printer's preface, Turba Philosophorum, William Rascalon of Worms, textual variants, alchemical practice, scholarship</keywords>

### PROPOSITION II.

**ISINDRUS.** I magnify the air <note>original: "aerea". Referring to the element of air or aerial things.</note>, because the work itself is improved by the air. When it is thickened, it [eventually] becomes rare; when it is heated, it [eventually] grows cold <note>This paradoxical statement likely refers to the alchemical cycle where an element reaches the peak of one quality and begins to transition into its opposite.</note>. Its density <note>term: spissitudo (thickness/density)</note> occurs when it is dispersed in the sky because of the sun's distance. Its rarity <note>term: raritas (thinness/rarefaction)</note>, however, occurs when the sun is exalted; then the air thins and becomes clear. A similar thing happens in the temperament <note>original: "complexione". For according to the change of the established disposition, in order to alter the divisions of the year, winter is changed; the air, therefore, is thickened at that time when the sun is distant from it. But when the air becomes rare, the sun is near; and by its proximity, heat reaches mankind.

### PROPOSITION X

**Eximenus.** All things were created from the four elements: namely the heaven, the thrones <note>A high rank of angels in the celestial hierarchy.</note>, the angels, the sun, the moon, the stars, fire, air, the sea and all waters, the earth, and things both diverse and similar. Nor is there any diversity in these things I have mentioned, except that each of those creatures is of a different nature, and its nature is varied according to different laws <note>original: "legibus". Here referring to the governing proportions or physical principles of their makeup.</note>. And this diversity is present in all creatures because they were created from different elements; for if they were made from a single element, they would have a total likeness among themselves. Truly, when the elements are mixed together, the mixture itself is neither dry by itself, nor moist, nor hot, nor cold. But when they come together, creatures emerge from them which are never perfected unless they first rot and are corrupted in appearance <note>original: "putrefiant & corrūpantur apud vifum". This refers to the alchemical stage of *putrefaction*, where matter must "die" and turn black before it can be transformed into a higher state.</note>. Then, however, God grants increase—namely life, food, nourishment, and governance.

Listen, dearest brothers, it is not in vain that I have recounted these descriptions of the elements to you. For in them lies a hidden secret: of these elements, two are visible, and their power and work are known; but the other two are neither seen nor touched, nor is their power or work seen, except through the first two elements <note>In classical alchemy, Earth and Water are the "tangible" elements, while Air and Fire are the "active" or "spiritual" elements that inhabit the others.</note>. And unless those four elements are joined, they accomplish nothing. However, when they are joined, they set aside their individual natures and become something else, and thus the Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy or the Great Work of transmutation.</note> is born: therefore, meditate upon these things. Moreover, know all you sons of the doctrine <note>original: "filij doctrinæ". This term refers to the initiated practitioners who have been properly taught the secrets of the craft.</note>, that no true tincture <note>A "tincture" is the goal of the work: a substance capable of "coloring" or transmuting base metals into gold or silver.</note> is made, except from our bronze <note>original: "ære nostro". Alchemists used the term "our" to distinguish their secret starting materials from common metals found in a blacksmith's shop.</note>. Therefore, do not consume your souls and money in vain, nor bring sorrow to your hearts. For you will achieve nothing unless you turn the aforementioned bronze into white, and make coins <note>original: "numos". This may refer to the physical shape of the material—flattened into discs—or symbolize the "currency" of the philosophical exchange.</note> by practice; then make that white into red, until the tincture is completed. Therefore, break that bronze, burn it, and deprive it of its blackness <note>The "blackness" or *nigredo* represents the first stage of the work, which must be washed away to reach the white stage (*albedo*).</note> by cooking, soaking, and washing, until it becomes white; then bind it by the Art.

### THE SIXTEENTH DISCOURSE

Frictes said: Know, seekers of wisdom: that the foundation of this art—for which many have perished—is indeed one thing that is stronger and more sublime than all natures according to the philosophers. But if not, repeat the work, taking the **white moisture**—which is the greatest secret, in which the true **tincture** consists—and moisten the sand <note>original: "arena". Here, probably refers to the granulated or powdered form of the stone.</note> (which was made from the stone previously moistened seven times) with it seven times, until it drinks all the water. Close the mouth of the vessel tightly, as has often been said, and behold, the **Tyrian stone** <term>lapis tyrius: likely referring to a stone of a deep purple or royal crimson color, named after the famous Tyrian purple dye of antiquity.</term> will appear to you.

### TWENTY-FOURTH STATEMENT

**Theophilus.** Investigators of the Art, know that the art of the **coin** and the secret of **gold** is a dark garment, which no one knows except him who has read through the books of philosophy with diligent and constant reading. For that which is hidden is greater than that which can be learned. Therefore, I make it known...

## STATEMENT XXX.

The **GUARDIAN** says: I marvel, O Assembly of Sages <note>original: "Turba sapientum"; the title of the work, referring to this gathering of philosophers.</note>, at the great power of this water, which, when it enters the body, turns it into earth, and then into powder. If you wish to test whether it is perfect, take it in your hand; if it is almost impalpable <note>Too fine to be felt as individual grains.</note>, it is at its best. If not, repeat the cooking of it until it is perfected. And you should know that if you take anything other than our copper <term>our copper: "aes nostrum," a specialized term for the secret starting material of the alchemists, which they claimed was not the common metal of the same name.</term>, and direct it with our water <note>original: "aqua nostra"; the secret solvent or "mercury" used to dissolve the solid matter.</note>, you will achieve nothing. On the other hand, if you direct our copper with our water, you will find everything I have described. Therefore, cook it with a gentle fire, and it will become a scaly stone <note>original: "lapis numosus"; literally "money-like stone," likely referring to a substance that forms flat, coin-like scales or flakes during crystallization.</note>, of which the Sages have said: "Nature rejoices in nature" <note>original: "Natura natura lætatur"; one of the most famous axioms in alchemy, suggesting that only substances of the same inner essence can successfully combine.</note> because of the closeness these two bodies have to each other along with the permanent water <term>permanent water: "aqua permanens," a substance that does not evaporate or "fly" from the fire, representing a stabilized spiritual state of the matter.</term>. Of these two, then, there is one nature, between which a closeness is mixed; if this were not so, they would not be mixed so quickly, nor would they hold one another, nor become one.

**DIAMEDES** says: Know, O Wise men, that from a human nothing is born but a human, and from beasts nothing but their own kind. And for this reason, I say that Nature is not improved except within its own nature <note>original: "Natura non emendatur nisi in sua natura."</note>, and therefore use the venerable...

The philosophers have said this: that when copper <note>original: "æs"; in alchemy, this refers not just to the metal copper, but to the base "body" or starting material of the work</note> is burned, it becomes better than it was before. Furthermore, when this copper of ours is burned, it becomes water; then, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened, and it becomes a **stone** <term>Stone: the Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the alchemical process</term> surpassing every metal. Afterwards, it is broken, soaked, and roasted with a more intense fire until it is colored and becomes like blood; then the money <note>original: "numus"; a recurring alchemical metaphor for the transformative substance or "coin" of the work</note> is added, and it **tints** <note>original: "tingit"; the process of alchemical transformation where the essence "dyes" or changes the nature of the metal</note> the copper into gold. Do you not see that seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> is not produced from blood unless it is diligently cooked? The same happens in our work: unless the seed becomes spiritual, no **tincture** <term>Tincture: the potent liquid or essence capable of transmuting metals</term> comes out of it.

## *STATEMENT XXXV.*

**NICARUS**: I command those who come after to take gold, and multiply and renew what they wish; then divide the water into two parts. With one part, it is necessary to burn our copper. For this copper, dissolved in this water, will be called the **Ferment of Gold** <term>Fermentum auri: a substance added to the alchemical mix to "leaven" or trigger the transformation into gold</term>. If you have guided it well, it will become water, which will be congealed by cooking, and then a redness will appear. You shall soak this redness seven times with water, or until it drinks all its water. Finally, cook it until it is dried out and turned into dry earth; then place it over an active fire for forty days, and it will **putrefy** <note>Putrefaction was a vital stage in alchemy, representing the breaking down of matter before its rebirth/purification</note>, and its colors will appear.

...because both are joined together in the boiling process <term>decoction: the reduction or concentration of a substance through heat</term>, where one contains the other and prevents it from escaping. If blackness <note>original: "nigredo"; the first stage of the Great Work, associated with death and decay</note> appears, it arises from "sickness" <note>this likely refers to the breakdown of the material's initial form</note>; it dies during the stage of rot <term>putrefaction: the decomposition of matter to prepare it for transformation</term> and becomes a rust <note>original: "rubigo"; in alchemy, this refers to a reddish tint or a metallic oxide appearing after the black stage, signaling a transition toward the final goal</note>. It does not behave as it did before, but having taken on a golden divine power, it brings the body back to life. Philosophers have called this nature "Spirit" and "Soul."

Furthermore, they said that the moist spirit is black, yet free from impurity. Just as a human being is composed of moisture and dryness, so in our Great Work there is nothing else but vapor and water. For this reason, the ancients stated that the work consists of two things. When joined, some call them a "composite," because these two are actually four: for within them reside dryness and moisture, spirit and vapor.

## DICTUM XXXIX

**AGADmon.** Cook the copper until it becomes a smooth and <term>impalpable: so fine it cannot be felt as individual grains</term> body, and place it in its own vessel: then <term>sublimate: to refine by heat</term> it five or seven times until the water descends, knowing that when the water is a powder, it has been diligently ground. If you doubt how water might become powder, know that the intention of the philosophers is that the body—which was not water before it fell into water—may become water together with water, and that water may be mixed with water, so that they become one. It must be known, moreover, that unless you turn both into water, you will not reach the precious work: for it is necessary that the body, occupied by the flame of fire, be destroyed and made weak when water is in water, until it becomes entirely water. The ignorant, however, when they hear the name of water...

### FORTY-SECOND SPEECH

**EFISTES** Pay attention, sons of learning, to what Hermes, the head of the Philosophers, said when he taught how to mix the natures. For he said: Take the stone of gold and mix it with the moisture (which is the <term>permanent water: original "aqua permanens"; a philosophical solvent that does not evaporate or "flee" when exposed to fire</term>), and place it in its vessel over a gentle heat until it liquefies. Then leave it until it dries out, and the water and the sand are held together; then let the fire be made more intense, until it dries out completely and becomes earth, and this will be the beginning of the secret <note>original: "arcani initium"</note>. Do this many times until two parts of the water disappear, and the colors appear to you. 

And know that the <term>whitening: original "dealbatio"; the alchemical stage of purification where the black "corpse" of the matter turns white</term> does not happen except by boiling, and for that reason, the process of grinding and moistening is repeated very frequently. I command you, however, not to pour the water all at once, lest the <term>Ysir: a specialized term for the elixir or the transformative substance being processed</term> be submerged; instead, pour it in little by little, grind it, dry it, and do this quite often, until they become water. 

And the philosophers said: Once the water is measured out, leave it until it is fixed below—that is, as the moisture dries and is turned into powder—and leave it in its glass vessel for forty days, until it produces various colors. By this regimen <note>original: "regimine"; the systematic control of the fire and the timing of the work</note>, bodies become spirits, and hot spirits become coloring agents <note>original: "tingunt"; the ability of the stone to 'tint' or transform the nature of metals</note>.

## SPEECH LXIII.

<margin><unclear>It lacks the lesser good which says that truth is made in a single day; for it is boiling that performs the great work.</unclear></margin>

ADMION says:
> You cannot, wise men, reach the usefulness of this art without a prolonged and continuous regimen <note>original: "regimine"; the systematic treatment or "cooking" of the alchemical substance</note>. Therefore, he who is patient in the regimen shall enter the art; but he who is not, let him not read our sayings, because having read them, they will only bring him harm. And so the Master said: He who labors in reading our books, and devotes himself to them, and is not entangled in various worldly thoughts, and prays to God, shall reign in a kingdom until he dies. For what is sought is not of small price, but is a gift of God; for that reason, patience and labor are needed. For we see that he who grafts trees hopes for fruit in time, and he who sows reaps after months.

> Watch, therefore, and learn to mix, to cook, to simulate <note>original: "simulare"; likely meaning to make the substances resemble one another in nature</note>, to roast, to heat, to whiten, to grind, to level the <term>Ethelia: original "Etheliam"; a technical term in the Turba referring to the spiritualized or vaporous part of the matter</term>, to make the rust <note>original: "rubiginem"; the reddish oxidation or "saffron" color that signals the approach of the final stage</note>, and finally to dye. These are many names, yet the regimen is but one; but the boiling is continuous, on account of which the philosophers have repeated often that the compound should be ground and cooked perpetually—and do not let the labor weary you. The goal, however, is that you adapt the complexions <note>the elemental temperaments or "humors" of the substance</note>; then cook it many times, soak the boilings, and cook until the spirits become impalpable <note>so refined and subtle that they cannot be felt</note>. And when you see the <term>Ysir: a specialized term for the elixir or the transformative substance being processed</term> clothed in a royal garment and turned into a Tyrian color <note>original: "colorem Tyrium"; the deep purple or red color associated with the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, then you will understand the sayings of the Philosophers.

<summary>Admion emphasizes that alchemy requires divine favor, prayer, and extreme patience, comparing the long process of "cooking" the matter to the slow growth of trees and crops.</summary>
<keywords>Admion, Turba Philosophorum, regimen, patience, Ethelia, Ysir, Tyrian color, boiling, spiritual alchemy</keywords>

**LARGUS** says: The copper <note>original: "Æs"; while often translated as brass or bronze, in alchemy it refers to the base "body" of the matter</note> of which the ancients spoke is not copper, nor is it the tin of the common people; rather, it is our body, which must be mixed with the body of Magnesia <term>Magnesia: a cryptic term in the Turba, not the modern element magnesium, but a "mother" substance or mineral earth capable of transforming metals</term> so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. Then, that stone is ground in a vessel with water of nitre <note>original: "aqua nitri"; likely a solution of saltpeter or a similar caustic alkaline salt</note> and is liquefied until it is destroyed. However, it is necessary for you to have the water which, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened, until it acquires the rust <note>original: "rubiginem"; the reddish oxidation or "saffron" color indicating the successful progression of the work</note>, which is the foundation of the work. Cook this, and grind it with Egyptian vinegar.

**CADMON**. I declare to posterity that the round thing, which converts copper into the four elements, is from each and every thing. The method of extracting it is this: let one part be taken from the copper, and three parts be taken from the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanente"; a central alchemical concept referring to a solvent that does not evaporate, often associated with Mercury</note>; then let them be mixed and cooked until they are thickened and become one stone, about which the philosophers said: Take one part of the sincere <note>original: "syncero"; meaning pure or unadulterated</note> body and three parts of the copper of Magnesia; then mix it with the right masculine vinegar <note>original: "aceto recto masculino"; a strong, "active" acidic solvent</note> mixed with earth, cover the vessel, and observe what is in it, and cook it continually until they become earth.

## SAYING XLVIII.

**MOS**es. This one thing that has been mentioned so often, the philosophers have named with many names: sometimes with two names, and occasionally even with three. I shall now tell you what it is: that one thing is <note>original: "igneum"</note> fiery; <image-desc>A marginal reference mark consisting of four dots in a diamond pattern with a curved tail.</image-desc> the second is the composite within it, and the third is the water of sulfur, by which the one thing is washed, ground, and governed until it is completed. And this is what the philosopher hinted at when he said: The quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: Mercury (Latin: *argentum vivum*)</term> that tints gold is the quicksilver of Cambar <note>original: "Cambar"; likely a Latinized Arabic term referring to a specific state of mercury, possibly related to cinnabar or a "leavening" agent</note>. Nevertheless, the philosophers make a distinction and say: sometimes it is Cambar, and sometimes it is orpiment <term>Orpiment: (Latin: *auripigmentum*) A deep yellow arsenic ore used in alchemy as a source of sulfur and for its color</term>, but you must understand it in this way: The quicksilver of Cambar is Magnesia <term>Magnesia: In this context, a "mother-substance" or mineral thought to contain the essence of the work</term>; but the second quicksilver, orpiment, is the sulfur that rises from the mixed composite. You must therefore mix that thick substance with the fiery poison, let it putrefy <note>original: "putrefacere"; the alchemical stage of breakdown or "death" necessary for rebirth</note>, and grind it diligently until it becomes a spirit within another hidden spirit; and then the tincture <term>Tincture: The final transformative substance or "dye" that changes the nature of metals</term> is created, which tints everything you desire.

### PROPOSITION 50

**Actomanus** said: The philosophers have very frequently discussed <term>rust: *Rubigo* in Latin. In alchemy, this usually refers to the deep red color or the "tincture" achieved during the final stages of the work, rather than common iron rust</term>. However, "rust" is a metaphorical name and not a literal one. I tell you, nevertheless, that rust is the second work, which is produced from gold alone. Because of this, they have called it the **Leech**, because it is hidden in the <term>sulfurous gold: Gold associated with the active, fiery principle of sulfur</term>, just as a leech is hidden in water. Therefore, rust is the "reddening" in the second work; for in the first work, to "make rust" is actually to whiten the work, in which the philosophers ordered that the flower of gold and gold be placed in equal measure.

### PROPOSITION LVI.

YSIMIDRUS. Regarding the governance of the brass and of the moist spirit, enough and more than enough has been discussed; I shall now complete what was omitted. It must therefore be known that the philosophers have assigned many names to this, and that it is sometimes called the "water of Ethelia" <note>original: "aqua Etheliæ." *Ethelia* is a Latinization of the Greek word *aithale*, meaning soot, vapor, or a volatile spirit.</note>, of which mention was made above. When this water is whitened, it whitens and tints. It is also called by them the "flower of gold," and before it performs its tinting and reaches its final purpose, it is called **brass** <term>brass: *æs*, a general term for the base metal or "body" being transformed in the work</term>.

But when it is joined with four things which the Sages called "fermented urines," <note>Alchemists often used "urine" as a "deck-name" or code for various salts or liquid extracts; "fermented" suggests they have been aged or chemically altered.</note> they call it the "Heart" and the "neck of gold." These names are invented, yet they are true and signify only one thing: namely, the **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*, or mercury</term> extracted by men, from which and with which all things are made. It is said to be the "worldly water" which destroys every shadow.

And it should be known that when this quicksilver extracted by men is whitened, it becomes sulfur—specifically, that which is contained by sulfur—and it is a poison that is compared to shining marble. This the philosophers have called "Ethelia," and "Orpiment" <term>orpiment: *auri pigmentum*, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term>, and "Sandarac" <term>sandarac: *sandarich*, a red arsenic sulfide</term>, from which the tincture and the pure spirit ascend by a slow fire, and from which the flower is sublimated. And this entire secret is nothing other than the quicksilver extracted by men—that is, through the agency of men. Furthermore, it must be known that to whiten the secret brass does not...

This is what **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage and mythical father of the alchemical tradition</note> intended to imply when he said: "Sift the things you know, and melt them more deeply."

# OPINION 64.

**BALGUS**. Someone described the fruit of that art to Tulleas <note>original: *Tulleas*; likely a reference to a specific (though perhaps corrupted) name of a sage in the alchemical tradition</note>, and began to teach me in a marvelous way, saying that its operation is found without labor. ### DOCTRINE LXXII.

**EMIGANUS:** The books of the Philosophers must be read: for not in vain have they said: "Look upon the falling boy, and do not hinder him; in him remains the secret <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: *arcanum*; a profound secret or hidden mystery of nature</note>, from which the Sages work good things." And I say to you, that the definition of this art is the liquefaction of the body and the separation of the soul from the body. Furthermore, I say that our copper has a soul and a body just like a human: it is necessary, therefore, for the body to be divided, and the soul to be separated from it. Hence the philosophers said that the splendor of Saturn <note>Saturn usually represents lead; here it signifies the dark, heavy initial state of the matter</note>, while it climbs into the air, appears only as darkness, and Mercury meets the rays of the Sun: then the quicksilver, by fiery power, vivifies and perfects the body.

### DISCOURSE LXXVIII.

**Agmon**. As a corollary, I will say that whoever does not liquefy and coagulate <note>original: *liquefacit & coagulat*; this refers to the fundamental alchemical axiom 'Solve et Coagula,' the dissolving and re-solidifying of matter</note> errs in many ways. Therefore, blacken the earth, and separate its soul and water, and afterwards whiten it, and you will find what you seek. I also say to you, that he who blackens the earth and dissolves the white substance with fire until it becomes like a **naked sword** <note>original: *gladius denudatus*; likely referring to a brilliant, metallic luster</note>, and who—after its whitening is complete—brings the soul back into it and fixes the whole with a consuming fire after it has been liquefied, will deserve to be called happy and be exalted above the circles of the world.

We do not doubt that this revelation of our **stone** <term>Stone: The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the work, capable of perfecting base metals and human health</term> is sufficient for the sons of doctrine; its powers cannot be corrupted. If it is placed in the fire, its strength is increased; if you wish to dissolve it, it will be dissolved; if you wish to coagulate it, it will be coagulated. No one can do without it, and everyone has need of it. And although it has many names, it is nonetheless called by one name; and where it is visible, there it is hidden. It is also a stone and not a stone, spirit and soul and body; it is white, volatile, hollow, and lacking hairs; no one, when it is cooled, can touch it with their tongue without injury <note>This may refer to the corrosive or caustic nature of certain chemical salts or acids used in the process</note>. If you make it fly, it flies; and if you say it is water, you speak the truth; and if you say it is not water, you speak falsely. Yet not

<summary>Agmon outlines the essential alchemical stages of blackening (Nigredo) and whitening (Albedo), describing the Philosopher's Stone through a series of riddles and paradoxes that highlight its dual nature as both physical matter and spiritual force.</summary>

## ALLEGORIES UPON
### the book of the Turba.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'I' set within a square woodcut frame, featuring an ornate pattern of scrolling vines and foliage.</image-desc>

THE ALLEGORIES <note>original: *allegoriae*; symbolic stories where physical processes are described through the actions of people or animals to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note> upon the book of the Turba <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, it portrays a gathering of ancient philosophers debating the secrets of nature</note> begin, and first concerning man. 
Take a man, shave <note>original: *tonde*; in alchemical practice, this usually refers to the "shaving" or stripping away of accidental impurities from the raw material</note> him, and grind him upon a stone or a plate until his body dies and its density <note>original: *spissitudo*; the coarse, physical thickness of matter that must be "killed" to reach the spiritual essence</note> vanishes. Be certain in knowing that when he has lost his density, he will become spiritual. Afterward, restore his soul to him; then place him in a bath <term>balneum; a "Mary’s Bath" or bain-marie, used to provide gentle, indirect heat</term> for 40 days, so that just as seed dies in the womb—which is indeed the principle of nature’s regeneration—the creation may rise and the intended purpose be fulfilled. Take a bull with flesh and blood, with horns and the shoes of its feet <note>original: *calciamentis*; referring here to the hooves</note>, and turn it into water, and mix it with blood, and draw it all out. Afterward, roast it until it grows red; then turn the copper <term>aes; a general term for base metals like copper or bronze</term> into divine tinctures. Take a *Cock, crowned with a red crest, and while alive* strip it of its feathers; afterward place its head in a glass vessel and keep it for an hour. Then store the cock again and grind it until it is softened and until it is purified, and spread it upon marble. Then, with the feathers removed from it, grind and shear it most strongly. Then leave it in horse dung <note>original: *equorum fimo*; a common alchemical method for maintaining a steady, low heat through the natural fermentation of manure</note> until it produces feathers again. And when you hear that cock, like a crowing cock, know that you have walked the right path.

->CONCERNING THE TURBA.<-
k 5

Take the viper, which is called *rexa* <note>original: *de rexa*; likely a corruption of the Arabic *al-raqs*, referring to a specific venomous serpent in medieval bestiaries</note>, and deprive <margin>4</margin> 
it of its head and tail; in these two places its venom liquefies, from which the spirit <term>spiritus; the volatile essence of a substance that can be driven off by heat</term> proceeds. 
Therefore, divide the head and the tail, and place each by itself in a glass vessel. Take the remaining body and cook it over a slow fire until the flesh is separated from the bones. And afterward, place it [the flesh] upon a metal plate, and store it so long until the body is turned into spirit and its flexibility <note>original: *flexibilitas*; the physical "softness" or elasticity of the matter that must be removed to make it brittle enough to grind</note> is taken away. 
For a flexible thing cannot be thinned [into powder]. Then join it to its head, and grind it with it as long as flexibility remains in the body. Dry such a body in the sun or by the fire, so that you may see what you seek. This then being completed, know that you have a body that penetrates bodies, and a nature containing nature, and a nature rejoicing in nature, which is called the *theriacal perfection of the philosophers* <note>original: *perfectio tyriaca philosophorum*; Theriac was a famous universal antidote and medicine; in alchemy, this refers to the completed Stone’s power to heal "leperous" or base metals</note>. 
There is in the sea a round fish, lacking bones and <margin>2</margin> 
scales <note>original: *corticibus*; literally "barks" or "shells," referring to the outer covering</note>, and it has within itself a fatness of wonderful virtue, which if it be cooked over a slow fire until its fatness and moisture entirely withdraw, and afterward it is ground most strongly, and soaked in seawater until it shines; then let it be buried <note>original: *sepeliatur*; often refers to "digestion" in a warm, dark place like a dung heap</note> for a week, and afterward be whitened by roasting. And when it has been well whitened, and its water restored to it: afterward it is soaked in its own moisture; then after the soaking in moisture, roasted until it appears yellow <note>original: *citrinus*; the "citrine" or yellow stage of the work, signaling the approach of the final red stage</note>, it becomes the *collyrium of the philosophers* <note>original: *coliriū*; an ancient term for an eye salve; symbolically, this medicine "opens the eyes" of the practitioner or clarifies the substance</note>: whose eyes, once anointed...

These metaphors describe the purification, grinding, and roasting of chemical substances to achieve the "theriacal perfection."</summary>

# ALLEGORIES

The ancient secrets <note>original: *arcana*; the OCR reads *cana* (ancient/grey), but the vocabulary list and context confirm it refers to the hidden mysteries or *Arcana* of the philosophers</note> of the philosophers could easily be perceived. In the moon of the sea <note>possibly a reference to the tides, or the "lunar" stage of the alchemical work characterized by whiteness and moisture</note> there is a planted sponge, having blood and sense, in the manner of a tree planted in the sea, and it does not move from its place. If you wish to rule <note>or "process"</note> it, have a sickle with you with which you may cut it; from afar take care that the blood does not flow out, because it is the venom of the philosophers <note>original: *venenum philosophorum*; a term for the volatile, corrosive, or transformative essence released during the breakdown of the initial matter</note>. Therefore, when you have taken that sponge, deprive it of its blood; then put it back in a glass vessel and guard it. Afterward, take its body and wash it with sea water until it is purified and becomes a white body lacking any disturbance. Afterward, return its blood to it: then grind it strongly until it is deprived of its smell by its own strength and becomes entirely dry.

Men have olives from which they extract oil, and that is combustible. However, the oil of the philosophers <term>oleum philosophorum; the "sulfur" or essential soul of the matter, which unlike common oil, is "incombustible" and permanent</term> is not extracted in this way. Nevertheless, its nature is combustible, yet it always persists immobile; and this is the way of making it. We take the olives that we have, clean and whole, and we grind them with their own water; afterward, we boil them. Then, placing them in a damp place, we leave them there until they are almost dissolved, and until the oil is separated from its thick body. We also make the dregs <note>original: *fecem*; the dross or "dead head" left over after distillation</note> descend below, the water stand in the middle, and the oil truly flow out on top. Afterward, we separate the water; placing it upon a glowing plate, we soak it with its own water, until flexibi- <meta>catchword: -lity (liatem)</meta>

# ALLEGORIES

...[ablu]tion <note>The word begins on the previous page as "abluen-" and concludes here as "natio" (ablution). It refers to the ritualistic or chemical washing of the matter.</note> consists of those things which cannot be extracted except by laborious and subtle ingenuity. Therefore, let the body be taken and washed, and let it be ground by the slow and tepid heat of a fire, in the manner of those who make flax white and gleaming with ash and white lime water; let it be whitened. Then leave it for one night in a moist place: afterward, having been washed with sea water, let it be moistened little by little until it is most fully whitened. Once it is whitened, let its **tinging spirit** <note>original: *spiritus tingens*; the active, "dyeing" principle believed to provide the power of transmutation and the final color to the Stone.</note> be returned to it, and it becomes the <term>elixir</term> <note>The "elixir" is the perfected substance of the Great Work, capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note>, firm and perfect at all times.

**Coral** is a certain vegetable growing in the sea, having roots and branches, and is generated in a moist state. However, when the North Wind blows, it hardens and becomes a red body. When a sailor who navigates the sea sees it, he cuts it beneath the waves; but when it emerges, it turns into stone, the color of which is red, and it is shaped into stones. The people of India also use it greatly.

<margin>⁘</margin> In a similar way, the Philosophers use "our coral" in our art: for they take it and grind it strongly, and imbue it in sea water for 21 days, and they leave it in a heat-bath <note>original: *balneo*; likely a *balneum Mariae* or water bath.</note> with much moisture until its **tinging spirit** stands out. Taking this spirit, they store it in a glass vessel and leave behind the dregs as if dead; and yet these are neither white nor red. Afterward, they place it in that sphere which we call a **sieve** <note>original: *cribrum*; while literally a sieve, in this context it refers to a specific type of circulating or filtering vessel.</note>. Then they imbue it with warm sea water, and this is repeated seven times...

And then they place it in a moist place, until it grows red, and its "sperm" <note>original: *spermale*; referring to the reproductive or creative seed of the matter.</note> is produced. And of this, the philosophers place it upon glass, and it makes it unbreakable. The philosophers take the stone which is called **Borites** <note>A legendary stone described in early alchemy, possibly representing a specific mineral like borax or a particular stage of the Work's coloration.</note>, which is said to be of an Indigo color and similarly varied. But the "body," which remains as if dark, they wash in the water of distilled salt; afterwards they leave it in the hot sun during the summer time, and this is repeated so many times until it flashes like white marble. Afterwards they place it in an **Athanor** <term>Athanor</term> <note>A specialized alchemical furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform heat for weeks or months at a time.</note>, and there they dry it. Dyers have a herb which they use in dyeing wool, taking only the **dye** <note>original: *tinctura*; the coloring principle or essence.</note> and leaving the wood behind. ENIGMA <note>original: *AENIGMA*; a riddle or mystery, often used in alchemy to describe truths hidden behind metaphors.</note>

# FROM THE VISION OF ARISLEUS THE PHILOSOPHER, AND THE ALLEGORIES OF THE WISE.

## ENIGMA I.

When certain more studious disciples of the philosophers had gathered once again, Pythagoras—among whom the elders were Arisleus <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often identified as the narrator of the "Vision."</note> son of Abladius, then Paris son of Belchiotus, Armenius son of Archia, Meditátalus, Phaliseus, the son of Echami, and Parmenides, and Eximesias son of Admiras—Auerca <note>Likely a corruption of a name appearing in the *Turba Philosophorum* tradition.</note> asked of Arisleus whether he could, by speaking, explain so that by example or parable it might be permitted for seekers of the **Art** <term>The "Art" (Ars) refers to alchemy, the practice of transforming base matter into gold or spiritual perfection.</term> to gather fruit from that **immortal tree**, which the aforementioned disciples of the philosophers and the others in the **Assembly** <term>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate between ancient sages.</term> had described?

And he [replied]: "I will indeed speak gladly, as best I can, but perhaps I will not satisfy your desire."

And Pythagoras said again: "Speak then as aptly as you can."

And he said: "I saw myself and certain others from the Assembly riding to the shores of the sea, and behold, the inhabitants of the sea were mating with one another, yet nothing was born to them; and they were planting trees, yet they bore no fruit; and they were sowing, yet nothing grew. And I said: 'What is the matter with you? Though you are many, is there no philo-" <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page mid-word: *philo-[sopher]*.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Vision of Arisleus," a core alchemical allegory where the philosopher Arisleus is asked to explain the secrets of the "immortal tree" through a parable. He begins a vision describing a barren seaside where the inhabitants mate and plant seeds but fail to produce any life or fruit.</summary>
<keywords>Arisleus, Pythagoras, Turba Philosophorum, Assembly of Philosophers, immortal tree, alchemical allegory, vision, barrenness, symbolic marriage</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Vision of Arisleus." The narrator, Arisleus, has arrived at the kingdom beneath the sea and is engaging with its inhabitants, who live in a state of sterility and ignorance. He is about to introduce the concept of alchemical "marriage" to the King of the Sea.</meta>

RIDDLES <note>original: *AENIGMATA*</note>

...[philoso]pher <note>original: *philosophus*; the text completes the word started on the previous page. In this context, a philosopher is not just a thinker, but an adept of the Alchemical Art who understands the secrets of nature.</note> is there, who may teach you?" And they said to him: "What is a philosopher?" He said: "One who knows the reality of things." And they asked: "Of what use is his knowledge?" And I replied: "If there were a philosopher among you, your sons would be multiplied, and trees would be born for you and would not die, and their fruit would never fail, and you would be kings, overcoming all your enemies."

Going forth, they reported these things to their lord, the **King of the Sea** <note>original: *Rex Marinus*; in alchemical allegory, the Sea often represents the *Prima Materia*—the raw, chaotic "First Matter" that must be organized and "fertilized" by the philosopher.</note>. And when we had been summoned by him, and he demanded gifts, we replied that we carried hidden gifts—namely, the art of generating, and of planting trees, and of sowing, from which trees and fruits whoever eats shall never hunger.

And he said: "That is a very great gift, if your master truly sent this. Tell me then, what do you have?" And I said: "Lord, although you are a king, yet you rule and command poorly: for you have joined males to males, knowing that males do not give birth. For generation comes from the joining of a male and a female; true generation occurs if nature is mixed with nature—male with female, like with like, and the fitting with the fitting <note>original: *conueniens conuenienti, aptūque apto*; a fundamental alchemical principle that "nature rejoices in nature," meaning substances must be chemically compatible to produce a result.</note>."

And he said: "Indeed I have a son and a daughter, and for that reason I am king of my subjects, since they have none of these; yet I have carried my son and daughter in my brain <note>The King's claim of carrying children in his brain suggests a purely spiritual or intellectual existence that lacks the physical "body" or "vessel" required for alchemical transformation.</note>." And I said: "Bring to us your son **Thabritius** <term>Thabritius (also Gabritius) represents the active, masculine principle, often associated with "Philosophical Sulfur" or the Sun.</term>" Having heard this, I also demanded that his sister **Beya** <term>Beya represents the passive, feminine principle, often associated with "Philosophical Mercury" or the Moon.</term> be brought to us.

<summary>Arisleus arrives at the court of the King of the Sea and explains that the kingdom is barren because the King has not properly joined the masculine and feminine principles. He calls for the King’s children, Thabritius and Beya, to begin the process of alchemical "generation."</summary>

Then I said to the King: "For what reason, in your haste, have you inflicted punishment upon us? At least hand over your daughter to us once more; perhaps she is destined to return life to your son Thabritis." 

And he said: "Do you wish to kill my daughter as well?" 

And I said: "Do not be hasty, O King, to inflict torments upon us: wait a little while, and hand over your daughter to us, and a little later you will have both your son and your daughter living once again." 

When she was handed over, she remained with us in the prison for 80 days, and we remained in the darkness of the waves, and in the intense heat of summer, and of the sea...

There is in our sea a small round fish, lacking bones and scales <note>original: *corticibus*; literally "barks" or "shells," referring here to the outer covering of the fish.</note>, and it contains within itself a fatness <note>In alchemical texts, "fatness" often refers to the internal sulfur or the "soul" of the substance.</note> and a wondrous power. When the eyes are anointed with its liquid, the secrets of the philosophers can easily be seen and understood.
