## DEFINITION OF THE STONE, AND from what beginnings it consists,

## EXERCISE I.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring foliage motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

As we are about to treat the <term>Philosopher’s Stone<note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and conferring longevity and spiritual perfection.</note></term>, we must first see from what beginnings and from what elements the Philosopher’s Stone consists. By the consideration of all philosophers, <term>Mercury<note>original: *Mercurius*; in alchemy, this refers not only to the common metal quicksilver but to the "primal spirit" or "root moisture" found within all metallic bodies.</note></term> is the father of all metals. The philosophical stone, moreover, is a metallic matter, converting the substances and forms of imperfect metals. Furthermore, it has long been proclaimed by all philosophers that this conversion does not occur except through its own likeness <note>A core alchemical principle: "like produces like." To create gold, one must use a substance that already possesses the "seed" or "form" of gold.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the Philosopher’s Stone be born from <term>metallic matter<note>original: *materia metallica*; the underlying physical essence common to all metals.</note></term>. From which metallic species it may be generated, all philosophers proclaim this, especially in this little book <note>referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), a seminal text composed as a debate among ancient sages</note>, saying: That in Mercury is everything which

Not that earth becomes water, but in such a way that earth, by means of its dryness and through the operation of the heat of fire, causes the moisture of water to consist with its own coldness. Thus, the nature of water is still observed—which is **fluxibility** <note>original: *fluxibilitas*; the ability to flow or fluidity.</note> in one part—while it loses its other part, which is **moistening** <note>original: *humectatio*; the quality of making things wet.</note>. Therefore, it is rendered as **dry water**, which flows but does not wet. 

That it is composed of earth through the operation of fire is clear: for by an excess of heat, the entire substance of **Mercury** is converted into **red earth** <note>original: *terra rubea*; likely referring to mercuric oxide, a red powder formed when mercury is heated in air.</note>. For everything is resolved back into that from which it is made, and is properly bounded by its own nature: because when that which flows is gathered together, it forms a mass. 

That it is indeed made of water is also clear: because it flows and is not contained by its own boundary, but by the resistance of an external one; for flowability is from the nature of water. 

Furthermore, the **Mercurial nature** is the one common matter for all metals. It behaves like the seed in vegetables and the **sperm** in animals. For from the seed in plants and vegetables, and from the sperm in animals, individuals are multiplied, preserving the species of every genus. And just as in vegetables and plants there is a certain germinative power, producing from the juiciness of the earth a certain nutritional saliva through the four natural virtues—which juiciness, according to the variety of the **digestion** <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation or refining of a substance through steady heat.</note> and according to its parts...

# ON THE CONVERSION OF NA-
## *tures and their mixing.*

### EXERCISE VI.

### PARMENIDES.

The method of the art of mutual conversion is as follows. First, dissolve the Stone into its Mercury. <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to the "First Matter" or the fluid essence of a substance rather than common quicksilver.</note> The authors call the Stone "metallic"; wash it, restore it, fix it, and soften it with wax <term>original: *incera*; "inceration" is the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy, meltable consistency</term>. That is to say: dissolve the coarse into the simple, wash the dark into the bright, restore the moist into the dry, and fix the volatile into its body. 

To "dissolve" is to divide and break down <note>original: *corrumpere*; literally to corrupt or decompose</note>, and to return the material to its "first matter." To "wash" is to bury <note>original: *inhumare*; the practice of placing the vessel in warm earth or dung to provide gentle, constant heat</note>, to distill, and to burn into ash. To "restore" <note>original: *reducere*</note> is to enrich, to wax, and to refine. To "fix" is to marry <note>original: *desponsare*; often called the "chemical wedding," referring to the permanent union of volatile and fixed principles</note>, to resolve, and to solidify. 

Through the first process, nature works inwardly; through the second, outwardly; through the third, above; and through the fourth, below. But modern practitioners ruin the end of the work: because when they cease their labor, they should instead have only just begun. One dissolves and solidifies, another dissolves and fixes; one disrupts the middle of the process, another the end. Thus they hesitate in the art like fools. In short, I say that they do not produce a tincture worth a single farth-

# ON THE MARRIAGE OF THE SUN AND MOON.

## EXERCISE VII.

### ZIMON.

This philosopher seems to suggest that both **perfect bodies** <note>original: *vtrumque corpus perfectum*; in alchemy, the "perfect bodies" are Gold and Silver</note> should be taken for the composition of the **Elixir**, whether it is intended to be **white** or **yellow** <note>original: *citrinus*; "citrine" or yellow is a stage of the work often following the white and preceding the red</note>. The reason is that neither **flows** easily without the other. However, the ultimate goal of the entire **alchemical secret** is that the **Elixir** should flow instantly—specifically before the **flight of Mercury** <note>original: *fugam Mercurij*; this refers to the evaporation or escape of the volatile quicksilver before it can be "fixed" into a stable state</note>. 

But I read no authors, or very few, who recommend this, or who specify when these two **bodies**—namely, the **Sun** <note>original: *Solis*; Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>original: *Lunae*; Silver</note>—should be applied: whether at the beginning of the work, such as during the **dissolution**, or at the end, during the **fermentation**. Therefore, let whoever wishes to try it see for themselves what ought to be done and chosen. 

This method does not particularly please me. Because if it were done this way, the **Elixir** would necessarily be neither white nor yellow, but of a **mixed color**. Yet it is possible that this opinion should be interpreted in this way: namely, when the **Elixir** is being prepared to reach the **red** <note>original: *rubeum*; the highest and final stage of the transmutation process</note> stage, the **filings of the Moon** <note>original: *Lunae limatura*; silver shavings</note> should be taken first and dissolved with **Mercury**, and from those joined together is collected the ear...

The author, Zimon, expresses skepticism about mixing them too early, fearing a muddied result rather than the desired pure white or yellow stages.</summary>

## EXERCISE IX.

### Z E N O.

In the alchemical work <term>alchymico opere; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, it is necessary first of all to completely mortify and exhaust the stone—that is, the body, soul, and spirit—since nothing yields fruit in this art unless it has first been mortified <note>original: *mortificatum*; in alchemy, "mortification" refers to the symbolic death or breakdown of a substance, often through putrefaction, to strip away its initial form</note>. But once mortified, the separation of the elements occurs, and the effect of each individual element is revealed. Therefore, if you wish to create the **Elixir**, it will be necessary first to entirely dissolve the stone itself into its constituent elements, a process which is signified to us by the seasons of the year <note>The alchemical stages were often mapped to the four seasons: for example, winter represented the "black" stage of cold and moisture, while summer represented the "red" stage of heat and maturity</note>. Then, you should join those elements by fire, with **Mercury** acting as the mediator; this is the greatest secret <term>arcanum; a deep mystery or hidden knowledge</term>, and thus the mastery <term>magisterium; the completed work or the "Masterpiece"</term> is complete. Indeed, the entire craft is situated in dissolving and joining. 

Moreover, these solutions or separations are performed by means of mercury: for mercury first dissolves the body and causes the separations, which are then joined together again by the **ferment** <note>A "ferment" acts like a starter in bread-making, a small amount of the perfected substance that "leavens" or transforms the whole mass</note> and mercury. But here, one must be carefully attentive: at the start of the work, **Mercury** is called **Water**; then, when the blackness appears, it is called **Earth**; then, once it has been sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to represent the "Air" stage</note>, it is called **Air**; then, once it has been turned red (now the air must by itself

### WITHIN THE ASSEMBLY

It is believable that any thing can be converted from its own nature into another, provided it is first reduced to that matter from which it was made from the beginning: for if that is done, I believe it can be led across to whatever nature you wish. Since all things were created from water: therefore it is necessary for that thing to be converted into water <note>This reflects the ancient philosophical belief, often attributed to Thales of Miletus, that water is the *prima materia* or the fundamental building block of all physical existence</note>. And therefore it is concluded that all spirits must be converted into water before they are sublimated. 

For **Mercury**, when it is dissolved into water, then puts down its dross <note>original: *feces*; in alchemy, this refers to the impure "sediment" or "lees" left over after a process</note>, and its coldness is turned into heat, and its moisture into dryness, and its heat is increased during sublimation, as is its subtlety and its **tincture** <term>tinctura; the power of a substance to "dye" or transform the color and quality of a base metal into gold</term>: because it receives heat and tincture from **vitriol** <term>vitriol; a glassy sulfate mineral used by alchemists as a powerful acidic agent to "fire" or "color" their mixtures</term>. 

Indeed, according to this doctrine, it can be seen that the **Stone of the Philosophers** can be composed of Mercury that has been purified, dissolved, sublimated, and resolved into lymph <note>original: *limpha*; here used to describe a clear, purified liquid state</note>. Likewise, it is composed of another Mercury—not indeed the common kind, but from that which is extracted from the common kind, which, once drawn out, is called the **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta essentia; the "Quintessence," the purest and most spiritual element that remains after the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water) are stripped away</term>. It must be believed that these two, namely the Fifth Essence and the aforementioned Lymph, ought to be joined together. 

In fact, the Fifth Essence itself is to be mixed with the "lymphatized" Mercury successively, until by turns the Fifth Essence has drunk up two parts of that lymph: then also, finally, the thinned body is to be joined to it. ## PANDULPHUS.

If the previous teaching does not please you, this philosopher offers another, which we will explain clearly in this manner. Take an equal weight of the water drawn from the stone and the stone itself; let the stone and the water be well mixed together and placed under the rule of its own fire, taking care that nothing leaks out. Then let it be permitted to rise into heaven, and then be commanded to descend to the earth—that is, repeat all the operations as is proper. For during the dissolving, it will ascend into heaven <note>referring to evaporation or sublimation</note>, and during the thickening <note>original: *coagulandum*; the process of a liquid becoming a solid or dense mass</note> it will descend, and the spirit is united with the earth; then let it be burned to ash <term>calcinetur; the process of calcination, or heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter and reduce it to a powder</term> once more, and it will be a fixed stone.

### EXERCISE XII.

### THEOPHILUS.

Theophilus teaches here that the poison <note>original: *venenum*; in alchemy, this refers to the transformative, caustic solvent that "kills" or breaks down the base metal</note> is to be divided into two equal parts. With one of these, the copper <note>original: *æs*; often referring to the metallic "body" or base substance</note> should be liquefied; with the other, however, it should be ground and imbued <note>saturated or soaked</note>. Let there be two parts of the Elixir to seven, or three to one, and let there be a fire of proper **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio; the stage of decomposition where the matter turns black, often compared to a "death" before rebirth</term>. 

It must be considered that the philosophers command the water to be divided into two parts for this reason: to signify that the Elixir, after **fermentation** <term>fermentatio; the stage where the Stone is joined with gold or silver to "fix" its quality</term>, should be imbued with as much water as was required during the fermentation—although some think differently and teach that a third part by number should be used. It should be moistened or "nourished" seven times, using the same proportion of water by which the copper itself was dissolved. 

And when the aforementioned portion has been applied to the Elixir seven times following the nourishment, then the Elixir is mature for **tinging** <note>the final process of transmuting or "dyeing" base metals into gold or silver</note>. Some, however, teach that before the said sevenfold imbibition or nourishment, the Elixir itself must be treated with the water which they call **Vinegar** <note>original: *Acetum*; likely the "Vinegar of the Philosophers," a specialized acidic solvent used to cleanse or dissolve the matter</note>...

...to be entirely dissolved, which is difficult both to believe and to do, and it is to be feared lest the Elixir, now **quickened** <note>original: *vivificatum*; brought to life or activated</note>, be strangled by that very solution. However the matter may stand, this must be perpetually observed: that you pour only as much "water" over the Elixir in a single **imbibition** <term>imbibitio; the process of "feeding" the dry alchemical body with liquid to increase its volume and potency</term> as you judge sufficient, little by little, and more frequently. Likewise, once your **king is born** <note>original: *nato rege*; the "King" signifies the Stone reaching a more perfected or solar state</note>, it is not permitted to deprive him of air or to keep him trapped in a closed vessel, lest the life he has received be suffocated. He is born and receives life through the **ferment** <term>fermentum; a substance added to the work to "fix" it or give it a specific quality, much like yeast in bread</term>; therefore, the vessel should not be opened any sooner than when you wish to begin the fermentation. Afterward, however, I do not think the vessel should be kept tightly sealed, for that would prepare a "suffocation" for the born king. 

And although "milk" <note>original: *lac*; a metaphorical term for the nourishing, white solvent used to "feed" the stone</note> must be diligently provided for his nutrition, he must nevertheless be guided with such a moderate fire that the milk cannot **fly away** <note>original: *evolare*; to evaporate or escape as vapor</note> in any manner.

# ON THE SOUL, THE SPIRIT, and the body.

### *MENABADUS.*

The entire discussion of the Alchemical **mastery** <term>magisterij; the supreme goal or "Great Work" of alchemy</term> depends on this: that the **Elixir** <term>a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing all diseases</term> be made from the body, soul, and spirit joined together, as the philosopher notes here. The **Body**, moreover, is called earth, bronze, lead, ash, **magnesia** <note>in alchemy, this often refers to a generic crude mineral or the "mother" of metals rather than modern magnesium</note>, lime, mother, key, holy virgin, the king's crown, talc, path, glass, golden wood, spirit of brightness, sea, salt, urine, alum, gum of Scotland, water of sulfur, spit of the Moon <note>original: *sputum Lunę*; typically a reference to silver or a white precipitate</note>, white gum, and so forth.

The **Soul** is called **Rebis** <term>from the Latin *res bina*, meaning "double thing," representing the union of opposites like male/female or spirit/matter</term>; stinking water, cleanliness of the dead, blood, water of blood, animal stone, blessed stone, and so forth. 

There are, moreover, mutual duties between these three, because the spirit guards the body, lest it be consumed by fire; and the clear body guards the spirit, lest it fly away from the fire. Because the body is **fixed** <term>fixum; a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when heated</term>, it preserves the spirit so it does not flee; and because the spirit is incombustible, it does not allow the body to be burned. This is because the spirit and body are made one through the mediation of the soul, which stays with both spirit and body. For if the soul were not present, then the spirit and body would be separated from one another by fire; but when the soul is joined to the spirit and body, this whole assembly cares nothing for fire, nor for any other thing in the world.

# THE PRINTER to the Reader.

n 4

**Dear reader,** know that here from the beginning of this book, truly titled *The Golden Hour* <note>original: *Aurea hora*; likely referring to the *Aurora Consurgens*, a famous medieval alchemical treatise often attributed to Thomas Aquinas</note>, we have deliberately omitted an entire treatise of parables or allegories. By these allegories, in the ancient manner of those who dwell in shadows <note>original: *tenebrionum*; refers to people of a "dark age" or those who hide their meaning in obscurity</note> (as the times and ages then allowed), the author allegorically dragged almost the entire Most Holy Scripture—especially the books of **Solomon** and the writings of the **Psalmist** <note>original: *Psaltes*; referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms</note> himself, but most particularly the **Song of Songs**—into alchemy, even against its will. He did this so thoroughly that it would seem (if we believe him) that all those works were written for no other reason than in honor and praise of Alchemy. Indeed (and this is a shocking thing), he most profanely twisted the very most sacred mystery of the incarnation and death of Christ our Lord into the <term>mystery of the stone</term> <note>the "stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work</note>, along with many other principal monuments of our faith. This was not done (as I indeed judge) with evil intent—for the author otherwise seems pious—but as that age of darkness brought forth: since they were ignorant of the true meaning of the sacred scriptures...

## GLOSS ON THE PROLOGUE
### of the treatise on Astronomy.

Aristotle <note>The text attributes this to a letter from Aristotle to his pupil Alexander the Great, a common tradition in medieval "pseudo-Aristotelian" texts like the *Secretum Secretorum*.</note> says to Alexander word for word: Saturn rules the earth, Mercury rules the <term>water <note>The symbol $\approx$ refers to the element of water, completing the fourfold elemental system.</note></term>, Jupiter <note>symbol: $\unicode{x2643}$</note> rules the air, and the Sun <note>symbol: $\odot$</note> rules the fire. Here, we do not simply acknowledge a coincidence in the planets’ actions, but rather the operations they perform continually and perpetually through that ultimate power which stands above all the specific forces of these works. And this is not the proper place for demonstrating such difficult matters; however, I have mentioned them because it is necessary and extremely useful for you, given the frequent discussions in this treatise where we will more precisely define the specific and individual natures of certain **planetary plants** <note>original: *uegetabilium Planetarum*; the author refers to "vegetables" or "plants" that fall under the influence of specific planets.</note>.

Knowledge of the properties of these things belongs to the philosophers; however, the knowledge of natural things belongs to physicians. I do not wish this to escape your wisdom: everything in the nature of plants that lacks light is ruled by **Saturn** <note>symbol: $\hbar$</note> and is attributed to him. And whatever plants are flowering and luminous are ruled by **Mercury** <note>symbol: $\unicode{x263f}$</note> and attributed to him. And whatever plants are flowering but do not bear fruit are attributed to **Mars** <note>symbol: $\unicode{x2642}$</note> and are ruled by him. Next, combine and join these in various ways, and you might say: Every plant that bears fruit is created by **Mercury** and **Mars**. Furthermore, some plants grow by way of branches, some through seeds, and some are born without seed or planting. It is therefore clearer than day from the aforementioned things, that any species of plants

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of "planetary plants" from the previous page, moving from the general rule of which planets govern light or dark plants to the internal mechanism of how these celestial influences shape a plant's physical properties and lifespan.</meta>

It possesses its own inherent disposition, through which it receives its <term>temperament <note>original: *complexionātur*; referring to the "complexion" or the specific balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—within a living thing.</note></term> and is transformed by the power of a single Planet. Furthermore, it is assimilated to and associated with the power of two or more **Planets**, depending on what it is capable of receiving. Whatever is attributed to the plant aids each of its individual properties. 

Specifically, the primary <term>natural virtue <note>original: *virtus naturalis*; the innate biological power or life-force that allows a plant to grow and function.</note></term>, as is required, determines its particular species, which is manifested in its taste, color, scent, and shape. The <term>natural soul <note>original: *anima naturalis*; in the Aristotelian tradition, this is the "vegetative soul," the lowest level of the soul responsible for nutrition, growth, and reproduction in plants.</note></term> gathers all these natural properties and powers from the plant itself; it expresses itself through them and causes them to endure for exactly as long a span of time as the planetary powers define and designate for it. This is because there is no act without motion, and there is no **operation** <note>original: *operatio*; the active process or functioning of a natural force.</note> without a defined limit.

## Geometrical Sayings in a Parabolic Style
### Chapter II.

Next, note that Geometry and Arithmetic have obscured this most noble science, both in part and in its entirety, through their various distinctions of numbers. For the limit and end of the entire <term>Work <gloss>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</gloss></term> is sealed within the divisions of numbers. Regarding this limit, however, many <term>sons of doctrine <gloss>original: filij doctrinae; a traditional term for students or initiates of alchemy.</gloss></term> have wandered and lamented. For the philosophers, in describing the limit of this science, added to and subtracted from the sum of the <term>root <gloss>original: radix; the fundamental starting material or the numeric base of the calculation.</gloss></term> by the parts making up the whole itself—using the lesser, middle, and greatest numbers. They did this so that the foolish might not be able to grasp the meaning.

For <term>Aristotle <gloss>Refers to pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical texts, specifically the *Liber Septuaginta* (Book of the Seventy).</gloss></term> says in the *Book of the Seventy Precepts*, in the chapter on "Alternations": The alternations of the seventy precepts are manifold: ten. For those things which agree in the first place, follow also in the second and third. For ten corresponds to ten; here finally it is necessary to follow the divisions. But let our reader attend to the prior order.

### *Natural things spoken according to the process of nature. Chapter III.*

Consequently, natural science—as it is the role of physicians and natural philosophers to consider—has surrounded this comforting, treasury-like science with its own processes, as the philosophers have placed this in many parts of their writings. ### Problematic Discourse Chapter V.
<note>original: *Sermo Problematicus*. In medieval philosophy and alchemy, a "problematic" discourse refers to a style of teaching through riddles or complex propositions intended to challenge the student's intellect.</note>

After the parabolic <note>A style of teaching using parables or symbolic stories.</note> style follows the problematic one, which **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy, often cited as the ultimate authority on the "Great Work."</note> pursues, saying: "I have considered a bird held in veneration by the wise, which flies while it is in **Aries**, **Cancer**, **Libra**, or **Capricorn**." <note>These are the four cardinal signs of the zodiac, representing the start of Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. This suggests the bird (likely a symbol for the volatile spirit) is active throughout the entire cycle of the year or the work.</note> "And you shall acquire it for yourself as an everlasting thing from pure minerals and rocky mountains. Divide its principal parts, which will remain with you after the division; though it may be small, and though blackness <note>original: *nigredo*. This represents the initial stage of alchemical transformation, often described as a state of decay or "the crow's head."</note> dominates it, yet it is tempered with earth, and you will perceive many colors within it."

The wise man calls it the **Earth of Wisdom**, **Bronze**, or **Lead**. Therefore, you shall roast it with a strong fire for a "minor number" of four days; for a "middle number" of seven; for a "greater number" of ten; and then it is called by the wise the **Silvery Earth**.

Its second part, being fluid, is called the **Water of Wisdom**. The third part is the **White Earth**; you must cause this to distill four times for the minor, middle, and maximum number of seven days. And then it is called **Manifest Gold**. The fourth part contains a great whiteness and is called the **Air of Wisdom**, **Gnumiau** <note>original: *Gnumiau*. An obscure, likely corrupted term from Arabic or Hebrew sources, used here to name a specific spiritual or gaseous stage of the alchemical substance.</note>.

### *On the Four Things from Man*
#### *Chapter VIII.*

From this, note truly that it is likened to four things from man: namely, to dung, urine, blood, and hair. It is said to be like dung in the quality of the foul, infected earth, or by reason of the bad odor that stains. And it is the <term>clay of wisdom</term> <note>original: *lutum sapientiæ*; a sealant used to airtight alchemical vessels, often symbolized by base or "dirty" materials.</note> by which the vessels are strengthened. It is likened to urine in the quality of cleansing or washing water, or that which removes the foulness of the earth; or by the sharpness of the drying salt. To blood in the quality of penetrating air, or softening the hardness of the earth, or by reason of the red color remaining upon the earth. To hair, however, in the quality of the burning fire that comes forth from the earth, etc.

### *On the Four Internal Things in the Human Body Chapter IX.*

It is also compared to four principal things within man: namely, to the brain, in the coldness of water; to the heart, in the heat of fire; to the liver, in the moisture of air; to the testicles, in the dryness of earth. For the seat of <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *flegma*; one of the four bodily humors, traditionally considered cold and wet.</note>

In the egg, therefore, there are four things, namely earth, water, air, and fire. These four aside, in the middle of the **yolk** <note>original: *rubei*; literally "the red part."</note> is a fifth thing, which is the **chick**. This is not to be understood as a common egg of birds <note>original: *volatilium*; literally "flying things."</note>, but as that of which the philosophers speak; and for this reason, all philosophers in this most excellent art have described the egg itself, and have provided many other examples in their work, so that the **sons of doctrine** <note>A traditional alchemical term for students or initiates of the craft.</note> might gain understanding from them and investigate the secrets of nature.

### ON THE BASILISK AND POISONOUS
### worms.

->*On the comparison of the science with the Basilisk and other poisonous worms on account of the similarity of nourishment. Chapter XI.*<-

After these things, [the science] is said to be similar to the **Basilisk** <note>A legendary serpent-king. In alchemy, the Basilisk often represents a volatile or poisonous stage of the matter that must be "killed" to be transformed.</note> and other poisonous worms, by reason of its nourishment, its feeding, or its infection. For just as the Basilisk is said to be nourished and fed by diverse food and drink until it becomes large and mature, and after this it dies and is killed, and from its powder miracles are then performed: so it is with the body.

Plato <note>pseudo-Platonic alchemical traditions often attributed mineral theories to the Greek philosopher.</note> maintains that **alums** <note>original: *alumina*; a group of astringent mineral salts used in dyeing and medicine.</note> illuminate, **salts** dissolve, and **vitriols** <note>original: *vitriola*; sulfate minerals, often green or blue, known for their corrosive power.</note> break apart or bind together. For raw **alum** is said to abound in moisture, but **calcined** <note>original: *calcinatum*; reduced to a powder through high heat to remove volatile components.</note> [alum] in extreme dryness: therefore, as long as moisture abounds, it is compared to alums. But when the offending moisture is removed, it is called calcined alum, white and fixed. Truly, the property of **salts** is to dissolve, and to corrode, and to moisten, and to create an acidic liquefaction: because it is said one must calcine bodies with salt, for salt corrodes their corrupting moisture. Now, salts make bodies flow easily in the fire. It should be noted that some salts are **fixed** <note>Stable in fire; does not evaporate.</note>, while others are **volatile** <note>Easily evaporated or transformed into vapor by heat.</note>. For every fixed thing is used for the body or for a bond, and such things are extracted from calcined things: as it is said, "Extract the **Salt Alkali**" <note>original: *sal alkali*; a basic salt derived from plant ashes, used as a flux or solvent.</note>. For they extract it, and yet they do not prosper in it: because they extract it from that in which there is no **Salt Alkali of the Philosophers**. 
<margin>S</margin>
For just as Salt Alkali is extracted from **quicklime** <note>original: *calce viva*; calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone.</note>, or from **potash** <note>original: *cinere clavellato*; literally "wedged ashes," a high-quality potassium carbonate derived from wood ash.</note>, or **salt of tartar** <note>original: *sal tartari*; potassium carbonate derived from the crusts left in wine barrels.</note> from calcined tartar itself through a suitable moisture, until no sharpness remains: *so our salt, which is the **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; the transformative essence of the Stone that "colors" or changes metals.</note>, is extracted from the lime of metals through **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactionem*; the stage of the work where the matter decays and turns black.</note>, until the whole compound puts off its own nature and puts on a foreign one.* Concerning such a salt, **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were highly influential in the Latin West.</note> says: First it becomes ash, then salt, and from that salt, through various operations, comes the **Mercury of the Philosophers**. ### *On the Many Kinds of Quicksilver*
### *Chapter XIII*

<margin>
Three things to be noted in quicksilver.
</margin>
In the comparison of quicksilver, it must be noted that quicksilver is threefold: this is to extract the **philosophical fire**. According to the vital soul, this is called **fire**, or the **soul**, or the **fifth essence** <note>original: *quinta essentia*; the purest, most refined element that transcends the four physical elements</note>.

<margin>
1 Concerning the first quicksilver, which is fire.
</margin>
Concerning the first, the **Assembly of the Philosophers** writes, saying: Quicksilver is fire, which consumes bodies. And again: it is therefore necessary for the flame of fire to seize the body, so that it may be destroyed and become weak. For it is necessary to extract this fire with a fire of the same nature, as **Senior** <note>original: *Senior*; referring to the alchemist Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic author widely translated into Latin</note> says. Our fire is water: if you know how to give fire to fire, and **mercury** <note>original: *mercurium*</note> to mercury, it is enough for you.

Concerning the second, **Senior** <note>original: *Senior*; referring to Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabic alchemical author known in the West as Senior</note> and other wise men say: That the **soul** <note>original: *anima*; in alchemy, the vital principle or volatile part of a substance</note> is extracted through **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactionem*; the stage of decay or blackening in the work</note>, and when nothing of the soul remains in the body, then you have washed the body of its filth. For through such quicksilver, the second is extracted, mortified, killed, extinguished, and **coagulated** <note>original: *coagulatur*; turned from a liquid or gaseous state into a solid</note>, as the Assembly of the Philosophers testifies, saying: "Know that the body does not tint unless it is first tinted." ### *On the Individual Qualities of All*
### *Metals. Chapter 16.*

From there it is truly compared to all metals in their qualities, natures, colors, softness, and hardness: and this in both their manifest <note>the outer, physical appearance</note> and their hidden <note>the inner, spiritual essence</note> aspects. It is compared to gold and silver by reason of the perfection of their colors which persist in the fire, and their weights, as well as their ductility—especially, however, to gold, since it is more noble and perfect than all the other three bodies <note>In this context, likely referring to the other primary metallic bodies in the alchemical hierarchy: lead, tin, and copper</note>. And because of this eternal perfection, it is called "philosophical gold," which is similar to it: as the Philosopher <note>A title often reserved for Aristotle, though here used for a general alchemical authority</note> testifies, saying: "Those of the present and the past have made nothing, except gold from gold and silver from silver; yet that gold or silver was not of the common kind" <note>original: "non tamen aurum illud vel argentum fuit vulgi"; a common alchemical warning that the "gold" they speak of is a spiritual or refined substance, not the metal found in coins</note>.

Moreover, it is philosophical gold which is not bought at a great price, as Alfidius <note>An early alchemical author of the Arab-Latin tradition</note> says: "Know that this stone, regarding which this secret is concerned, God has placed as something not to be bought for a great price, because it is found cast out in the way <note>A recurring alchemical trope: the "First Matter" is everywhere and overlooked by the ignorant</note>, so that it may be possessed by both the poor and the rich: namely, so that anyone might easily arrive at it through reason and knowledge." And Morienes says: "Every thing which is bought at a great price is a lie: because..."

...of ours, is placed as a father in generation. <note>original: "stri," likely completing "nostri" (of ours) from the previous page.</note> Wherefore it must first be seen what the **philosophers' calcination** <term>calcination: the process of reducing a substance to a powder by heat, or in alchemy, by a "corrosive" liquid</term> is, and it must be known that the philosophers' calcination is threefold: twofold for the body, and the third for the spirit.
---
<margin>1</margin> The first is the beginning of our work, of which it is said: calcination is the deprivation of cold humidity by the combustion of that which removes it; or the incineration of dry earth. And the philosophers have exemplified this in wood, in which there are three humidities: the first is watery and cold, and this prevents the wood from burning.
---
<margin>2</margin> The second is oily or greasy, and it causes the wood to burn; these two are vaporizable in fire and combustible.
---
<margin>3</margin> But the third is left behind in the ash, and it is very slight and subtle, fixed and eternal, not at all flammable; it is **vitrifying** <note>original: vitrificans; the quality of turning into glass</note> and provides a glassy transparency. And in such a way the philosophers' calcination is commanded to be done, as was said regarding the wood: and it is truly done through the **philosophers' vinegar** <note>original: acetum philosophorum; a metaphorical term for a powerful acidic solvent</note>, or through **permanent water**, and by no other thing.
---
And note this: For such humidity, as was said, which is the principle of **liquefaction** <note>melting or dissolving</note>, must be in bodies: as **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says, "The principle of all liquefiable things is water." And **Avicenna** <note>a Persian polymath and influential alchemical authority</note> relates: "We have therefore considered in natural principles that the subject of liquefaction is humidity, mixed with dry earthy parts, in which it is moved while the fire dissolves them, and..."

<summary>This page defines the "philosophers' calcination," explaining it through the metaphor of wood containing three types of moisture: one that hinders burning, one that fuels it, and a third subtle substance that remains in the ash to form glass. It establishes that this process must be achieved using the "philosophers' vinegar" or "permanent water."</summary>

The action of the **Fifth Essence** <term>Fifth Essence: also known as the Quintessence, the purest and most refined part of a substance that remains after the four elements are balanced</term>, is either **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of vaporizing a solid and then collecting it as a solid again to purify it</term>, or **inceration** <term>inceration: the process of adding liquid to a substance until it achieves the soft consistency of wax</term>, or **imbibition** <term>imbibition: the repeated "drinking" or absorption of liquid by a dry material</term>, or indeed the interpretation of all these aforementioned things. For this **calcination** <term>calcination: the reduction of a substance to a powder by high heat</term> is performed for this reason: so that the parts dried by the fire and constricted may become spiritual, or be refined and made rare through the spirit, which is the "resolving water" <note>original: aqua resoluens; a solvent that breaks down matter</note> that moistens the burnt earthy matter itself. And the heat impressed upon it is that which corrupts, along with the humidity, transforming the substance into an airy breakdown <note>original: aeream resolutionem</note> through the process of digestion. For in the first calcination, two types of moisture are removed: namely, the cold and watery moisture, and the burning moisture. In this second calcination, however, the earthiness and the fieriness are removed through the breakdown caused by our "water." For all things which this water dissolves, liquefies, and softens, it then disturbs; from this, through decoctions <term>decoctions: the process of boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</term>, airy breakdowns result by way of evaporation.

This is the "solution of the philosophers," which occurs when the dry earthy parts soften: in such a way that their dryness, which is hardness, is turned into softness. This softness is called the moistening water, like rainwater or another form of humidity: because it is said that the more a thing is dried, the more it is softened, since only the "dryness" of **Alchemy** tinctures <note>original: tingit; to "tincture" means to permanently change the color or nature of a substance</note> and nothing else; this is the rarity <note>meaning the refined or subtle state</note> of the elements.

It is also called "inceration" for this reason: when the earth is deprived of its own moisture, it is necessary to "wax" it; that is, to drench it with moisture so that it may flow and have "entry" <note>the ability of a substance to penetrate and transform another</note>, and that it may represent the power and the metallic form, as the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: Turba philosophorum; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a debate between various ancient philosophers</note>...

<summary>This page describes the "Action of the Fifth Essence," explaining how calcination and "inceration" refine dry matter into a spiritual, soft, and metallic state using a symbolic "resolving water." It emphasizes the paradox that extreme alchemical dryness leads to a refined "softness" capable of transforming metals.</summary>

This second part is also called **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: in alchemy, a stage of symbolic decay where the substance turns black (nigredo), breaking down its old form to release its inner essence</term>, or **corruption**, by reason of what is manifest. For everything that putrefies and is corrupted to the sight, casts off its manifest matter and represents the matter of the hidden. The Philosophers, moreover, intend to corrupt or destroy the manifest, which is earthy, and to draw out the hidden, which is silver and gold, as **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicenna"</note> testifies, saying: When the copper <note>original: "æs"; refers to the base metal or "latten" being transformed</note> is made subtle and is decocted in vinegar with medicines until it dies, its whiteness then penetrates to the exterior, so that its inward part becomes outward <note>original: "intrinsecum fiat extrinsecum"</note>, resembling silver in its whiteness. When we have done this, we find its power to be staining, remaining, and of greater **tincture** <term>tincture: the transformative "dye" or spiritual essence of the Stone that has the power to change the color and nature of metals</term> and penetration, such that it does not differ from the color of pure silver in any way; indeed, it is filled with tincture, and is of a more complete whiteness. For such a putrefaction is generative, because it generates something of the same kind as itself. Whence **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith: the Latin name for the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: Know that no generation occurs without corruption; therefore, apply your study to putrefaction. And the **Assembly of Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba philosophorũ"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic sages</note> [says]: This putrefaction is the greatest, and it attracts the greatest secret.

It is also called the **separation of the elements**, as was mentioned before in the first **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine powder or ash</term>; for in this stage the elements are separated, namely: **earth**, **water**, **air**, and **fire**. The Earth is left behind there, so that the other three elements in it...

For everything that is dense and hard is neither staining <note>original: "tingens"; the ability of the alchemical "tincture" to change the color and nature of a metal</note> nor penetrating; therefore it must be ground down so that it becomes most subtle and penetrative. Whence in the *Assembly* [Turba]: "when all things have been carefully made into powder, it is ground."

And it must be noted that there is a twofold contrition: one of the common people, which is done by the hands of craftsmen. Of this it is said: "grind by day and roast by night." The second is that of the philosophers, and it is done by the fire of **decoction** <term>decoction: a process of extraction or maturation achieved through prolonged, steady heating</term>. Whence the *Assembly* says: "This contrition, however, is not done by hands, but by the strongest decoction." And the *Assembly*: "Therefore it is necessary for the sons of doctrine <note>a traditional term for students of the alchemical art</note> to burn 그 thing without fear until it becomes ash. And know that you have mixed it most excellently, because it receives from it the **spirit of life** <term>spiritus vitae: the vital essence or soul that animates matter</term>." **Roasting** <term>assatio: the process of dry heating or parching a substance</term> is so named and was invented so that the accidental moisture of the thing may be dried out and destroyed by a gentle fire. And it must be noted that in this roasting, the drying occurs both to the body and to the spirit itself. And one must be extremely careful lest the spirit—which dries the body and is dried by the body—becomes volatile: for if it flies away from the body, the body cannot be made perfect. **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were central to medieval alchemy</note> teaches such a drying, saying: "But since this has goodness, it is not burned over the fire entirely, but is only heated," etc.

**The philosophers** have established **five distinctions** through which their **tincture** <term>tincture: a transformative substance, also called the Elixir, capable of changing the properties of metals</term>—whether the white or the red Elixir—is completely composed and finished; without these, no tincture can exist. 

**The first** is to remove the superfluous <note>original: "superflua euacuare," meaning to purge the raw material of impurities</note>. 
**The second** is to alter the medicine into a white and yellow <note>original: "citrinum," a lemon-yellow or golden hue often associated with the penultimate stage of the work</note> color. 
**The third** is to provide metallic fusion. 
**The fourth** is to make such fusion permanent in the fire. 
**The fifth** is to grant the proper weight to every infused metal. 

And these five can be found within the number three, namely: **measure, number, and weight**, which are the perfection of all necessary things.

<margin>3</margin>
Then follows the **third part** of this work, which is described in this way by **Hermes** <note>original: "Hermete," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy</note>, King of the Greeks and father of philosophers:
> **The wind carried it in its belly.** <note>original: "Portauit illud ventus in ventre suo," a famous line from the Emerald Tablet, a foundational alchemical text</note>

The philosophers call this part **distillation**, or **clarification**. Therefore, after the matter has been **calcined** <note>original: "calcinata," reduced to a powder through intense heat</note> by a liquefiable moisture and stripped of its former name <note>original: "denominatiuo priuata," meaning the substance has lost its original identity and characteristics during the process of breakdown</note>, and then released from its fiery earthiness, it is necessary to **distill** it—that is, to clarify it—and to bring forth the transparency and clarity of the air. For distillation is defined as the clarification of a thing until it reaches transparency; and this distillation is the completion of the entire serenity of the work through clarity. And this is done three or four, or five, or six, seven, eight, or nine times,

### *Concerning the effects of this medicine or Tincture. The Final Chapter.*

Fifthly and finally, we must proceed to discuss the power, nobility, and effect of this praiseworthy philosophical tincture <term>philosophical tincture: the final, perfected form of the Alchemical Stone, capable of "dyeing" or transforming both metals and the human body</term>; which is a "tower of strength against the face of the enemy." <note>original: "turris fortitudinis est à facie inimici," a reference to Psalm 61:3, suggesting the tincture provides divine-like protection against disease and decay</note> And it should be known that the ancient sages discovered four principal effects or virtues in this glorious, comforting, and helpful treasury of knowledge. 

**First**, it is said to heal the human body from many infirmities. 
**Second**, to restore imperfect metallic bodies <note>meaning the transformation of "base" metals like lead into "perfect" gold</note>. 
**Third**, to transmute ignoble stones into certain precious gems. 
**Fourth**, to make all glass ductile <term>ductile: able to be hammered or shaped like metal without shattering</term>, or malleable.

Regarding the first effect, all the philosophers agreed that the hematite stone <note>original: "lapis hematites." While this literally means "bloodstone," in alchemy it refers to the "Red Stone" at the final stage of the work</note>, when perfectly reddened, not only performs miracles in solid bodies but also in the human body; of this there is no doubt. For it cures every infirmity when taken internally and heals when applied externally as an ointment. Indeed, the philosophers say that if a portion of it is given in water or warm wine to those who are paralyzed, frenzied, suffering from dropsy <note>an old medical term for swelling caused by fluid retention</note>, or lepers, it cures them. Other sages say that it often eliminates "the rosy drop" <note>original: "guttam rosaceam," likely referring to the skin condition rosacea or similar pustules</note> through anointing; and from this, even heart trouble...

One day I entered the house of the elder <term>Habielsam</term> <note>Habielsam is likely a Latinization of an Arabic name, representing a legendary alchemical teacher, often identified in this tradition as a master of the hidden arts.</note> for the purpose of visiting him, and I sat at his right hand. Two men were there, one of whom I knew, but the other I did not. And when they spoke in my presence concerning the <term>Art</term> <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, the sacred science of transformation.</note>, I perceived through what I observed that the art had been brought upon them, yet the word was obscured; they did not understand what they were looking for in the sayings of the wise, and they were in a state of astonishment. A companion turned his face toward me, secure in our friendship, and said to me: "What is the meaning of the wise in this matter? 'Take lead, and that which is likened to lead; and take <term>azoc</term> <note>original: "azoc," a term for mercury or the "universal solvent" Azoth, derived from Arabic.</note>, and that which is likened to azoc.' This is the order of the science which the Egyptians knew, along with its Enigma, its logic, its power, and its abundance. Here are four things, of which two are manifest: for he named lead, and that which is likened to it. What then are these four?" he asked. "And these words of the Wise possess an obscurity, and are among the <term>Sophisms</term> <note>In this context, "sophisms" are not logical fallacies, but rather deliberate riddles or "blinds" used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note> of the Wise," he said. "How is this so?" I replied. By this, the Wise man intended only two things, which are the male and [the female] of them...

...designated the male here: because he named him at the beginning of the discourse, clearly so that there may be no doubt in the speech; and yet this word is as effective as if you were to say: "Take Adam, and that which is likened to Adam." The male is hot and dry; the female, however, is cold and moist. For fire is an enemy until the elements become agreeable to one another, namely through fixation. And know that **if you make fire and water to be in harmony, that is, the volatile spirit...**

And know that it is not burned all at once in the vessel <note>original: "sapulo"; likely a corruption of "capulo" (a bowl) or "spathula"</note>, but gradually; that is, it is not fixed all at once by a single regime. Furthermore, the fire of the first **cooking** <term>decoctio|The process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or mature it</term> ought to be light. This is for the first stage, when the whole is still volatile, until it makes use of the fire and becomes unyielding <note>original: "implacabilis"; meaning the substance has reached a state where it no longer evaporates or changes easily</note>. Then, increase the fire gradually, because the more it is cooked, the more it is fixed, and so on.

And she <note>Euthicia</note> said: "Reveal then what the philosopher Syrnas <note>This name likely refers to a Greek philosopher or a corrupted version of a name like Serapion</note> says: 'that there is one thing in which the whole work is performed; and unless it is present, you will find nothing.'"

# TO EUTHACIA

Those who work this stone are ignorant [of how] to examine it alongside those things extracted from dead metals, which certain philosophers call the **Heart of the Sun** <term>Cor solis|A symbolic name for the pure solar essence or hidden "gold" found within crude mineral matter</term>.

And she said: "What is the **Heart of the Sun**?"
He responded: "A powder."
And [she asked]: "What is the powder that is both the container and the contained? And what is the contained?"
He responded: "The **stone that is not a stone** <note>original: "Lapis qui non est lapis"; a classic alchemical riddle referring to a substance that is physically mineral but possesses spiritual, transformative powers</note>, which you asked me about before."

And she asked: "Which of them is the male?"
He responded: "The **Red** <note>original: "Rubeum"; likely the Red Sulfur or the solar principle that provides the "seed" for gold</note>."
And she: "Which is the female?"
[He replied]: "The **Black Earth** <term>Terra nigra|The 'nigredo' or black stage, representing the initial decomposition and purification of the matter</term>."

And she asked: "Do these things suffice, so that I need nothing else?"
He responded: "It is necessary for you to have a **refinement** <term>emendatio|The act of "correcting" or purifying the substance through chemical processes</term>."
And she: "What requires refinement?"
He responded: "The container."

And she asked: "Which of them is stronger?"
He responded: "The stone that is not a stone is stronger than the other enemy; but the red is stronger than that, for by its own strength it has fortified its companions."
And she: "What is the container?"
He responded: "It is that which is **fugitive** <note>original: "fugans"; referring to volatile substances that "flee" or evaporate when heated</note>, which makes its companions flee [with it]."
And she: "In what way does it make them flee?"
He responded: "When it turns them into **spirits** <term>spiritus|The volatile essence of a substance separated from its heavy, "earthly" body</term>, after their earthly parts have been separated from them."

And she asked: "Which colors are most prominent in these bodies?"
He responded: "**Whiteness** <term>Albedo|The second major stage of the alchemical work, associated with purification, light, and the production of silver</term>."
And she: "From where does that Whiteness come?"
He responded: "Not from one part alone—namely, by [simple] completion—but through **reiteration** <note>original: "reiteratione"; the repeated cycle of distillation, sublimation, or washing used to purify the substance</note>, and indeed from many parts."

And she said: "Perhaps it is this [Whiteness] which turns gold into coins, because the refinement of the work is whiteness?"
He responded: "This is its beginning, and not its perfection."
And she: "Tell me more..."

...if what has been said satisfies you, I will nevertheless set down an example for you because you ask it of me. Regarding the making of the lead of copper <note>original: "æris plumbum." In alchemy, this often refers to a specific alloy or a stage of "blackening" copper to make it look like lead or to prepare it for further transformation.</note> in every way, which you did not propose to ask of me. **And she said**: "I did not ask, because all things must be made from it and through it; yet I wish it to be an example for those who come after. Tell me then."

<margin>From wood</margin>
**He responds**: "In the beginning, I give you an example from wood. For craftsmen finding a crack in wood or in stone take some of the dust of that wood, 
<margin>glue</margin>
and they mix it with glue <note>original: "colla." This refers to a binding agent, but in an alchemical sense, it represents the "gluten" or spirit that joins bodies together.</note>, and then they fill that crack or stone. Thus its color becomes like itself, so that no one seeing it would be 
<margin>Carbuncles</margin>
repulsed by it. Likewise, when carbuncles <note>original: "Carbumuta" in text, "Carbuncula" in margin. <margin>physician</margin>
taking flesh and blood, or human dung, with which they treat and cure those things. Furthermore, 
<margin>Of ships</margin>
ship owners repair the timbers of their ships; 
<margin>stone-cutters</margin>
and stone-cutters, when they find a hole in any stone, fill it with the flour <note>Fine powder or dust.</note> of that stone mixed with glue, and then it becomes like itself. In the same way, millers repair their 
<margin>of the mill</margin>
mills: for they take a little bit of the millstone, grind it, and prepare it with glue, then join it back to the stone. Similarly, anyone repairing any stone grinds a little of it and mixes it with glue of a 
<margin>vessels</margin>

<margin>potters</margin>

<summary>Rosinus uses the analogy of various craftsmen—carpenters, shipbuilders, and potters—to explain the alchemical principle that a substance is best repaired or transformed using its own "glue" or essential nature. This "like-to-like" principle is fundamental to the alchemical process of joining "spirit" and "body."</summary>

**And she**: "Why then do they speak of ivory, stones, and bones?"

**He responded**: "You have already learned what I answered regarding this. Know that '**living water**' is a fictional name; it is their **poison** <note>original: "venenum." In alchemy, 'poison' is a transformative agent that 'kills' the metal (breaks down its form) so it can be reborn in a perfected state.</note>, which is the water of sulfur. This is because when their water is cooked with that, it penetrates body with body. ...however, it is in the first composition. I tell you, moreover, that **sulfur water** <note>original: "aqua sulphuris." In alchemy, this is rarely literal sulfur water; it usually refers to a chemically active, "soul-bearing" liquid capable of changing the properties of metals.</note> is the **living water** <note>original: "aqua viua." Often refers to mercury (quicksilver) or a potent solvent that acts as the "life-force" of the chemical process.</note> extracted from the **lead of copper**, which liquefies and congeals all things. For first it prepares all things through boiling, then it congeals them, without any foreign substance entering into it. And know that this water contains every **tincture** <note>A "tincture" is the concentrated essence or "spirit" that imparts color and quality—such as turning silver into gold.</note> mixed with it.

Similarly, let that **gum** <note>original: "gumma." Alchemists used "gum" or "glue" to describe viscous, resinous intermediates that bind the volatile spirits to the solid bodies of metals.</note> be our living water.

And she asked: "Is this living water not a single, unique thing?"

He responded: "No. And therefore, in every work we name it the tincture itself—namely, among common woods, ivory bones, skin, hair, and pottery. For in all these things we call it 'living water,' because wherever it is applied, it enters, penetrates, and purifies."

And they gave it diverse names after it was composed from its various types and boiled, and it is called "gum." Take the gum of thorns and almonds, and mix it into the **urine of milk** <note>original: "urinæ lactis." Alchemists frequently used biological metaphors; this likely refers to a specific distilled liquid or a milky byproduct of a chemical reaction.</note> and especially that herb in which nothing but **sublime saffron** <note>original: "crocus est sublimis." Saffron often symbolizes the golden color or the "deep yellowing" stage of the alchemical work.</note> is found.

Do you not see how **Hermes**, thrice-graced <note>original: "Hermes gratia trinus," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, testified that this gum is the foundation of compositions? For it is the composition itself; and they guard the initial work through the agents. But when they desire, they mix the tincture with it, and from that point they achieve their intended goal.

And know that the **spirit of the Moon** <note>original: "spiritum Lunæ." The Moon represents Silver in alchemical symbolism. The "spirit" is its volatile or purified essence.</note> and every white substance is composed from the **lead of copper**. It is mixed from these spirits, then it is governed—and from there the tincture is extracted, which...

# TO EUTHACIA #

<page-num>293</page-num>

It is a shining stone, free of any blemish, and nothing is stronger than it—and [it exists] through its own forms (or spirits). <note>The "shining stone" (lapis nitidus) is a common metaphor for the purified matter or the Philosophers' Stone itself at a specific stage.</note> Agathodaemon <note>original: "Agadamon." A legendary figure in early alchemy, often depicted as a teacher of divine wisdom.</note> says: "Do not impose more things upon our **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymiæ."</note> lest it be extinguished." Now therefore I have signaled that the art of the **gum** <note>original: "gummæ." In alchemy, "gum" refers to a thickened, resinous intermediate substance that binds the volatile spirits to the solid "body" of a metal.</note> exists as a distinct thing by itself, and its preparation must be performed step-by-step. And so I have signaled to you that they perhaps guard it after the prior regimen is completed; but when they have need of it—namely, that which contains it—they mix it with the **tincture** <note>original: "tincturæ." The concentrated essence that imparts color and transformation.</note>—that is, the content of that which they wish to act upon in a similar way.

And know similarly, unless the gum is mixed with moisture, it burns and is consumed; therefore, the ancient philosophers ordered it to be cooked gently in moisture, until the **soul** <note>original: "anima." The volatile essence or "life-force" of the mineral.</note> surrounding it, which is suitable for our work, is lightly extracted from it. And know that they named that moisture itself by the name of "milk of the earth" <note>original: "lactis terræ." A poetic term for a white, nourishing liquid or a specific state of mercury.</note> and the name of every white creature. In the beginning, however, I say to you: when you cook it, place the moisture with the Plate <note>original: "Lamina." A thin sheet of metal, likely copper or silver, being acted upon by the vapors.</note>—as much as <margin>-</margin> covers it—and cook it gently, just as the philosophers ordered you, until you make it a completed gum, unburnt and inviolate.

"Gall" <note>original: "Fella." Likely referring to bile, used as a "Deckname" or code-word for a corrosive acid or a bitter reagent.</note> is a fictional name for **sulfur water**, and sulfur water is similarly a fictional name. He who can use these "galls" to make the body rot <note>original: "putrescere." Putrefaction was the necessary first stage of the Great Work, where the substance "died" and turned black (the nigredo).</note> for forty days, until it is transformed by cooking, creates a **dyeing poison** <note>original: "venenum tingens." In alchemical Latin, "venenum" (poison) often refers to a potent, penetrating medicinal elixir or reagent that "attacks" and changes the nature of a base metal.</note> that never fails.

# ROSINUS #

<page-num>269</page-num>

<header>ROSINUS</header>

...it has been proven, and when it has been reddened, he called it gold itself. However, very many are ignorant of this **copper** <term>Copper (Latin: aes): In alchemy, this often refers to "the philosophers' copper," a base material undergoing purification, rather than the common metal.</term>: but he who knows it maneuvers in the governing of the process, until he produces from it the color of the preparation in the **Iccir** <note>original: "Iccir." This is likely a Latinized corruption of the Arabic "al-iksir," or Elixir.</note>, and the color of gold is never mixed in the Iccir with gold and coin.

And she said: "Explain to me then what you said, that the philosophers have placed two modes in their books: one true, and the other false."

He responds: "It must be noted that to describe the truth, they never placed a word of the one without placing many false things with it, and they transfigured it with simulated names: wherefore we find no one who has placed the pure word stripped of the false, except for this one when..."

<margin>$\therefore$</margin> "...he said, 'Know that no **tincture** <term>Tincture: A potent substance or liquid capable of transmuting or coloring base metals into gold or silver.</term> is ever made except from the **red stone**.' But the other philosophers have disguised this stone as a 'coin'; a few called it leaden, red, the color of apples, <insert>colored like a flower, green, lemon-yellow, saffron</insert>, and black, and they have **mortified** <note>original: "mortificarunt." Mortification refers to the alchemical process of "killing" or breaking down a substance to its base state, usually through putrefaction or blackening, before it can be reborn.</note> it with all colors."

And she said: "How zealously they have hidden this stone!"

He responds: "It is the key of the work. But they have hidden the Earth by a multiplication of names, just as they did the stone, saying it is sand, because it is that from which the colors are extracted from their elements. The best copper among us is of the 'thing' <note>original: "aes rei." A cryptic phrase suggesting the copper is inherent to the primary material being worked on.</note>, and he who knows the copper of the thing dies in his own distress. Therefore, hide it likewise, if you can, and know that it is perhaps better than that which in its veins..."

<summary>Rosinus explains to Euthicia that alchemists intentionally used confusing names and false paths to hide the "red stone," which is the essential key to the Work. He emphasizes that the "true copper" and the "Earth" are the sources of all alchemical colors once they are properly processed.</summary>

...we have placed. And she said: Therefore explain to me what you said—that none of the philosophers has been found who named that which is raised in affirmation <note>original: "eleuatũ in affirmatione" — likely referring to the "exaltation" or sublimation of a substance to a higher state</note> by a single name. He responded: Now I say this very thing; however, they call it **copper** <term>Copper (Latin: aes): In this context, it refers to the "philosophers' copper," a spiritualized or purified metal rather than the common metal.</term>, the body of **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: A mysterious "mother" substance or mineral used as a starting point for the Philosopher's Stone; not the modern element magnesium.</term>, and **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver (Latin: argentum vivum): Mercury, representing the fluid, feminine, and transformative principle in alchemy.</term> itself. And she said: Is the truth then in this? He responded: Not at all. And she: Why? He responded: Because those names are taken from the species that are composed within it, for quicksilver is not made except from liquefied bodies. And therefore Democritus <note>Democritus was a Greek philosopher often cited by alchemists as an early authority on the nature of matter.</note> says, "**Cambar** <note>Cambar: An obscure alchemical term, sometimes referring to a "spiritualized" lead or a specific metallic salt.</note> and quicksilver are extracted from bodies." And she: Explain to me the clean **sulfur water** <term>Sulfur Water (Latin: aqua sulphuris): Also called "Divine Water," it is a transformative liquid, often acidic or caustic, used to dissolve and "color" metals.</term>, which is everything. He responded: I have already informed you that if you work the sulfur water properly, you will make gold from it—purple gold, I say, which is the perfection of the intention. And she: What then does the philosopher mean by "to dissolve any body and to tint <note>original: "tingere" — to dye, color, or transmute.</note> every body"? He responded: Clean sulfur water, because it is both the tinting agent and the tincture itself. And she: How is it tinted? He responded: It is tinted in **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: A stage of decay (often symbolized by the color black) where the substance dies to its old form so it can be reborn.</term>. But how does it tint? He said: Cook it in the **fire of dung** <term>Fire of dung (Latin: ignis stercoris): A low, steady, moist heat provided by fermenting manure, used for gentle digestion of alchemical materials.</term>. Therefore, the tinter and the tinted thing are made through it, in which is the tincture of any body. Therefore, hold it as certain that there is never any tincture unless it is cleansed by the sulfur water.

According to the sulfurous nature, diverse metals are procreated in the earth, even though their primordial matter is one and the same naturally. This occurs solely by the action of heat—namely, by more or less heat arriving, or not arriving with temperance; and in this, all philosophers agree. 

And I will demonstrate this to you: because every thing is and becomes that into which it is resolved. Just as ice, when it is changed—being turned into water by means of heat <note>original: "colore" (color); likely a scribal error for "calore" (heat), as the context refers to the melting of ice.</note>—was therefore previously water; so all metals are turned into the water of quicksilver, and therefore they were previously quicksilver. However, I will demonstrate below the method of seeking to reduce them into quicksilver. 

This being established, the opinion of those who said that the species of metals cannot be transmuted is refuted. What they say is true, unless the metals are first reduced to their **prime matter** <term>Prime Matter (Latin: prima materia): The primitive, formless base of all substance which must be reached before a new form (like gold) can be imposed.</term>. # ROSINUS

...with these same [waters] he sublimates the bodies, not by the **common sublimation** <note>original: *sublimatione vulgari*</note> which the unlearned intend, believing that to sublimate is merely to ascend upward. For this reason, they take calcined <term>Calcined: Reduced to a powder through high heat.</term> bodies and mix them with "superior" sublimates—namely, **mercury** and **arsenic**—and cause the bodies to be sublimated by a fierce fire, making them ascend with the spirits. They claim the bodies have been sublimated, yet they are deluded; for they find these bodies afterward to be unclean. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Indeed, our way of sublimating is not merely to ascend upward, nor is it to create a black and impure earth from what is thick and corrupt. Rather, for us, **to sublimate** <term>Sublimation (Latin: sublimatio): In chemistry, this is when a solid turns directly into a gas. One of these is the goal: namely, **whiteness** <term>Albedo: The "white" stage of the Great Work, representing a high degree of purity and the transformation of the matter into a silver-like state.</term>, in the procreation of which is the water of the fermented body.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The knowledge of our **Great Work** <term>Great Work (Latin: magisterium): The central goal of alchemy, referring to the creation of the Philosopher’s Stone.</term> is likened to the order of human creation. For first there is **Sexual Union** <note>original: *Coitus*</note>. Second, **Conception**. Third, **Pregnancy**. Fourth, **Birth**. Fifth, **Nourishment**. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This one thing I will make you understand: that our **seed** <note>original: *sperma*</note> is **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver (Latin: argentum vivum): Liquid mercury, considered the "seed" or fundamental fluid of all metals.</term>. When the earth is joined to the "imperfect body" (which is called our "earth"—because earth is the mother of all elements), this they call **Union**. While the earth begins to retain some of the **arsenic** <note>In alchemy, "arsenic" often refers to a volatile white spirit or sulfurous substance used to "whiten" metals, rather than just the modern chemical element.</note> with itself, then it is called **Conception**, when the male acts upon the female. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And this is what the philosophers have said: "That our Great Work is nothing but the male and the female and their conjunction." With the arrival of the water—that is, the arsenic—it grows much in the earth and is increased; and it happens that when the earth is **whitened** <note>original: *dealbata*</note>, then it is called **Pregnancy**, because it is now "pregnant." 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Then the **ferment** <term>Ferment: A substance added to the mixture to trigger a transformation, similar to how yeast causes dough to rise.</term> touches the prepared "imperfect body," as was said, until they become one in body, species, and appearance; and then it is called **Birth**. For then our **Stone** is born, which is called "The King" by the philosophers, as is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>: "Honor our King coming from the fire, crowned with a diadem." 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And one must bring him up to a perfect age. His father is the **Sun** <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold or the "perfect" masculine principle.</note>, and his mother is the **Moon** <note>The Moon represents Silver or the "imperfect" feminine principle.</note> for the "imperfect body"—taking the Sun for the "perfect body." And **Nourishment** follows, so that he may be increased further, just as he would be nourished more in his own milk and seed, from which are made...
