...abundantly, the **arsenic** <note>In this context, arsenic refers to a volatile white spirit or "philosophical sulfur" used for whitening, rather than modern metallic arsenic.</note> is truly imbibed more and more often, so that it "drinks" two parts, and let this be enough.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let us descend, therefore, to the **practical application** <note>original: *practica*</note>. I have told you, then, that first of all, **bodies** <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to solid metals like gold, silver, or lead.</note> must be reduced to the **First Matter** <term>First Matter (Latin: materia prima): The original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made; in alchemy, the goal is to return metals to this state so they can be "reborn" as gold.</term>, which is the **First Work**. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Take, therefore, one pound [of the metal], provided it is clean **filings** <note>original: *limatura munda*</note>, and mix ten pounds with arsenic, by **grinding** and **waxing** <term>Waxing (Latin: incerando): A process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency.</term> it with a little salt, until the whole becomes an **amalgam** <term>Amalgam: A mixture or blend; specifically, a soft alloy created by mixing mercury with another metal.</term>. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Afterward, in other vessels with its own **blessed water** <term>Blessed water (Latin: aqua benedicta): Not religious holy water, but a potent alchemical solvent or distillate used to purify substances.</term>, it resolves the "earth" into water through continuous distillations, until the whole has been resolved into **quicksilver** <note>original: *arg. viu.* or *argentum vivum*</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;This they call the **First Work**. The **Second Work** follows, and is done thus: Place this water in an earthen vessel over a slow fire, until you see it appear as **blackness** <term>Blackness (Latin: nigredo): The first official stage of the Great Work, representing decay, the "death" of the old metal, and the beginning of purification.</term> on top; remove this as delicately as you possibly can; cook it in this way and take away the blackness until no blackness appears, but the water appears clear. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thus you have the "earth" and the "water." The **Third Work** follows and is done thus: Take this earth, place it in a glass vessel, and pour the **blessed water** over it—that is, until nothing protrudes, so that the water floats four finger-widths above it. Cook it with a gentle fire for one day, and add water again; cook it thus successively until the earth becomes **white and clear**, and this is what the philosophers have said. This earth **putrefies** <term>Putrefaction: The process of breaking down a substance through heat and moisture, often associated with the transition from the "black" stage to the "white" stage.</term> and is cleansed with its water; when these things are made "putrid," with the help of God, the whole **Great Work** <note>original: *magisterium*</note> is directed—

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Regarding this dissolution, the philosopher **Parmenides** <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher; here he is cited as a character in the "Turba Philosophorum," a famous medieval alchemical dialogue.</note> speaks in the **Turba** <term>Turba Philosophorum (The Assembly of the Philosophers): One of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various ancient sages.</term>: "...hearing the dissolution of a certain dry oil." &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The second "word" is that there should be earth. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The third "word" is that the purification of the earth must come first, of which Morienus says: *This earth rots with its water and is purified, and then it becomes clean with the help of God.* Regarding which the philosopher says in the *Turba*: "Join the dry with the moist"—the dry being the earth and the moist being the water. Behold, now you have water and earth—that is, the earth **whitened** <note>original: *dealbatam*; referring to the "Albedo" or whitening stage, a sign of successful purification in alchemy.</note> with water.

...the refinement of the philosophers, through which the humidities <note>In alchemy, "humidity" or "moisture" refers to the flexible, life-giving essence of a substance that prevents it from becoming brittle and dead.</note> are preserved and are not dissolved from one another, but rather are coagulated. Afterward follows **solution** <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note>; a solution of **salt gem** <term>Sal Gemmae: Rock salt or pure crystalline sodium chloride.</term> is made with sal ammoniac and alkali. ...our [operation], of which one part congeals many for the philosopher. **Note:** when the **spirit** and **soul** are extracted from the **body**, the body remains dead; return its soul to it, and then they revive. <note>original: "ruu̅t," likely a transcription error for "vivunt" (they live). The metaphor of death and resurrection is central to the alchemical process of dissolving and reforming matter.</note> And know that those things which are resuscitated from death are perpetual. Likewise, **Sun** and **Moon** <term>Sun and Moon: In alchemical texts, these almost always refer to Gold (Sol) and Silver (Luna).</term> are prepared as the ferments of metals in the process of coloration. Note also that the sharper and more penetrating the **waters** with which the spirits are soaked, the better they are. Likewise, all **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: The stage where the substance is broken down, often turning black, symbolizing death before the new "life" of the philosopher's stone emerges.</term> occurs in moisture, and every earth rots when combined with water. 

Likewise, there are many types of **calcination** <term>Calcination: The process of reducing a metal to a powder by heating it in air.</term>, but the best is that done with **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Another name for Mercury.</term> and fire—that is, with the "water of life" while it is washed, as it is called in the first book, "a deadly poison." <note>original: "venenum mortiferum." # ROSINUS
<note>original: "ROSINVS." This is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist and mystic whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note>

To truly make the coarse into the simple; to **wash** <term>Wash: "Abluere" in Latin; the process of purifying a substance by removing its "shadow" or impurities.</term> is to render the dark into the light. To **reduce** the moist upon the dry, to **imbibe**, to **fix** that which would fly away, and to dominate over its own body.

To **dissolve**, therefore, is to divide, to break down, and to restore the primary nature. To **wash** is to distill into humidity, to **calcine** <term>Calcine: To reduce a solid to a powder through heat.</term>. To **reduce** is to **incerate** <term>Incerate: From "cerare," to make a substance soft and pliable like wax, often as a precursor to melting.</term>, to impregnate, and to re-sublimate. To **fix** is to betroth, to dissolve, and to regulate. The first kind of work of the **Stone** is to dissolve; the second, to distill; the third, to calcine the earth and to **whiten** <term>Whiten: Known as the "Albedo" stage, where the matter is purified of its blackness.</term> it by sublimating; the fourth, to re-dissolve, distill, calcine, and re-coagulate. Wherefore, to know how to sublimate with **Mercury** is nothing other than the ash which gives what it does not have. Or otherwise, when it extracts the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidum radicale." In alchemy, this refers to the essential, life-giving fluid inherent in all matter, which must be preserved during heating.</note> from gold, it is nothing other than the ash which does not give what it does not have: because **sublimation** covers the art just as chaff covers the grain.

And note that **sulfur** and sulfurs, **orpiment** <term>Orpiment: An arsenic sulfide mineral ("auripigmentum") used for its yellow color and chemical properties.</term> and orpiments, and **zandaric** <note>original: "zandaric." This likely refers to Sandarac, which could mean a red resin or a red arsenic sulfide (realgar) depending on the context.</note>—all these are names of the **divine water**, that is, the **Mercurial water** of the perfected bodies, foliated and clean. Its whitening is its preparation through sublimation (which is distillation) until it becomes white and clear, in which there is no dross. And this is the sublimation of Mercury and zandaric. But the **washing of the body** is the reduction of water upon it for so long that nothing remains in it of the **soul** (which is the **tincture** <term>Tincture: The essential color or quality capable of transforming matter.</term>) that does not ascend with the spirit. But when both are dissolved—namely, the bodies and the spirits—then a close and particular mixture occurs, which fire can still separate. # ROSINVS

...in the first stage it is black, in the second more lucid, in the third even more clear, and so on for up to 15 cycles of **dissolving and coagulating** <note>original: *soluendo & coagulando*; the repetitive process of turning a solid to liquid and back again to purify it</note>. In every **coagulation** <note>the process of a liquid thickening or becoming solid</note>, take care that the matter does not retain any of the salt, but wash it again and again. 

And note that when the elements have been divided, purified, and mixed together, you should perform a test: place a particle of the matter, about the size of a barley corn, upon an **ignited plate** <note>original: *laminam ignitam*; a red-hot metal sheet used to test the stability and melting point of the substance</note>. If it flows and stains the surface of the plate with its color, the work is good. If it does not, know that some harm has occurred during the **solution** <note>original: *solutione*; the process of dissolving the body</note>, for a body that is not well dissolved lacks the capacity for **entry** <term>entry: the ability of the alchemical tincture to penetrate and transform the interior of a base metal</term>. 

<margin>459</margin> These failures are caused either by a shortage of time or by the weakness of the **heat of the dung** <note>original: *caloris fimi*; a "bain-marie" or slow-cooker method using the natural heat generated by decomposing horse manure to provide a gentle, constant temperature</note>. If the substance penetrates but not deeply, this happens because of a lack of **air** <note>one of the four traditional elements</note>. For the **soul** <note>original: *anima*; the volatile or animating principle of the substance</note> entering the body runs swiftly through all its veins like an ointment. 

If, however, a part of it flies away, this happens because of a multitude of **spirits** <note>original: *spirituum*; volatile components like mercury or sulfur</note> that are not yet **fixed** <note>original: *fixatorum*; rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by heat</note>. But if the substance is laid down and flows, staining and penetrating deep into the whole plate without flying away, yet it leaves behind a dark smoke, this is due to insufficient **clarification** <note>original: *clarificatione*; the process of making the substance pure and transparent</note> of the separated elements. 

Therefore, arrange the **airy substance** by discernment—namely, within the body of the common earth—and arrange the **earthy substance** according to the moisture of the air and the heat and dryness of the sun (or a gentle fire), until they agree and are joined. Then, add to them two operative virtues: water for the **white work** <note>original: *album*; the albedo stage, producing silver</note> and fire for the **red work** <note>original: *rubeum*; the rubedo stage, producing gold</note>.

COMMANDMENT. This is the **stone that is not a stone** <note>original: *lapis non lapis*; a classic alchemical paradox indicating that the "Stone" is not a common mineral, but a substance with spiritual or organic properties</note>; it has a soul and blood and a reason similar to both. When they say it is fixed in it, that is to say, you have your knowledge there, and in no other thing. And just as man is composed of the four elements <note>The classic elements of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water, which alchemists believed must be balanced to achieve perfection.</note>, so also is the stone, and thus it comes from man. You are its mineral source, meaning it is enclosed within you and you hold it hiddenly; and it is extracted from you when it is reduced and dissolved by you. Because without you it cannot be completed, and you cannot live without it; and thus the end looks back to the beginning, and vice versa.

It is born in two mountains, that is, from **Venus** <note>In alchemical shorthand, Venus represents the metal Copper, but here it often signifies a "feminine" receptive principle or a specific refined essence.</note> and **Mercury** through the persistence of nature’s <term>decoction</term> <note>original: *decoctionis*; a process of slow, steady heating or "cooking" to extract the essence of a substance</note>. From this, the body and the spirit—and all volatile things—take their sustenance. Those things that are not fixed receive their coloration and fixation from it. 

Do not take it unless it is fresh and prepared with its own blood—that is, with Venus not yet melted, or well prepared. Its life or its operation comes to you from the blood, that is, from living Venus. Let it die in the air, namely through the rising of the fire, or <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again, used here to represent spiritual purification.</note> and purification. And if this stone were not of an airy nature—that is, of the same preparation—it would not be joined to Mercury, nor would their operation be perfect and firm. But because both are prepared and similar, they are mixed and united, so that fire does not separate them.

...calamine, talc, etc. Some are not fixed, such as **quicksilver** <note>original: "arg. viu." (argentum vivum); mercury.</note>, **arsenic**, **orpiment** <note>original: "auripig." (auripigmentum); a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>, **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "salarmo." (sal armoniacum); ammonium chloride, valued for its ability to dissolve metals.</note>, and so forth; if the spirits vanish through smoke, they cannot withstand the fire. Some truly are dissolved into water, and with them occurs the **inceration** <note>The process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency through the gradual addition of liquid.</note> of bodies and spirits, such as **vitriol** and **atramenta** <note>Metallic sulfates; "atramenta" specifically refers to black or dark minerals often used in making inks.</note>. There are, therefore, these 4 principal spirits in our art: **arsenic**, and **sal ammoniac**—because without it, the spirits would not be dissolved nor could they enter; for it dissolves and fixes all spirits, penetrates all metals, and softens them. ->*And one art demands one thing, which everyone well knows:*<-
->*they prepare this thing, yet this thing is many.*<- <note>original: "Ac ars una rem poscit, quod quivis bene noscit: hanc rem aptant, plura tamen haec res est."</note>

Likewise, this art requires neither many expenses nor great labor. Wherefore Morienus says: "Every thing which is bought at a great price is found to be false and useless in this work." Why then is it said that so many species are necessary in the art, if there is only one thing? Morienus resolves this: "Its root is one, which gives and renews its color."

### THE VERSES FOLLOW.

*Mary sounds forth wonders, briefly thundering such things.*
*With two gums, she fixes the fugitive in the depths.* <note>original: "Gummis cum binis fugitiuum figit"; in alchemy, "gums" often refer to semi-solid resins or spirits, and the "fugitive" is a common term for Mercury, which evaporates (flees) when heated unless "fixed" into a solid state.</note>
*In the hours of the hair, let the end overcome three strong things.* <note>original: "crinis"; likely refers to the "hair" or rays of the sun, symbolizing specific degrees of heat or stages of the chemical reaction.</note>

*The daughter of Pluto joins the partnerships of love,* <note>original: "Filia Plutonis"; Pluto, god of the underworld, represents the "dark" or "hidden" earth/matter used at the start of the work.</note>
*She rejoices in the roasted seeds, joined through three.*

# OF KHALID, SON OF YAZID
<note>original: "CALIDIS FILII IAZICHI." Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704 AD) was an Umayyad prince credited in alchemical tradition as one of the first great patrons and practitioners of the art in the Islamic world.</note>

What shall the ignorant or foolish man do, who does not understand the natures of things, nor knows the complexions <note>In medieval science, "complexions" refers to the specific combination of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determine a substance's properties.</note> of things? But when I saw this state in my chosen and most beloved disciple, moved by piety and love for him—and indeed by the nod and will of God—I published this book of mine as my death approached. In it, I have omitted certain things that my predecessor philosophers reported in their books, and I have said certain things which they themselves concealed, and in no way wished to speak of or reveal in their writings. 

I have explained and set forth those things which they covered up with their obscure and figurative speech. And I have called this my ***Book of the Secrets of Alchemy***. In this book, I have named whatever is necessary for the seeker of this science, or of the <term>magisterium: the mastery of the alchemical Great Work</term>, using a language suited to his understanding and to the senses of the inquirer. 

And I have named in this book four masteries, higher and better than those the wise men of old performed. Of these, there are the Elixirs: one mineral and another animal. The other two remaining are mineral, and are not a single elixir; their craft is the cleansing of what they call the **bodies** <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" (corpora) usually refers to the seven metals—gold, silver, mercury, copper, iron, tin, and lead—which must be purified before transmutation.</note>. 

One mastery is indeed to make gold from <term>living azoth: a term for "mercury of the philosophers," believed to be the essential soul or spirit of matter</term>, the creation and generation of which follows the same order of generation found in the mines, existing in the heart and the deep interiors of the earth. And the wise men explained these four masteries and crafts in their books regarding the composition of this mastery.

<summary>Khalid ibn Yazid explains that he wrote this "Book of Secrets" near the end of his life to clarify the obscure writings of earlier alchemists for his disciple. He introduces four primary alchemical works, including the creation of gold from "living azoth" following the natural processes of the earth.</summary>

But regarding these matters, much was lacking, and the [ancient philosophers] did not wish to include the details of their operations in their books; or, if a seeker found them, he could not understand them, for they found nothing more difficult to explain than that. Therefore, in this book of mine, I shall describe the work itself and how it is performed. 

Thus, whoever reads this book of mine should first study some geometry and learn its measurements, so that he may correctly construct the <term>furnaces: original "clibanorum," the specialized ovens used for sustained, controlled alchemical heating</term>, and not exceed their proper proportions through either increase or decrease, nor [mishandle] the quantity of the fires. Unless the matter of the mastery finds a suitable vessel for itself, the deed and its work will be destroyed; its operators will not find what they seek, nor will the thing itself reach the intended effect of "generation" <note>In alchemy, "generation" refers to the "birth" of the philosopher's stone or the transformation of a substance into a higher state.</note>. For when the matter does not find the cause of generation—that is, the root and the heat itself—the operations will inevitably result in failure. 

This same principle applies to the quantity of weights; when these are mismatched in the composite substance—with parts of its nature exceeding their proper limits through increase or decrease—the specific property of the composite is destroyed, and the resulting mixture becomes useless and void. ...observe that in soap, with which cloths are washed and cleansed and made white, there is generated in its proper composition this specific <term>property: a unique power or characteristic inherent to a substance</term>. This arises because of the balance, the correct proportions, and the required measures of the compound, which share in both length and breadth <note>The author uses spatial dimensions—length and breadth—to describe the physical balance of ingredients in a mixture</note>. Because of this shared participation, the elements come together, and it then becomes apparent that the truth of the intended result was within it; from this, the power which previously lay hidden is made known. This power they call a "property," and it is the cleansing virtue generated within the compound.

But when the quantity of the compound itself exceeds its proper limit—whether through addition or subtraction—that power of balance oversteps its boundary and turns into its opposite, following the imbalance of the mixture. Understand that it is exactly the same in the composition of our <term>mastery: the "Magisterium" or the Great Work of alchemy</term>.

And in the same way, the soul acts upon the body. In this same manner, the water is thickened by the earth, and it becomes similar to the earth in density, because earth is thicker...

...is water. <note>original: "est aqua"</note> And you should know that between the **solution** <term>solution: the process of liquefying or dissolving a solid substance</term> of the body and the **congelation** <term>congelation: the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid into a fixed state</term> of the spirit, there is no difference in time, nor is there a separate task. They are not independent of one another, just as there is no separate moment in time between water and earth when they are joined, such that one could be distinguished or separated from the other in their effects. Instead, they have a single goal and a single result; one and the same operation encompasses both of them simultaneously, *before* the composition.

I have said "before the composition" specifically so that whoever reads this book or hears of this solution and congelation does not mistake it for the "composition" named by the **Philosophers** <note>In alchemical texts, "the Philosophers" refers to the ancient authorities and masters of the craft, such as Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. To do so would lead them into error in both their practical work and their theoretical knowledge.

In this **magistery** <term>magistery: the highest "masterwork" of alchemy; the process of creating the Philosopher’s Stone</term> or craft, "composition" is the joining or **marriage** <note>Alchemists used the metaphor of "marriage" or "matrimony" to describe the permanent chemical union of two opposite substances, often represented as King and Queen or Sol and Luna.</note> of the congealed spirit with the dissolved body. Their union and their transformation take place over the fire, for heat is their nourishment. The soul does not leave the body, nor is it joined to it in a complete, total union, except by the transformation of both substances away from their original powers and properties, and after the conversion of their very natures. 

This is the true solution and congelation that the philosophers spoke of previously. Yet you must know that the wise have hidden this solution and congelation; they spoke of it using subtle reasoning and obscure, veiled language, so that the understanding of the seeker might be kept far from their true meaning. Let this be an example of the sayings of the **Philosophers** <note>original: "philosophorum"; the ancient authorities of alchemy</note> which are veiled and obscure among them: "Anoint the leaf with **poison** <note>original: "toxico"; in alchemical literature, 'poison' or 'venom' often refers to a transformative, volatile, or corrosive agent, such as mercury or a strong solvent, that "kills" the base metal to prepare it for rebirth</note>, and through it the beginning of the office—that is, the **magistery** <term>magistery: the masterwork or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> itself—will be proven to you." Similarly, the saying of the **Sage** among them is: "Unless you convert the bodies into subtlety, so that they are fine and impalpable to the touch, that which you seek will not be achieved for you." And: "If they have not been ground down, return to the operation until they are crushed and become subtle; for if you do this, what you desire will be directed to you."

In this manner, they set down many such words regarding these matters. Nor could any of those testing these claims reach the truth of such a concealment until a clear opening of the instructional demonstration appeared to them, removing their previous doubts.

Furthermore, they named "composition" as following **solution** and **congelation**. Later, they even said that composition is not completed except with ***marriage and putrefaction*** <term>putrefaction: the "death" or decomposition of the alchemical matter, usually marked by a black color, which must precede its purification</term>.

And again, their teaching later explained solution, congelation, and division, as well as marriage, putrefaction, and composition. This is because ***composition is the origin and life of a thing*** <note>original: "compositio, rei est origo & vita"</note>. For unless there were composition, a thing would not be produced into being. And **division** is to separate the parts of the compound; thus, the separation was its conjunction.

## Concerning decoction and its effect.
### Chapter 4.

And you should know that the philosophers have named "Decoction" <term>decoction: from the Latin 'decoctio', meaning to boil down or cook; in alchemy, it refers to the prolonged application of heat to mature a substance</term> in their books. And they said that they perform decoction upon things. And it is this process which generates them and changes them from their original substances and colors into other substances and other colors. And do not stray from what I tell you in this book, and you will proceed correctly. 

Look, brother, at the seed which sustains the life of men: how the heat of the Sun works upon it until the grain emerges from it, which humans and other animals eat. Afterward, nature works upon that grain within a person with its own heat and transforms it into flesh and blood. And the operation of our mastery <term>mastery: the 'magisterium' or the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> is just like this. Thus our seed—which the wise say is such that its perfection and its process is fire—is the cause of life and death; it does not grant life except through an intermediary and its own spirituality <term>spirituality: the 'spiritus' or volatile essence of a substance</term>, which are not mixed except by means of fire.

### *On the quantity of fire, and its benefit and harm.*
### Chapter VIII.

And let the practitioner likewise know the quantities of fires, and the benefit of this thing, as well as its harm, for it proceeds from the proper use of fire. ### On the solution of the composite stone.
### Chapter XII.

But afterwards the philosophers applied their ingenuity <note>original: "subtiliauerunt se," meaning to refine one's thinking or use subtle methods</note> to dissolving them, so that they—the body and the soul—might mix well. For all things that are joined together in grinding <term>contritione: the act of crushing a substance into a fine powder to increase its surface area</term>, and roasting <term>assatione: a dry-heat process used to remove moisture or change a substance's temperament</term>, and watering <term>rigatione: the process of moistening or "feeding" a substance with liquid</term>, have a proximity and a binding to one another. Therefore, the fire is able to take the nature from the weaker part until it fails and vanishes; and similarly, it turns back upon the stronger parts until the body remains without the soul.

Wherefore, when they are thus dissolved and congealed, they receive their parts into one another—namely, their large and small parts—and from these came a union <note>original: "complexio," referring to the balanced combination of qualities</note>, and it is their taking up <note>original: "assumptio"</note> of each other, and thus those two were converted into one and the same thing. And when it was so, the fire takes from the soul as much as it takes from the body, neither adding nor diminishing; thus, perfection was achieved through them. 

For this reason, it is necessary to have a specific chapter in the science of the Elixir <note>original: "Elixiris," the transformative substance capable of transmuting metals or prolonging life</note>, namely the discourse on dissolving simple bodies and souls. ## CONCERNING THE QUALITY OF THE *Philosophical* STONE. *Chapter One.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' with a floral and vine motif inside a square border.</image-desc>

This stone from which this work is made has within itself all colors. For it is white, red, and most ruddy; it is lemon-yellow and most intense yellow-gold, sky-blue, green, and heavy. Within this stone are the four elements <note>The classic Aristotelian elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>. For it is watery, airy, fiery, and earthy. That which is in the manifest part, the cold and moist, is a corrupting watery smoke. It therefore behooves us that this moisture and coldness be made equal to the heat and dryness, so that it does not flee from the fire. For between that coldness and moisture, there is one hot and dry particle; it therefore behooves that the cold and moist... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

## Concerning the hidden heat and dryness existing in the moist and cold.
### Chapter III.

<margin>what the precious stone is</margin>
The wondrous work of the three words is the work of the precious stone, in which there is a watery and burning <note>original: "aduſtiua"; referring to a corrosive or "stinging" quality often associated with acids or salts in early chemistry.</note> coldness and moisture, and within that same thing is a hidden heat. And so, that which concerns the "three words" is read and understood differently by certain people, so that not everyone may clearly and openly understand the cause within these three words. <margin>hidden heat and dryness</margin> This [cause] is sought in the moist and cold, within which there is hidden heat and dryness; and it is necessary for us to know this so that we may make the manifest hidden, and the hidden manifest <note>This "inversion of qualities" is a core alchemical concept: making the external physical properties (manifest) disappear to reveal the internal spiritual or transformative powers (hidden).</note>. And this hidden thing is <margin>the hidden is of the nature of fire</margin> of the nature of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"; in alchemy, the Sun represents Gold or the active, masculine, and fixed principle of fire.</note> and of Fire, and it is the most precious oil of all hidden things, and <margin>tincture water vinegar spirit</margin> a living tincture <term>tincture: a potent substance or "medicine" capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</term>, and the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a term for the universal solvent that does not wet the hands, often identified with philosophical mercury.</note> which always lives and remains, and the vinegar of the philosophers, and the penetrating spirit. But the watery and burning coldness flees from the fire and destroys itself.

### *Concerning the works of the planets and their images existing in Mercury. Chapter V.*

I say, therefore, that in <term>Mercury: here referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the fundamental watery principle or "soul" of all metals, rather than just the liquid metal we know today</term> are the works of the planets, and their images <note>original: "imaginationes"; likely referring to the formative influences or astrological "signatures" the planets imprint upon matter.</note> in their places, just as they work in the fetus in its parts and times. For in the fetus, in the first month when the seed is received by the womb, Saturn works by congealing and constricting the matter into one mass through its coldness and dryness. ## On the observation of the planets in the work of Alchemy. Chapter VI.

From these three months <note>Referring to the divisions of the gestational period mentioned on the previous page</note> we must understand that you, with a sharp wit, must know how to compose and extract two: for from two, three are not understood; but from these three, two and seven are understood. Wherefore all who desire to know this art should sharpen their wit to open the treasure from three words, in which the whole preparation and power of the stone is hidden. In this stone there is heat and dryness, and this dryness is the "living oil" and the "living tincture," and it is a tinctured dryness and the very depth of tinctures; and this is the "hot and moist conjunction" <note>original: "calidum & humidum coniunctiuum"; a reference to the balancing of opposite qualities—the Four Humors—required to create the Philosophers' Stone</note>.

Everyone, however, who has seen this from the beginning, recognized it from the word that was spoken; and those who heard of the three words were greatly amazed. Here is their explanation: because just as from the beginning of conception until the birth of the child, each planet in its place gives its image by the divine power so creating—so I, Rachaidebi <note>Likely a Latinized name for an Arabic alchemist, possibly Khalid ibn Yazid or Rhazes, who were frequently cited as authorities in medieval European texts</note>, say: and it is true, that in all alchemical works each planet in its place makes its own image until the completion of the work; and then Alchemy is born artificially. But if I speak more truly, it is born naturally according to all the planets, just as God showed to the first-formed man <note>original: "protoplasto hominis"; referring to Adam, the first human, who in alchemical lore was often said to possess innate knowledge of all natural secrets</note>, naturally having the nature of all tinctures:

# A LITTLE TREATISE OF ARISTOTLE ON THE PRACTICE
## *Of the Philosopher's Stone.*
### *begins.*

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' containing intricate foliage and scrolling decorative patterns.</image-desc>SINCE every body, according to the Philosopher <note>In medieval texts, Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher."</note>, is either an element or generated from elements, generation is of the highest necessity for our Mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>original: "magisterio"; referring to the completion of the Great Work</note>. This generation, however, cannot consist of anything except the four natures, which are the four elements. Indeed, there are four elements: air, water, fire, and earth, without which all generation is deprived of its effect. For of the elements, two are stony and two are watery: the stony ones are fire and earth, while the watery ones are air and water. Likewise, two of them are friends, and two are enemies. Earth and water are friends; fire and water are enemies.

Therefore, make peace between the enemies, and you shall possess the whole Mastery. But you cannot make peace between the elements except through their mutual conversion <note>In alchemy, "conversion" refers to the process of changing one element into another by altering its qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> into one another. Moreover, it is quite possible to convert them well into one another. Because, as the Philosopher says: It is within the natural aptitude of all elements that they may be changed into one another. For fire is changed into air, and air into water. Likewise, fire is changed into water, and water into earth, and vice versa.

It emphasizes that the alchemical "Mastery" is achieved by reconciling opposing elements—specifically fire and water—through their mutual conversion.</summary>

Therefore, convert the elements, and you shall find what you seek. For our composition, as Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist of the 7th-8th century, famously the teacher of Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says, is a change of natures, and a mixable connection of their heat with cold, and moisture with dryness. For the coldness of water, the heat of fire, the moisture of air, and the dryness of earth, when bound together harmoniously, constitute the complete first generated thing. For the elements are, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says, convertible in a circle. And thus they are generated and corrupted <term>corrupted</term> <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breaking down of a substance's form so that a new form can emerge.</note> into one another, but this is perfected only through operation and guidance.

There are truly four modes of operation: namely, the dissolution of the stone into spiritual water, the separation of the stone into a spiritual state, the reduction of the stone into natural earth, and the wedding <term>desponsatio</term> <note>original: "desponsatio"; an alchemical metaphor for the chemical union or "marriage" of substances, often sulfur and mercury.</note> of the stone into spiritual lime <term>calcem</term> <note>original: "calcem"; refers to the "calx," a powder or oxide remaining after a metal has been burned or heated.</note>.

The dissolution of the stone is achieved through grinding <term>contritionem</term>; the separation of the stone through distillation; the reduction of the stone through waxing <term>incerationem</term> <note>original: "incerationem"; the process of softening a dry substance by adding liquid until it reaches a wax-like consistency.</note>; and the wedding through fixation.

Therefore, the first step of our guidance or work is the dissolution of the stone into spiritual water, as the Philosopher says. Since the first mode of preparation is that the stone becomes Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; in this context, the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a refined state of matter, rather than common quicksilver.</note>. For it is the first body acting upon coarse things, so that it may return them to its own manner. For if it were to leave coarse things in their coarseness and did not refine the being, the stone would not be dissolved, nor would it putrefy. because your labors in the solution of these things aim at the heavier parts being cast aside, so that the work may be completed with the lighter parts. This is indeed achieved through sublimation <term>sublimatio</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then collecting the purified solid that forms when it cools.</note>. Slaughter, therefore, your sons, and take their blood, but throw the flesh to the dogs, lest they bark at you <note>original: "Iugula ergo filios tuos... ne latrent super te." A striking alchemical allegory: the "sons" represent the raw materials; their "blood" is the spiritual essence or soul, while the "flesh" is the gross, impure matter that must be discarded.</note>. And this is because blood is the soul, and the soul is life, and life is our stone. For nothing is suitable for our stone that has not been alive, and has not sought the heaven of the air. Turn your stone, therefore, into blood, and blood into air, and air into earth, and you shall have the whole mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>The "Mastery" or "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), the successful creation of the Philosophers' Stone.</note>.

The second stage of our governance is the separation of the stone into a spiritual state: which separation indeed occurs through the division of the elements and their full purification <term>depuratio</term>.

Regarding the purification of the separation, as Rasis <note>Rhazes (854–925 AD), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential figures in the history of alchemy and medicine.</note> says: The nature of the stone is to be divided into the four elements, and to cleanse them individually by distillation. For fire extracts that which resides in the inner parts. For it consumes the impurities of the stone through distillation, and refines it through the levigation <note>The process of grinding a substance into a smooth, fine powder, or here, a metaphor for refining via air.</note> of the air; and therefore our stone is divided into four elements, so that it may be more refined, and better purified from filth, and so that it may be more firmly joined afterward; but this is because putrefied things, being more thoroughly digested, are more easily divided. Putrefaction <term>putrefactio</term> <note>A stage where the matter is allowed to decay or ferment in a closed vessel, often turning black (the "nigredo" stage).</note> must necessarily precede the division of the elements, so that the elemental parts may be dissolved within it, and thus it may be rendered more fit afterward for extraction through the four elements.

Apply a very gentle fire beneath it for a philosophical month <note>original: "mensem philosophicum." In alchemical tradition, this usually refers to a period of forty days, symbolizing a complete cycle of transformation or gestation.</note>, so that it may become more foul and corrupted.

For as the philosopher says: Corruption is the putrefaction <term>putrefactio</term> of a thing's substance, resulting from the retention of vapor and the action of fire. For if it were dispersed through the air, it would not putrefy at all. Therefore, seal your vessel so that it cannot breathe. When the philosophical month is over, gently distill the four elements—namely water, earth, air, and fire—placing each one aside. However, take the greatest care that you do not burn the tincture <term>tinctura</term> <note>The essential, concentrated essence or "soul" of the material that possesses the power to transform other metals.</note> with too much fire during their separation. For the secret is, as Rasis <note>Rhazes (854–925 AD), a Persian polymath and influential alchemist mentioned on the previous page.</note> says, to prepare the elements subtly so that they are safe from scorching in every distillation, until the tincture is taken from them. If the tincture is burned, its effect will be ended.

Therefore, continue the fire gently, and first receive the water that comes out. For the first thing that distills, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose chemical and medical works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says, is water, but it is not yet pure. Afterward, fire mixed with air drips out. Keep those together until you divide them. What remains at the bottom, burnt, is the black and dry earth. And so you have the four elements separated into parts, but not yet purified. The first element, therefore, is pure water—cold and moist in nature—which must indeed be distilled seven times, and it will be bright and clear...

The fourth degree of our governance <term>regimen; the systematic management of heat and chemical processes over time</term> is the betrothal <note>original: "desponsatio"; an alchemical marriage or union of elements</note> of the stone into the bodily lime <note>original: "calcem corporalem"; a powdery substance remaining after calcination</note>, so that it may be fixed in that body from which it was taken in the beginning. And this is because when the spirit has dissolved the body and the soul, so that they exist in their own form, it does not remain fixed unless you have "occupied" it. This occupation, indeed, consists in joining it with the body from which you prepared it in the beginning, because in that body it is restrained from the flight of the spirit toward the persistence of the body. And for this reason **Plato** says: When the spirit has dissolved the soul and the body together, it does not stand fixed. Join it therefore with the body, so that it may generate something like itself. Nor should you join it with just anything, so that it might remain stable, except with that from which it originated. If you do this, it becomes **Iccir** <note>original: "Iccir"; likely an Arabic-derived alchemical term, "al-iksīr," which refers to the Elixir or the stone itself</note>. And know that for all practitioners, their purpose fails after the completion of the work if they omit this secret. Note these words, therefore, and mark these mysteries. For white and red sulfur, as **Aristotle** says, congeals quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; mercury, the "living silver"</term> into gold and silver. Join your work, therefore, with the body, so that it may generate its like. If you do this, that which you join will be [established] over other bodies; otherwise it will not be fixed <note>original: "figetur"; rendered stable and resistant to evaporation by heat</note>, because nature is not contained except in its own nature. And this is because, as **Plato** says: Nature follows nature, and nature contains nature, and teaches it to fight against the fire <note>This "fight" refers to the substance's ability to remain solid and unchanged even in the furnace</note>.

Make, therefore, a betrothal <note>original: "desponsationem"; the allegorical marriage of chemical principles</note> between the husband and the wife, and you will possess the entire mastery <term>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</term>. But their preparation, as **Avicenna** says, is this: That you first cleanse the husband on one side and the wife on the other, so that once they are purified of filth, they may be better joined; for if you do not prepare the bodies, they cannot be loved <note>original: "amari"; in an alchemical context, this refers to the chemical affinity or attraction that allows substances to bond</note>. Create peace, therefore, among the elements, so that they may love one another in a suitable embrace.

For the sharp mastery of the philosophers places the soul into the lime <note>original: "calces"; the fine powder or ash remaining after a substance has been burnt or calcined</note> of the bodies; then the vigor of the spirits crushes them into the smallest lime of the leads. Likewise, when you wish to add the ferment <term>fermentum; a substance—often gold or silver—added to the alchemical mixture to "leaven" the whole and act as a catalyst for transformation</term> into the Elixir, first mix it with the spirits, because unless you do this, its nature would not be impressed upon them. Mix the ferment well, therefore, with the elements, and you will have the mastery.

-> THE END. <-

# AVICENNA ON THE
## CONGELATION AND
### conglutination of stones.
### Chapter I.

Pure earth does not become stone, because it does not create continuity <note>original: "continuationem"; the internal cohesion or binding that holds a solid mass together</note>, but rather discontinuity. For the prevailing dryness within it does not permit it to be bonded together <term>conglutinari; to be glued or joined as if with a binding agent</term>. Stones, however, are formed in two ways: by bonding and by solidification <term>congelatio; literally "freezing," but here referring to the hardening of a liquid or substance into a solid state</term>. In some stones, earth is the dominant element; in others, however, water is dominant. For sometimes the mud is first dried out, and something is created that is midway between mud and stone, and thereafter it becomes stone. Viscous <note>sticky or thick in consistency</note> mud is more suitable for this transformation, for it is cohesive. On the banks of the Geon <note>The Gihon, one of the four rivers of Paradise mentioned in the Bible, often identified by medieval scholars as the Nile or a river in the Middle East</note>, earth has been observed which appears to be converted into stone over a period of 33 years.

Stones are also formed from water in two ways. One is when water falling drop by drop solidifies <note>A reference to the formation of stalactites and stalagmites</note>. The other is when something settles out from running water and rests upon the surface of the bottom of that water, and thus becomes stone. For there are certain places where poured waters are converted into stones of various colors; yet these waters, if taken up from the source, do not solidify, but if they are poured near their own riverbed, they do solidify and become stones.

<summary>This page introduces Avicenna’s theories on mineralogy, explaining that stones form either through the bonding of earth or the solidification of mineral-rich waters. It distinguishes between mud-based stones and those created by sedimentation or dripping water.</summary>

We know, therefore, that there is within the earth that mineral power which solidifies waters. Therefore, the principles of stones are either formed from a muddy substance, or a viscous one, or from a substance in which [water] prevails, which is solidified by a certain mineral power; or earth prevails within it, causing it to coagulate. In the same way <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Sal armoniacum"; a salt historically used in alchemy, usually identified with ammonium chloride, valued for its volatility</note> is solidified, but the earthly power is not sufficient on its own to transform it into salt; rather, heat assists it. This heat, upon arriving, coagulates it through a hidden power; and perhaps it is made from cold, dry earth; and earth is made from water when the qualities of earth overcome it, and vice versa.

There is also a certain thing which some ingenious men use when they wish to coagulate a dry substance; it is composed of two waters and is called <term>virgin's milk</term> <note>original: "lac virginis"; in alchemy, this typically refers to a milky white liquid formed by mixing two clear solutions, such as litharge dissolved in vinegar and sal ammoniac</note>, which is its most certain effect. 

Therefore, stones are formed from mud through the heat of the sun, or from water coagulated by a dry, earthly power, or from hot water that has been dried out. Similarly, certain plants and certain animals are also turned into stones by a certain <term>lapidifying</term> <note>original: "lapidificatiua"; stone-making or petrifying</note> mineral power. This occurs in stony places or through a sudden disharmony <note>original: "disconuenientia"; an imbalance of elements or a sudden environmental shock</note> caused by a certain power which exits the earth at the hour of an earthquake, which converts things into stones. ### On the Cause of Mountains.
#### Chapter II.

Mountains also are sometimes formed from an <term>essential cause</term> <note>original: "causa essentiali"; an internal or primary mechanism of change, in this case, seismic activity</note>, and sometimes from an <term>accidental cause</term> <note>original: "causa accidentali"; an external or secondary factor such as erosion</note>. From an essential cause, as when the earth is elevated by a violent movement of the earth <note>an earthquake</note> and becomes a mountain. From an accidental cause, as when a deep hollow occurs because of winds or the flow of water; this happens gradually until a vast depth is created, resulting in a great height emerging alongside it. This is the primary cause of mountains. There are also certain earths that are soft and others that are hard. The soft ones are carried away by water currents and winds, while the hard ones remain, creating an elevation. Just as there is a generation of mountains, so too is there a generation of stones; for the flow of water continually brings them viscous clay, which is dried out over a long span of time and becomes stone. It is also quite possible that there exists a <term>mineral power</term> <note>original: "vis mineralis"; a formative force or "virtue" thought to transform elements into minerals</note> converting waters into stones. And for this reason, the remains of aquatic animals and other creatures are found within many stones <note>this is an early medieval recognition of fossils</note>. Mountains were formed over vast periods of time, as we have said, provided they are not currently eroding. The substances...

However, the clays that are found on high places are not made of that stony matter, but rather consist of what is worn away from mountains—be it terrestrial soil or some other substance brought by waters along with mud and vegetation. These materials are mixed with the clay of the mountain, or perhaps they are the ancient mud of the sea, appearing as a single substance. This is because one part of it becomes stone, while another part does not, but instead is softened and dissolved by some prevailing quality <note>In medieval science, a "prevailing quality" refers to the dominance of one of the four primary qualities: heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>. The sea undergoes retreats and advances; it hollows out certain places and elevates others, and at times it covers the entire earth. From this movement, it scrapes away certain soft materials, leaves the hard ones behind, and has piled them up in certain locations. These soft materials piled up by the sea, once they were cut off and dried out, were converted into mountains.

### *On the four species of mineral bodies. Chapter III.*

Mineral bodies are divided into four species: namely, into stones, <term>fusible substances</term> <note>original: "liquefactiua"; minerals that can be melted, typically referring to metals</note>, sulfurous substances, and salts. Among these, some are of "rare" <note>meaning porous or less dense</note> substance and weak composition, while some are of strong substance; some are <term>ductile</term> <note>capable of being hammered thin or stretched into wire without breaking</note>, and others are not. Of those that are of weak substance, some are salts, such as those which quickly liquefy from moisture, like alum, <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "calcamentum"; a term for metallic sulfates used in making dyes and inks</note>, and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sal armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, highly valued in alchemy for its ability to clean metals</note>. Others are oily and do not easily liquefy by moisture alone, such as sulfur and <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum"; literally "gold pigment," an arsenic sulfide mineral used as a yellow dye</note>.

### MINERALS.

But quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> belongs to the second category, although it is an element of <term>ductile substances</term> <note>Materials that can be hammered or stretched thin without breaking, such as metals.</note>, or similar to some ductile ones. Moreover, all ductile substances are <term>fusible</term> <note>original: "liquabilia"; capable of being melted.</note>, and for the most part, those that are not ductile are also not fusible, and they cannot be softened except through great force. <margin>⸫</margin><note>The following passage is underlined in the original: "And the matter of ductile things is an aqueous substance mixed with an earthy substance in a strong mixture"</note> And the matter of ductile things is an aqueous substance mixed with an earthy substance in a strong mixture, and one cannot be separated from the other. Its aqueous substance is congealed by cold after the action of heat upon it, which is <term>epthesis</term> <note>original: "epthesis"; from the Greek *epsēsis*, meaning "boiling" or "decoction." In medieval alchemy, it refers to a process of refining or "ripening" a substance through controlled heat.</note>. An example of this can be seen in wine that has not yet frozen because of its oiliness; and for this reason, it is not ductile. 

Stony things, however, among mineral substances are materially aqueous, but they are not frozen by water alone, but also through dryness, which transforms the aqueous nature into an earthy nature. There is no moisture in them that is excessively oily, and therefore they are not ductile. Because their <term>coagulation</term> <note>The process of a liquid becoming a solid.</note> results from dryness, they are not easily dissolved for the most part, except through natural solvent methods. <note>The following phrase is underlined in the original: "Moreover, alum and sal ammoniac are of the genus of salt"</note> Moreover, <term>alum</term> <note>A type of astringent mineral salt.</note> and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sal armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, highly valued in alchemy for its ability to sublimate.</note> belong to the genus of salt, because the portion of fire in sal ammoniac is greater than the portion of earth. For this reason, the whole substance is <term>sublimated</term> <note>The process of a solid turning directly into a gas when heated.</note>; it is essentially water mixed with a hot smoke that is extremely subtle and possesses a high degree of "fieriness," which has been coagulated through dryness. <margin>⸫</margin><note>The following phrase is underlined in the original: "Truly, the aqueousness of sulfurous things"</note> Truly, the aqueousness of sulfurous things is mixed with earth in a strong mixture through the boiling of heat until they have become oily, and afterwards they were congealed by cold.

Vitrils <note>original: "Atramenta"; literally "inks" or "blackening substances." In this context, it refers to metallic sulfates or vitriols used in alchemy and dyeing.</note>, however, are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; and within them is the mineral power of certain <term>fusible bodies</term> <note>original: "corporum liquabilium"; substances that can be melted, typically metals.</note> which are formed from them. For example, <term>chalcanthum</term> <note>original: "calcamentum"; a corruption of the Greek *khalkanthos*, referring to copper sulfate or "blue vitriol."</note> and <term>alachar</term> <note>A Latinized Arabic term referring to a type of vitriol.</note> are generated from the larger grains of the vitril, and its saltiness is only dissolved along with that which is in that sulfurous part, and afterwards it solidifies. This substance then receives its mineral power from certain bodies. Therefore, that which receives the power of iron will be red or saffron-colored, like <term>alathar</term> <note>Another Latinized Arabic term, likely referring to red vitriol or an iron oxide.</note>. But that which has received the power of copper will be green. Hence, it is possible for these two to be produced artificially.

<margin>∴</margin> *Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; mercury.</note> is like water that is mixed with an extremely fine earth in a strong sulfurous mixture, to the point that it does not rest upon a flat surface;* <margin>∴</margin> and this is due to the great dryness that exists within it, and for that reason, it does not stick to what it touches. Its whiteness comes from the clarity of that water and from the whiteness of the fine earth that is within it. *Its unique property is that it is solidified by the vapor of sulfur,* and perhaps in this way it is congealed by lead, or easily by the vapor of sulfur. Moreover, it appears that quicksilver and things similar to it are the element of all fusible substances; either because all fusible things, when they are melted, are converted into it—though they are not melted until they are heated—and when they have been melted, they appear red. But lead, without a doubt, when it is melted, is quicksilver; however, it does not melt unless it is heated, and when it melts—

->AVICENNAE<-

...sulfur <note>The Latin text begins with "phur," completing the word "sulphur" from the previous page.</note> is bad, possessing a foul and weak vapor; therefore it does not solidify well. And craftsmen produce a solidification through artificial means that is almost similar, although artificial things are not formed in the same way as natural ones, nor do they possess such certain similarities. For this reason, it is believed that natural composition occurs in this way, or in a manner close to it. But art is weaker than nature and does not equal it, however much it may labor. 

Let the practitioners of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiæ"</note> know that the **species** <note>In medieval philosophy, the "species" is the essential nature or "whatness" of a thing that makes it what it is (e.g., the "gold-ness" of gold).</note> of things cannot be transmuted; but they can make things similar to them. They can tint a red substance with a lemon-yellow color so that it appears to be gold, and they can tint a white substance with whatever color they wish until it is very similar to gold or **copper** <note>original: "æri"; this term could refer to copper, bronze, or brass.</note>. They may also wipe away the impurities of lead, yet it will always remain lead, even though it may look like silver. 

Indeed, other qualities will be so excellently presented in it that men are deceived, much like those who take salt and mistake it for **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "salem armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, a salt used extensively in alchemical processes for its volatile properties.</note>. Furthermore, I do not believe it is possible for the **specific difference** <note>original: "differentia specifica"; the defining characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note> to be removed by human ingenuity, nor is it the case that one **complexion** <note>The specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature.</note> can be converted into another. This is because these sensible qualities <note>Qualities that can be perceived by the senses, such as color or smell.</note> are not the essential differences by which a species is changed; rather, they are **accidents** <note>original: "accidentia"; non-essential properties that can change without changing the identity of the substance itself.</note> and properties. 

Moreover, the essential differences of these metals are not known to us. Since the difference is unknown, how can it be known whether it has been removed or not, or how it could possibly be removed? However, the stripping away of accidents—such as vapor, color, and weight—or at least their reduction, is not impossible.

<meta>catchword: quia</meta>

<summary>Avicenna argues that alchemy can only mimic the external "accidents" of metals (like color and shine) but cannot achieve true transmutation because the essential "specific difference" of a substance is unknown to humans.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, transmutation, Avicenna, species, specific difference, accidents, gold, lead, sal ammoniac, sulfur-mercury theory</keywords>

However, this does not happen through melting alone, but rather through external factors that occur within it.

# THE INTERPRETATION OF 
# A CERTAIN EPISTLE, 
## which is circulated in the name of 
## Alexander, King of the Macedonians, 
## most sharply declaring to the wise 
## the hidden composition of the 
## Philosophers' Stone.

Alexander, treating in this Epistle the **Art of the Sun** <note>original: "arte Solis"; a traditional alchemical term for the process of making gold.</note> according to the image and likeness of the world, says briefly that you must be grounded in this demonstration; for he shows that the art is derived from the creation of man, in whom all things are present. For just as the **microcosm** <note>original: "minor mundus"; literally "lesser world," the concept that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe</note> is composed of four different virtues, so too is this art composed from the natures of the woman <note>In alchemical allegory, the "woman" or "mother" often represents the receptive, material principle or the "matrix" in which the Stone is formed.</note>: some of which we briefly recount,

### EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE

I speak not in philosophical riddles, and above all, caution must be applied in the solution of **liquefaction** <term>liquefactio: The process of turning a solid substance into a liquid state, often regarded in alchemy as a method of "freeing" the spirit from the body of the metal.</term>, so that you do not exceed the proper measure in the ascent <note>This refers to the "rising" of vapors during distillation or sublimation.</note>, because the entire **secret** <term>arcanum: A deep mystery or hidden secret of nature, often referring to a powerful medicinal or transformative substance.</term> of the alteration of all natures consists in liquefying. And know this: how a substance is changed from nature to nature, until it becomes a substance that is neither fleeing <note>original: "fugiens"; referring to volatile substances that evaporate easily</note> nor altering, but remains fixed and constant. From these things, the beginning joins the black elements together, because they are clearly discerned. And soon nature appears through nature. <note>The following phrase is underlined in ink</note>A rare [thin] state of things therefore joins the nature of fixed things to liquefaction, and it is the water which is called by the Sages the **water of wisdom** <term>aqua sapientiæ: A metaphorical term for the universal solvent or the "mercurial" water used to dissolve metals.</term>; next are the secrets which are tempered and moist. For unless you thin the natures and turn them into water, they will not be able to provide color; thus, you shall moisten the body by this watering. 

And know that **whiteness** <term>albedo: The second main stage of the Great Work, representing purification and the transition from the black "nigredo" to a silver or white state.</term> is found in the coagulation, and that these are the species of the spirit, and they improve one another. I also say to you, my son who desires to be improved, that you should not place raw and disordered species into it, but rather those that are putrefied and properly joined, both ascending and descending. I have <note>The following phrase is underlined in ink</note>without doubt discovered certain **elevated ointments** <term>vnguenta: Oily or fatty substances produced during alchemical digestion, thought to contain the concentrated essence of the work.</term> that are clear and illuminated, and I found in them hidden secrets; if you govern these well, the nature of those things which you hold hidden has appeared and shall appear clearly to you—that is, the **white earth** <term>terra alba: The purified, solid remains of the alchemical matter after it has been washed and distilled, associated with the "silver" stage of the work.</term> through clear and known silver. And know that certain bodies require solution, while others require elevation <note>sublimation or distillation</note> so that they may tint [others], and become clear and illuminated.

<summary>This page provides practical instructions on the alchemical processes of liquefaction and refinement, emphasizing the transition from a "black" state to the "white" stage of perfection (albedo). It warns the practitioner to use only "putrefied" (broken down) materials and highlights the "water of wisdom" as the essential agent of transformation.</summary>

# OF KING ALEXANDER

...all bodies may be dissolved. Know also that according to nature there are secrets hidden within them: for if the hidden nature is governed [correctly], those things will appear to you which appeared to **Hermes the Philosopher** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy and the purported author of the Emerald Tablet</note>, and it is the **white earth** <term>terra alba: A purified state of matter, often associated with the 'white stone' that allows for the transmutation of base metals into silver.</term> which is near to silver. Therefore, prepare the bodies which heal you with that white earth, so that they remain fixed and constant, and place it above so that the fire does not consume it with its flame, but liquefy them just as you would melted wax. 

And remember that this is called the **water entering again** <term>aqua intrans: A term for a recursive solvent or a liquid that is repeatedly distilled and reintroduced to a substance to break it down.</term>. Therefore, in the arts which you study, believe that there will be two hammers, one of which is owed to the **Sun** <note>original: "Soli"; symbolizing Gold in alchemical tradition</note>, and the other to the **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"; symbolizing Silver</note>. Afterwards, two orders follow, whose governance is fittingly figured by the doubt in our head <note>This likely refers to the intellectual difficulty or the dual mental application required to master the process</note>. Behold, I have numbered them, I have revealed the **celestial secret** <term>arcanum celeste: A divine or cosmic mystery that links the movements of the stars to the transformations of matter on earth.</term>, I have illuminated the difficult and hidden science, and I have confirmed the perfect way of governing this knowledge. 

I swear, therefore, that I have concealed nothing; I have not described any species with a false description, nor have I placed types in the wrong categories. Therefore, if you read and understand my letters, you will reach your goal and give thanks to God. But if someone’s composition is weak and their understanding is brief, they will not reach their goal; let them not blame their own ignorance on me, nor say that I have erred, but rather blame themselves for failing to reach their purpose.

## ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE
### *A small work metaphorically describing the secrets.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring ornate foliage and scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
THE MODEL of our science is an old man above death; in him, the natures are joined with their completion: earth, water, his fire, and air. And all these are found in **Saturn** <term>Saturnus: The alchemical name for the metal Lead, representing the cold, dark, and heavy beginning of the "Great Work."</term>. With him, the gates of the sciences are opened, as **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says, along with his first predecessors: Take the stone suspended above the sea, like an old man of white wax; above the fountain, like the boy of the **hypocistis** <note>original: "ypoquistidos"; a reference to a plant parasite (Cytinus hypocistis) used in ancient medicine, here likely symbolizing a specific stage, color, or extract in the alchemical process</note>.

Its name is "The Conqueror." With it, kill those things that are alive, and bring life back to those that have been killed; to it belong both death and life, and both this and that come from the east and the west. With this, you will possess the knowledge in which the **Arabs** <note>A reference to the medieval Islamic alchemists, such as Geber or Rhazes, whom the author suggests did not reach this specific finality</note> have faltered <note>original: "pigritauerunt"; literally "were lazy" or "shrank back," implying their efforts stopped short of this ultimate secret</note>. I have told you the truth by Him who caused the author of the stone of paradise to arise, the light of life.

In it are two opposites at once, namely fire and water: and the one gives life to the other, while the other destroys the one. Both are joined together in the **Lion** <term>leo: A common alchemical symbol for a powerful solvent or the "fixed" state of matter that resists the fire.</term>; by Him who is death and life, I have told the truth and I do not lie. Our **gum** <term>gumen: A metaphor for a resinous or sticky substance that binds the chemical components together during the process.</term> coagulates our milk, and our milk dissolves our gum. Afterward, the redness of the east shall appear, and the redness of blood. This clean stone, without any stench, is found in the highest places,

Fire and light are in the essence of clarity: and fire and light are our spark, and our glowing firebrand, and with both this and that you will find knowledge. I have spoken the truth by the one who unites all things.

Our **ladder** <note>original: "scala"; a common symbol for the successive stages of distillation or purification.</note> is our tower of **viscous earth** <note>original: "terra viscosa"; a term for the "fat" or "sticky" soil-like substance that represents the base matter before it is purified.</note>, and this viscous earth is our mud, and our **cerate** <note>original: "cerotum"; a wax-based medicinal unguent. In alchemy, it refers to the stage where the matter becomes soft and pliable like wax.</note> made from wax and tallow: and here and there is our ship in our sea full of **giants** <note>original: "gigantum"; "Giants" often represent the powerful, unruly forces of raw minerals or the "heavy" elements that must be subdued.</note>. I have opened what the ancestors have hidden. I am not envious or stingy as they were; by the one who illuminates all things, I do not lie.

The Earth is placed before your eyes, both East and West, and here and there is the narcissus with our **lily** <note>original: "lilio"; a symbol of the "White Work" or purity.</note>: and here and there with our **old man** <note>original: "sene"; the "Old Man" often represents the "First Matter" or the sulfurous principle at the beginning of the work.</note>, and our old man and our **vessel** <note>original: "vter"; literally a "womb" or "skin-bag," referring to the alchemical flask where the "birth" of the stone occurs.</note> is our body: and our body is our **Stone** sought by many, but found by few. And I have explained this out of piety, and revealed it to all by the God of nations.

->The end of the Unknown Author.<-

# MERLIN'S ALLEGORY
## Perfectly containing the deepest secret of the Philosophers' Stone. <note>original: "Lapis Philosophicus"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>

A certain **KING** <note>In alchemical allegory, the King usually represents Gold or the "Solar" principle of nature which must undergo a transformation.</note> desiring to overcome other powerful ones, prepared himself for war against them. And when he wished to mount his horse, he commanded one of his soldiers to give him to drink of the **water** <note>original: "aqua"; likely referring to the "mercurial water" or universal solvent used to dissolve solid matter in the early stages of the Great Work.</note> which he most loved. The soldier, answering him, said: "Lord, what water is that which you seek?" And the King said: "That water which I seek is water most desired by me, and it loves me above all others." And the soldier, considering this, went immediately and brought it to him. 

But the King, receiving it, drank and drank again, until all his limbs were filled, and all his veins were swollen, and then he became greatly **discolored**. <note>The King's discoloration represents the "putrefaction" or "nigredo" stage, where the material turns black or changes hue as it begins to break down.</note> This being done, his soldiers said to him: "Lord, behold the horse; mount, if it pleases you." He, answering, said: "Know that I cannot mount." The soldiers said: "Why can you not?" He answered: "Because I feel myself weighed down, and my head aches; and as it seems to me, all my **limbs are divided** <note>original: "membra mea ab inuicem diuiduntur"; this describes the chemical process of *solutio* (dissolution), where a solid substance is broken down into its constituent parts by a liquid.</note> from one another. I command you, therefore, that you place me in a bright chamber, and let it be established in a warm place, and thus...

# RACHAIDIBI, VERADIANUS, RHODIANUS, AND *Kanidis, Philosophers of the King of the Persians*

## *A Fragment of a Most Acute Dialogue Concerning the Matter of the Philosopher’s Stone.*

RACHAIDIBI, son of Zetheibida, philosopher to the King of the Persians and the Prince of the Romans, said: The seed <term>Seed: (Latin: *sperma*) In alchemical theory, this is the generative "starting material" or essence required to "grow" the Stone, much like a plant grows from a seed.</term> of the stone is cold and moist in its manifest <term>Manifest: (Latin: *in manifesto*) The outward, physical qualities of a substance that can be seen and felt.</term> state, and in its hidden <term>Hidden: (Latin: *in occulto*) The internal, essential nature or "soul" of a substance that is not immediately apparent to the senses.</term> state it is hot and dry. He says therefore: make that which is cold and moist hidden, and place that which is hot and dry in the manifest; and thus its coldness and moisture shall be hidden, so that it might never be diminished, for if it were diminished, the stone itself would be diminished. When, therefore, the coldness and moisture are hidden, act by hiding them, so that you may thus compose that heat and dryness which was in the hidden and in the manifest; and so, from the spirit, a body may be made in two stages, and it will become a mass <note>original: *globus*; literally a globe or sphere, but here referring to an embryonic cluster of matter.</note>, and blood, and flesh.

RODIANUS says: The seed is white and liquid. This liquid first forms a mass in its proper place for five days; and it receives flesh and blood, and limbs and an image, and the imaginative power from God Most High; and it comes to its birth, and shines, and arises in its own time. These two are... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

# A BRIEF TREATISE
## *OF AVICENNA.*
<note>Avicenna is the Latin name for Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath. While many alchemical texts were falsely attributed to him, they remained foundational to the European alchemical tradition.</note>

->I shall DIVIDE this<-
