In the **first chapter**, I shall speak of **Mercury** and its nature, as well as the **sulphur** <note>Alchemy often taught that all metals were composed of varying proportions of Mercury (the principle of fluidity and shine) and Sulphur (the principle of combustibility and color).</note> that it contains within itself.

In the **second**, I shall speak of the nature of **perfect bodies** <note>Referring to Gold and Silver, which were considered "perfect" because they resist fire and corrosion.</note> and their sulphur.

In the **third**, I shall speak of the **conjunction of body and spirit**, and the **dissolution** of the **stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> into **prime matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"; the base, formless substance from which all material things are created.</note>.

In the **fourth**, I shall speak of the **extraction of water from earth**.

**QUICKSILVER** <note>original: "ARGENTVM viuum" or Mercury.</note> is cold and moist <note>These are the two primary Aristotelian qualities associated with water and liquid states.</note>, and God created all minerals from it or with it: and it is airy and fugitive from fire, but when it has stood in the fire for a little while, it performs strange and wondrous works.

## *On the nature of perfect bodies, that is, of the sun & the moon, and of their sulfur.*

### *Chapter II.*

**Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"; associated with the Sun/Sol</note> is the most perfect body, the lord of stones, the King and head of all others. Neither does the earth corrupt it, nor do burning things consume it, nor is it diminished in the fire; rather, it is improved by it, because in the fire it is moistened by a certain metallic humidity, nor is it altered even by water. Its constitution <term>complexio: the specific balance of the four qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness)</term> is tempered, and its nature is perfectly balanced in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; nothing superfluous or lacking is found within it. For it is created from the most subtle and clear substance of **mercury** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver"</note>, and from a small amount of the substance of pure and clean **sulfur** <note>Alchemists believed all metals were made of Mercury and Sulfur in varying degrees of purity</note>, of a fixed redness, which clearly tints the very substance of the mercury.

Gold is held to be the body and the ferment <note>The following four words are underlined in the text</note> of the white and red Elixir <note>The "White Elixir" turned metals to Silver; the "Red Elixir" turned them to Gold</note>. In a damp place it is corrupted, and its taste is acidic; in fire it is diminished, and it is consumed by sulfurs.

Also note, that entry, submersion, connection, conjunction, complexion, composition, and mixture all mean the same thing in this art <note>the "art" refers to alchemy</note>. For nothing is submerged, joined, or connected without also being mixed. For if a substance has not been putrefied, it can neither be dissolved nor melted; and if it has not been dissolved, it will come to nothing.

Also know that in every work there are three dimensions: namely width, height, and depth. This is clearly seen in any body that is subject to our sight. For example: Our Stone <note>original: "Lapis noster," the Philosopher's Stone in development</note> in its first creation is white, and so it appears on its "face" or surface. For this reason, we call it "cold and moist," because that is its nature. Hence let us consider why our stone is called "aquatic": because it is cold and moist, its natural state is called the "manifest body" or its "height" <note>height: here used to mean the external or visible surface of the material</note>. "Width," however, is that intermediate state through which one travels to reach the "deep" state. Truly, regarding that which is in the middle between depth and height—as if between contained things or opposites—a transition through them is impossible unless one quality is destroyed. Since its "high" <note>surface</note> state is cold and moist, let one quality—namely, moisture—be destroyed through putrefaction; then the substance becomes thickened,

## *On the extraction of water from the earth.*
### *Chapter 4.*

After the material has been putrefied <note>original: "putrefacta," referring to the alchemical stage of decay or blackening</note> to produce the "body" and the "spirit," this can only be achieved in the air—that is, through sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor, then allowing it to solidify again, used to purify substances</term>.

Know then that our Stone <note>original: "lapis noster," the developing Philosopher's Stone</note> is divided into two primary parts: namely, the upper part which ascends, and the lower part which remains fixed <note>original: "fixa," meaning it does not evaporate when heated</note> at the bottom. Nevertheless, these two parts are united in their power.

And so the Philosopher <note>This refers to the famous opening of the Emerald Tablet, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "That which is below is like that which is above." This division is necessary to perform the miracles of the "one thing"—namely, the Stone. The lower part is the "earth," which is called the "nurse" and the "ferment"; the upper part is the "soul," which brings the whole stone to life and causes it to live again.

-># THE WORKS OF AVICENNA<-

Wherefore, once the celebrated separation has been performed, many miracles are achieved through the joining of the stone. It should be noted that, although for some authors our stone is not divided into four parts—specifically into the four elements during the first operation, as was mentioned above—it is nonetheless said to have four principal parts <note>The text mentions four parts but proceeds to list three: the volatile spirit, the fixed base, and the fermenting earth. The fourth is often considered the resulting "union" or the "water."</note>. These are: first, the part which ascends to the top and is not "fixed" <term>fixed: a substance that is stable when heated and does not evaporate; "non-fixed" refers to volatile spirits</term>; second, the part which remains below, which is called "fixed"; and third, the earth or ferment <note>original: "fermentum," a substance that acts like leaven to transform and "ripen" the whole chemical mixture</note>, which nourishes and leavens the entire stone, as has been said. 

Regarding that non-fixed <note>volatile</note> part, it is necessary to have a sufficient quantity of it and provide it to the stone, which must be entirely pure and without any filth, until it carries the whole stone upward by the power of the non-fixed spirit through sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term>. And this is what the Philosopher <note>This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy, quoting his "Emerald Tablet."</note> says: 

> It ascends from the earth into heaven. 

Afterward, it is necessary to treat the stone that has been thus exalted upon a marble surface, using the element extracted from the stone itself during the first operation. This element is called the "water of the stone" <note>original: "aqua lapidis"</note>. It must be processed <note>original: "affari," likely a technical variant for cooking or refining the substance</note> so many times until, through its own refinement, the stone descends once more into the earth. In this way, it receives the higher power by ascending and the lower power by descending, so that the physical body becomes spiritual by ascending, and once it is spiritual, it becomes physical again by descending. 

And thus you shall possess the glory of the clarity of this world, and all darkness, poverty, and sickness shall flee from you; for once composed in this way, it cures every illness. And this is the stone of all strength,

   The Philosophers have said that water alone, through itself, performs all things: it dissolves all things, it congeals all things, and it destroys all things without any external aid. ### *On the founding or also the pouring out upon its own earth. Chapter V.*

Therefore, pour the water upon its own earth, and mix it by grinding; immediately begin soaking it little by little, boiling <note>original: "decoquendo"</note> it weekly, and afterward gently calcining <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts and reduce it to a dry powder</term> it, until the earth drinks a fifth part of its own water. Know that the earth must be nourished, first with a small amount of its water, and afterward with more, just as one observes in the upbringing of an infant. For this reason, grind the earth many times, and soak it little by little every eight days: boil it, and afterward calcine it moderately in the fire. Let not the labor of repeating the work many times weary you, because the earth does not bear fruit without frequent irrigation <note>original: "irrigatione," used here as a metaphor for adding liquid to the dry alchemical matter</note>. Now you must know that when you have mixed the body <term>body: the solid, physical matter or "base" used in the work</term> with moisture, and the heat of the fire reaches it, the moisture turns upon the body and dissolves it. At that point, the spirit <term>spirit: the volatile, gaseous, or "living" part of the substance that easily evaporates</term> cannot escape from it, because it drinks itself into the fire. Otherwise, spirits are naturally prone to flee <note>original: "fugabiles"; referring to volatility or evaporation</note> until they are thoroughly mixed with the body; then the spirit attempts to fight against the fire and its flame. However, these parts do not come together except through proper tempering, persistence, and long labor. 

Indeed, the ancient philosophers bestowed many names upon our Stone, such as **amalgam**, **vitriol**, and **blood**—due to its red color. Among infinite other names, they even called it **iron** because of its "impossible fusion" <note>This likely refers to a state where the material becomes extremely resistant to melting or reaches a high degree of "fixity"</note>. For when this body is deprived of its moisture, it is necessary for the dry body not to flow, whereas previously, through the moisture, it was flowing and was volatile. 

By necessity, bodies are "fixed" <term>fixed: rendered stable and resistant to the heat of fire, no longer evaporating</term> through the deprivation of moisture. This process is called **calcination** <term>calcination: the reduction of a solid to a powder by intense heat</term> by the philosophers; it is also called the **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the chemical breakdown or "death" of the material, usually seen as a blackening stage</term> of the matter, or the pulverization of parts previously made solid by moisture. Through calcination, the spirits are now fixed: the soft becomes hard, the volatile becomes fixed, and thus it is changed "from nature into nature."

The *Turba* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various philosophers</note> says: *Let there be a change of complexions* <note>original: "complexionum"; in medieval science, this refers to the balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note>, namely from cold and moist to hot and dry—or, as the physicians say, from "phlegmatic" to "choleric." By the heat of the sun and by a gentle boiling <note>original: "decoctione"</note>, the spirits are coagulated. Truly, by intense and ex—

[By too] much heat the work is destroyed, as Bonellus <note>Bonellus is a figure frequently cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts</note> says. For if you kindle a strong fire before the increase of the red <note>The "Red" refers to the *Rubedo*, the final stage of the Great Work which signifies perfection</note>, it results in nothing that profits us. Indeed, all the philosophers and true practitioners assert that a light fire should be used, and they testify to this for the reasons mentioned before. For they say that we must rule the fire gently until our **sulfur** <term>sulfur: in alchemy, this is the active, masculine, and "combustible" principle that must be rendered stable or "non-combustible" through the work</term> becomes non-combustible. 

Regarding the seed, it is said: One must not reap the seeds until the time of the harvest has arrived. The philosophers called this stone of ours a **Salamander**, because just as the Salamander is nourished and lives—that is, is perfected—by fire alone, so too is our stone.

## On the method of the sublimation of the earth.
### Chapter VI.

A certain great philosopher says: "That which you seek is in the dregs." <note>original: "fecibus"; the "feces" or dregs are the solid remains left at the bottom of a vessel after distillation</note> Therefore, let the dregs be taken when they are extracted from the **alembic** <term>alembic: a specialized apparatus used for distillation, consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap</term>, and let them be ground strongly and soaked with their "own water" <note>original: "aqua sua"; this usually refers to the liquid that was previously distilled from the same material, now being recombined with the solids</note>, and let them be dried in a slow fire or in the sun; let this be done many times. For by such preparation, that smoke <note>The "smoke" refers to the volatile vapors produced during heating that eventually solidify</note> is made ready for **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance so it rises as a vapor and collects as a purified solid on the upper parts of the vessel</term>. 

Regarding this, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and the most influential figure in medieval alchemy</note> says: "Therefore, from the multiple repetition of soaking and roasting, the greater part of its wateriness is destroyed. The remainder, however, is removed through sublimation."

Therefore, let the aforementioned dregs be taken and prepared for sublimating, by administering to them first—

Indeed, no thing can come from the first to the third, except through the second, because there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through a middle state. Therefore, a perfect **yellow** <term>citrinatio: "citrination" or yellowing; the stage between the white (albedo) and red (rubedo) in the alchemical process</term> cannot be produced from black, unless it has first been white, because the yellow is composed of a little red and the purest white. Nor can white be made from yellow, unless it was first black.

Thus gold cannot be made into silver <note>This refers to the "regression" of a metal back to its base state or "prime matter" so it can be reconstructed</note> unless it has first been "corrupted" and turned black. And this is the first order, which is called the first operation, which is performed so that the purest and most subtle substance may be drawn out.

The second is solution, so that the material may be dissolved into water.

The third is putrefaction, because **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: Nothing animate was ever brought to birth, nor anything growing, except through putrefaction and transformation; thus it is necessary for putrefaction to occur, because the corruption of one thing is the generation of another <note>original: "corruptio vnius est alterius generatio"; a fundamental Aristotelian concept used by alchemists to explain how matter must "die" to its old form to be reborn as something higher</note>.

The fourth is washing <term>ablutio: the cleansing of the alchemical matter to remove "accidental" impurities</term>: for it is necessary that the putrefied and dirty thing be washed and cleansed of its corrupting impurity. And the masters have rightly said: as long as water remains upon the earth, so much more is the earth washed and waxed <term>ceration: from the Latin "ceratio," the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>, so that washing and waxing are the same thing.

The fifth is coagulation: for it is necessary that by gently cooking in our sun <note>in alchemy, "our sun" refers to the controlled heat of the furnace or a specific stage of internal heat, rather than literal sunlight</note>, the water be changed into earth, and be perfectly coagulated and dried, and turned into powder.

The sixth is calcination. Whence you should know that a calcined thing is more fit than one not calcined, and it is simply fixation <term>fixio: the process of making a volatile substance "fixed" or stable so that it no longer evaporates when exposed to fire</term>. Thus there were many philosophers who called calcination "fixation," and they spoke well, for all these stages are involved in sublimation. For certainly

<meta>catchword: if anyone (original: "fi quis")</meta>

If someone sublimes <term>sublimatio: in alchemy, this is the process of vaporizing a substance and then re-condensing it to purify it, often symbolizing the "spiritualization" of matter</term> perfectly, he accomplishes the whole work.

And you should know that this whole thing is perfected in one furnace and in one vessel <note>The phrase "one furnace, one vessel, one path" is a common alchemical maxim emphasizing that the entire transformation takes place within a single, unified system representing the universe</note>. And any intelligent person can carry out these seven dispositions. Therefore, do not be negligent in sublimation. For just as the cleansing was, so will the perfection be.

### *Now I wish to tell you what Sublimation is.*

Sublimation is the elevation of the most subtle parts from the fixed parts. The non-fixed <note>volatile</note> parts are elevated through smoke—that is, through the wind <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "wind" often refers to the volatile spirit or the air element that carries the essence of the work</note>—because, as we have said, it is necessary to take care that they do not escape; rather, they are fixed along with the fixed parts, and they remain, and they provide a swifter fusion <note>original: "fusionem," referring to the melting or merging of the substances into a single state</note>. You should understand that true sublimation is when we create a separation of the parts that are raised above from those that remain below. Indeed, we want them to come together simultaneously in their own proper nature, because in our stone—after the first purification which is completed through solution—we find nothing diminished or superfluous.

For this reason, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and the most famous figure in early alchemy; his works were the "gold standard" for medieval European practitioners</note> said: Let the stone be sublimed with it, until it eventually reaches the purity of sublimation. For he said "with it," which is to say, without any other addition or any foreign [substance]...

Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in both Islamic and Western alchemy</note> says: "For the Stone of the philosophers is a single medicine, in which the whole <term>magisterium: the 'Mastery' or the completion of the Great Work</term> consists. Afterward, apply a slow fire until the greater part is turned into powder, which happens in *30 days*.

And when the operations which we have mentioned are done, then have been completed: <term>sublimatio: sublimation</term>, <term>solutio: dissolving</term>, <term>distillatio: distillation</term>, <term>descensio: the process of making a substance sink or filter downward</term>, <term>putrefactio: the 'rotting' or blackening stage where the matter decomposes</term>, <term>ablutio: washing or cleansing</term>, <term>ceratio: softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</term>, <term>coagulatio: thickening or solidifying</term>, or <term>fixio: fixation, making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>.

And you should know that the philosophers have set down many such diverse names for operations and labors, which however in reality are nothing but one and the same; and by a single operation, everything happens simultaneously, at once, and in the same [time...]

### *On the Multiplication and Fixation of the Stone. Chapter VII.*

Now follows the joining of the powders, so that they may bear fruit, and their fruit may remain for eternity; and I will teach how to <term>fix: (fixatio) the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or escapes when heated</term> the sublimated powders, so that they can remain in the fire, and be united and mixed with metallic bodies.

For fixation is the fitting adaptation of a "fleeing" <note>original: "fugientis," referring to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur that vaporize easily</note> thing to the fire. Indeed, the reason for its invention is so that every <term>tincture: a concentrated substance used to "color" or transform base metals into gold or silver</term> and every alteration may be prepared, and changed into another nature. It is fixed in this way: Take that which has been <term>sublimated: purified by heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid</term>, and divide it among <term>cucurbits: gourd-shaped glass vessels used as the base of a still</term> or urinals, as the quantity of the matter requires. And the sign of its fixation is when the matter no longer rises into the <term>alembic: the "cap" or lid of the still that directs vapors into a cooling tube</term>. Or you could strengthen the fire greatly, and then the sign appears immediately. Or place some of the substance upon an iron plate; if it remains fixed and does not smoke away, do not repeat the process.

## *Summary of the whole.*

### A

I say, therefore, that the sum of the entire work is nothing other than this: that the stone <note>original: "lapis", the legendary Philosopher's Stone</note> known from the chapters of these books should be taken, and with diligent labor, the work of sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid as it cools</term> of the first degree should be applied to it, so that it may be cleansed of all corrupting impurity. Then, once it is dissolved, its "white" or "red" addition <note>the "white" stage refers to silver-making, and the "red" to gold-making</note> should be refined until, in the final mode of sublimation, it becomes volatile <note>original: "volatile"; able to be vaporized</note>.

Furthermore, let it be fixed by the methods of fixation <term>fixation: (fixio) a process that makes a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates</term>, until the whole substance rests calmly within the harshness of the fire. Then indeed, you should make the fixed part volatile again by using the reserved non-fixed part through the method of solution and sublimation. You must make the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved; and again the volatile, and the volatile fixed, until it flows and transforms in a certain "solar-making" <note>original: "solifico", meaning gold-making</note> and "lunar-making" <note>original: "lunifico", meaning silver-making</note> completion. And in this way is worked the most precious secret <term>arcanum: a deep mystery or "holy grail" of alchemical knowledge</term>, more precious than any price in the world, and the

O pious father, may God increase in you the spirit of understanding, so that you may weigh in your mind what I am about to say. For the elements are not generated except from their own **sperm**, and the sperm is **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for mercury, which alchemists believed was the base "seed" of all metals</term>. Just as it is apparent in the generation of man, in which there is no mingling of anything except through sperm, and in plants [it is not done] except by seed, regarding their generation and growth. 

Others, looking [at the matter] more subtly, sublimate <term>sublimatio: the process of vaporizing a solid to purify it</term> **Mercury**, and fix <note>make a volatile substance solid or resistant to fire</note> it, and join it with bodies, and yet they find nothing. The cause of their error is this: For the seed cannot be transformed, neither as it is now nor as it was before, nor does it profit anything unless it is cast into the woman’s **womb** <note>original: "matricem," referring here to the specialized alchemical vessel where the "gestation" of the work takes place</note>. 

Thus Mechardus the Philosopher says: "Unless the stone is cast into the woman’s womb, so that she may nourish it, it does not profit." O my father, thus you have, according to your desire, the description of the **philosopher’s stone**.

->Praise be to God.<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 489 regarding the creation of the physical world. # THE RESONANCE
<page-num>490</page-num>

...[fire], it desires its own perfection all the more, and it is perfected as one with another because of the harmony of its properties with its **fifth instrument**, which shares in the celestial cause. Furthermore, there is also a desire for the perfection of nature—namely, the cycle of birth leading to decay, and decay leading back to birth. This occurs because its instinct or "appetite" does not come directly from the Creator of nature. If it did, the object would be made by the Creator alone and not by a created being, and thus it would be perfect and eternal without any destruction. 

Therefore, when this instinct comes from nature, nature herself cannot make that thing perfect unless it is completed through divine intellectual science—just as human nature is set right by divine intelligence. Thus, through the **mastery of our work** <note>original: *magisterium operis*; the alchemical Great Work</note>, one can understand the nature of the first elements as they were primordially created following the division of the third substance. 

Do not assume that their substance is the simple **fifth element** <note>original: *elementum quintum*; the quintessence</note>. <margin>The Sun. I, heating the earth, <unclear>wear it down</unclear>. And it speaks of the distance and boundary of the sun; the moon acts as a mediator. Thus, in our art, the tincture is remote because of density and thickness; the moon refines it. Hermes, Aristotle: the moon is the mother. The Letter of the Sun to the Moon. In [my] sister.</margin>
The sun does not warm the earth, nor does it impress its power upon the earth except through the mediation of the moon, which, among the other stars, is most receptive to the light and heat of the sun, acting as a medium <note>In medieval science, a "medium" is a middle substance or agent through which an effect is transmitted from one thing to another.</note> between the sun and the earth. Therefore, as the philosophers say, there are two obstacles why one body does not impress its power upon another: namely, remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is there between the sun and the earth, because the sun is far distant from the earth, and because the moon mediates there.

So also in our alchemical art, the sun <note>original: *sol*; refers here to philosophical gold</note> does not perfect the tincture alone except by the mediation of the moon <note>original: *luna*; refers here to philosophical silver</note>, because it is remotely distant, since it has not yet reached that subtlety <note>In alchemy, "subtlety" refers to the refinement of matter until it is fine enough to penetrate and transform other substances.</note> required for it to tinge <note>To "tinge" is the alchemical process of permanently changing the color and nature of a base metal into gold.</note>; and also because of those mediums, namely, density and thickness. Therefore, the moon is necessarily required there, so that she may refine the sun itself, making it rare and volatile, and separate its impurity. Since she has more need of his light and nature than the other planets—that is, the metals <note>The text explicitly links the seven planets of ancient astronomy with the seven metals of alchemy.</note>.

Therefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the *Emerald Tablet* is attributed.</note> and Aristotle say in *On Plants* <note>original: *de Plantis*; a work often attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages, though now thought to be by Nicolaus of Damascus.</note>: "The Sun is its father, the Moon is its mother." <note>This is a famous quote from the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Western alchemy.</note> Therefore, the moon is the mother and the field in which the solar seed must be sown; and thus we need nothing else from which our stone and our alchemy may be made, than the sun and the moon. Hence, in the *Letter of the Sun to the Moon*, in the solar year when the moon begins to be joined with the sun in thinness and to be illuminated by him, the sun first says: "In my sister the moon, the degree of your wisdom grows, and not with any other of my servants."

The **first matter** <note>original: "Prima materia"</note> of all things is found within each of them, in the form of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"; here referring to the philosophical principle of fluidity and transformation rather than common quicksilver</note>: which matter is called the generative genus, a real being, the material limit of nature, in which nature takes its material principles in the act of generation, since it is the first subject in nature. For then **species** <term>species: the essential, defining form of a substance (e.g., "Goldness")</term> are changed into a different form than they were before; yet, it is not actually the species themselves that change, but the **individuals** belonging to those species. This is because the individuals themselves are the objects of sensible actions <note>i.e., they can be touched, heated, or broken</note>, due to the fact that they are perishable among themselves.

Species, however, since they are universal, are not subject to sensible actions, and therefore they are not perishable among themselves. The species of silver, which is **silverness** <note>original: "argenteitas"</note>, does not change into the species of gold, which is **goldness** <note>original: "aureitas"</note>, nor vice versa. This is because true species cannot be changed; however, the individuals of those species can indeed be reduced back into their first matter. 

For when the form of a thing has been destroyed and dissolved into the first matter, then a new form is necessarily introduced, because **the destruction of one is the generation of another** <note>original: "corruptio vnius eſt generatio alterius"; a fundamental Alchemical and Aristotelian principle that matter is never lost, only changed</note>. But because matter cannot be destroyed in such a way that it does not remain under some form, once one form of the metals is destroyed, another is immediately introduced—specifically through the **transmutation** of Mercury into sulfur, for our intended operation. Furthermore, every individual multiplies the form of its own species, and not that of another, as **Aristotle** and **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lully</note> say. Fur-

### The beginning of the Work follows.

There are four regimens or stages <term>regimina</term> <note>specific procedures or "rules" of laboratory practice</note> of this art: The first stage of the regimen is performed by **calcining** <note>original: "calcinando"; the process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a powder or ash</note>, that is, the body must first be calcined. The second by **dissolving** <note>original: "soluendo"</note>, because it must be dissolved into liquid. The third by **distilling** <note>original: "distillando"</note>, because it must be distilled or **sublimated** <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note>. The fourth by **congealing** <note>original: "congelando"</note> with a gentle fire. And in these four regimens and stages consists the right and true preparation. Therefore, the body and the spirit of **Mercury** <note>original: "spiritus Mercurij"</note> are necessary to perform the miracles of this thing, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in Arabic and European alchemy</note> says.

And for this art only two things are required, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the hermetic tradition</note> says. Confidence consists in two things, to which a third is joined. And he says: *I have seen three faces—that is, three species—in one father, that is, the lineage.* For Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says that three species suffice for the entire mastery: namely, **white smoke** <note>original: "fumus albus"</note>, which is the **fifth essence** <term>vis quinta</term> <note>the quintessence; the purest, most spiritual element beyond the four physical elements</note>, namely the **celestial water**; and the **green lion** <term>leo viridis</term> <note>often a symbol for vitriol or a raw, acidic mineral substance used as a solvent</note>; and the **copper of Hermes** <note>original: "æs Hermetis"</note>, from which and with which they prepare the work itself in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.

# ->THE TRUMPETS<-
<note>original: "B V C C I N Æ"; plural of 'buccina,' a curved trumpet or war-horn. This is the title of the section continuing from the previous page's "Clangor" (The Trumpet-Call).</note>

To tinge <term>tinge</term> <note>original: "Tingere"; in alchemy, to "tinge" is to permanently change the color and quality of a metal, essentially dyeing its very soul</note> is to transform that which is tinged into its own nature by the act of tinging, and to remain with it without any separation, as in the nature of the fixer, the tinging agent, and the tinged subject.

The Stone <term>Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis"; the Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note> is a body composed of the **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence</term> <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the quintessence, or the most refined and spiritualized state of matter</note> of metals. Oil <term>Oil</term> <note>original: "Oleum"; not common oil, but the "radical moisture" or essential liquid extract of a metal</note> is the sliminess of all metals floating upon the menstruum <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstruum"; a powerful solvent used to dissolve solids into their primary liquid state</note> after their dissolution. Moreover, it is necessary that bodies be converted into oil, because if they are not converted, they will remain solid within themselves, and what we seek will not happen; this would result in the loss of all the principles of this art.

The solvent <term>menstruum</term> is that by which the bodies of metals are dissolved by a natural dissolution, and their spirits are led from potential to actualization. According to this definition, it is shown that the dissolution of metals must not be done except with the aforementioned principle; if it were done otherwise, nothing would be achieved in effect.

This is the strength of the entire mastery <note>original: "magisterij"; the "Mastery" or Great Work of alchemy</note>.

Likewise, Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of alchemy and medicine</note> says that the white and the red <note>referring to the *albedo* and *rubedo*, the white and red stages of the Great Work</note> proceed from a single root; they sprout without any body of another kind intervening—that is, from the Sun <note>original: "sole"; in alchemical shorthand, the Sun represents Gold</note>. And because of this, the wise say: "Our bronze <term>bronze</term> <note>original: "æs"; here referring to the base material of the work, not necessarily the common alloy</note>, like a human being, possesses a spirit, a body, and a soul." ...beyond what they said: there are three, and these three are one, and in the one are three. **Spirit**, **body**, and **soul** are one, and all things are from the one. And this is the **preparation**, which they call **conversion** and **division**, because it is turned from one thing into another. This is just as human seed is converted within the womb <note>original: "matrice"; the matrix or womb</note> in a natural preparation, from one thing to another, until a perfect human is formed from it, from which was its **root** and **beginning**.

Neither does it change from this, nor depart from its root and its division from thing to thing, without the entry of another thing upon it: except for the **menstrual blood** <note>original: "sanguis menstruorum"; in alchemy, this refers to the "menstruum," a solvent or catalyst that "nourishes" the metallic seed in the vessel</note> from which the seed was made—that is, from a blood similar to it—and in that blood it finds its growth. In a similar way, the **egg**, without anything else entering it, is converted from one state to another, and is divided from thing to thing, and finally becomes a flying chick, just like the other from which it had its root and beginning. Likewise, all things born of the earth rot and are changed, and **decay** <note>original: "corruptio"; the alchemical stage of putrefaction where matter breaks down to be reborn</note> enters into them; then they sprout and are increased, just like the growths from which they had their root and beginning.

And for this reason, **minerals** are not nourished in a way that they depart from their root; instead, each thing returns to that which it was, nor is it converted from this into anything else. He who says otherwise speaks falsely. This, then, is the **conversion** and **division** which the wise desire.

Likewise, the **sperm of the philosophers** <note>the "seed" of the Philosopher's Stone, often equated with a highly purified form of Mercury</note> is **living water**...

...[water], but the earth is an imperfect body. This earth is deservedly called the **matrix** <term>matrix: a Latin term for womb or breeding ground</term>, because it is the mother of all elements. Likewise, the whole benefit of this art lies in the **Sun** <note>representing gold</note> and **Mercury**. Indeed, a small amount of such a color infused into white—that is, into the **Moon** <note>representing silver</note>—converts a great quantity of white into a lemon-yellow color.

The preparation of these things from beginning to end is the honored **fixed water** <term>fixed water: a liquid that has been stabilized so it no longer evaporates under heat</term>: for that water manifests the tincture during **projection** <term>projection: the final stage of alchemy where the "stone" or powder is cast upon a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver</term>, and it is the mediator between opposites, and it is itself the beginning, the middle, and the end. Whoever understands these things grasps wisdom.

And note that whatever is not good in an **imperfect body** is perfected by that which is good in a **perfect body**: because a perfect body, remaining in its denseness <note>original: "grossitie"; thickness or material coarseness</note>, can have very little power to separate the **sulphurous earth** from an imperfect mixture, and to convert that imperfect mixture into its own perfect nature. It is necessary, therefore, for the perfect body to be **subtilized** <term>subtilized: refined, thinned, or made more spiritual and volatile through alchemical processes</term> before it can possess such power.

<header>THE CLANGOR</header>
<note>original: *CLANGOR*; part of the title *Clangor Buccinae* (The Blast of the Trumpet).</note>

...into spirit, and makes the living from the dead, and effects the marriage between the man and the woman. <note>original: *matrimonium inter virum & mulierem*; a common alchemical metaphor for the union of opposites, such as sulfur and mercury or fixed and volatile substances.</note> Indeed, it performs the entire benefit of the art.

And note that **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*; the metal mercury, regarded by alchemists as a primary "spirit" or life-force of all metals</term> or the **spirit** is twofold: namely, **preparing** and **tinting**.

The **preparing spirit** dissolves the body and cleanses it from corrupting causes, and it extracts the second spirit existing in the body, which is the **tinting** spirit. It leads the bodies back to itself through dissolution, and it softens their hardness. It illuminates the bodies, raising and exalting them by segregating and removing their darkness and impurity from the purest parts. It returns them to a sublime nature, breathes life into them, and refines them until it makes what was solid into something spiritual. These are the benefits and effects of the spirit, or quicksilver, which prepares the body and extracts from it the tinting spirit.

This spirit, however—that is, the quicksilver—is at first coarse, impure, and **fugitive** <note>original: *fugitivus*; meaning it evaporates or "flees" easily when exposed to heat</note>, because of the **sulfur** it encountered and was mixed with in the passages of the earth. But by the operation of the art—which is performed through **distillation** and **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, used here to purify the mercury</term>—it is renewed, cleansed, purified, cooked down, thickened, and **coagulated** by means of white and red sulfur.

And this preparing spirit is itself twofold. The first is a dry, non-viscous vapor of great **acidity** <note>original: *acedinis multæ*; likely referring to a sharp, reactive chemical property or "sharpness" rather than just pH</note>, exceedingly subtle, fleeing the face of fire, and having a great power of penetrating and easily resolving mineral bodies. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the two types of alchemical spirits. <page-num>525</page-num>

<header>->THE TRUMPETS<-</header>
<note>original: *BUCCINÆ*; part of the title *Clangor Buccinae* (The Blast of the Trumpet).</note>

Mercury is called by many different names used interchangeably, but Mercury is a spirit. Therefore, in the final terminology of logic, it is called the **dry spirit**. <note>original: *spiritus siccus*; alchemists often used "dry" to describe substances that were powdered or did not wet the hands, even if they behaved like liquids.</note> It is necessary for such a spirit to be shut away in a well-sealed **flask** <term>flask: *ampulla*; a glass vessel used for heating substances in a laboratory</term>, and this is according to the intention of **Albert**. <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous medieval scholar and theologian credited with many alchemical works.</note> For this spirit is generated from **astringent substances** <note>original: *rebus ponticis*; literally "Pontic things," referring to sharp, acidic, or sour substances like alum or vitriol</note>, and he himself calls it the **fiery dry humidity**.

Another preparing spirit is humid in its vapor, not **oily**, but **viscous**; it possesses the greatest acidity and is moderately refined. It easily flees the sharpness of fire, vanishing into it, yet it possesses the power of dissolving bodies and spirits, being essentially water in its own nature. This is also the view of Albert and many others, though they describe it under the guise of other substances. Such a spirit is also called **Mercury** by a shared name, and this is done through comparison and metaphorical speech.

For Mercury, as the philosophers say, has the greatest power of altering and penetrating bodies; it does not rest on a flat surface and does not wait for the test of fire. <note>original: *ignis examen*; the "examination" or "trial" of fire refers to how a substance reacts to high heat—Mercury typically evaporates or "flees" rather than melting.</note> The same is true for these two spirits, and for that reason, both are called "Mercuries." Use this to understand the sayings of the Philosophers, and your understanding will be easy here and elsewhere; you will see that the philosophers do not contradict one another, as many have thought.

Thus, it should be noted that **oily** is one thing, and **viscous** is another. For the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> is generated from a viscous humidity, but **metals** are generated from an oily humidity.

<summary>This page distinguishes between the "dry spirit" and the "viscous spirit," both of which are referred to as Mercury by alchemists. It clarifies that the Philosopher's Stone is derived from viscous substances, while common metals come from oily ones.</summary>

But the tinting spirit is **Philosophical Mercury** with its red **or white** sulfur, naturally mixed together within the ore itself and in the depths of the earth, moderately prepared and left to the judgment of the craftsman until its perfect completion. Another quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> is the permanent tincture, which is extracted from perfect bodies <note>original: *corporibus perfectis*; in alchemy, these are typically gold and silver</note> through dissolution, distillation, sublimation, and refinement. And indeed, the operation of these two parts consists, or is entirely based, in dissolving and coagulating. To dissolve is to change the body into the nature of the spirit

Assiduus the philosopher <note>Assiduus may refer to a specific "diligent" philosopher or is a corruption of a name like Adastus.</note> says: Fire is coagulated and becomes air, air indeed is coagulated and becomes water, and water indeed is coagulated and becomes earth.

Behold, the enemies <note>The "enemies" are the opposing elements (e.g., fire and water) which naturally repel each other.</note> have met in one nature; when they are driven together—that is, coagulated—they become friends; and when they are thinned out, they become enemies, namely in the separation of the elements. But if you reverse this rule, through the opposite you turn the body into a spirit. Therefore, you must thin out the whole in the earth—that is, to spiritualize the earth <note>original: *terram spirituare*; to make the solid earth-like matter volatile or subtle.</note>, which is to make it a **tinting agent** <note>original: *tingentem*; a substance capable of projecting its color and nature onto other metals.</note>—and then you have completed the whole.

Whence Plato says: Know, all you crowds, that all thickness rests in the earth. For the thick part of fire falls into air, and the thick part of fire and air into water, and the dense part which is joined together from the thickness of fire, air, and water, falls into the earth.

Gratianus says regarding how the body becomes spirit: *The earth is dissolved into water*, water into air, and air into fire, and this is the way by which the body becomes spirit.

Likewise, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: Join the male with the female in their own moisture, because without male and female no offspring is generated. 

Likewise another says: When the **King** <note>The King often symbolizes the "fixed" red sulfur or the gold-state of the matter.</note> saw the water freezing itself, he was certain that the matter was true, just as the sought-after will of **sulfur** with **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, masculine principle (fire/soul), and Mercury represents the passive, feminine principle (moisture/spirit).</note> assigns; understand nothing else. It follows: then let it be done in a large glass vessel, and place it in...

Because there are only two formal elements in our **stone** <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the ultimate goal of the work.</note>, namely water and earth, although virtually all four elements are within it. And where it is said that our stone is made from the four elements, this is not to be understood literally—that it is earth, nor that it is water, nor air, nor fire—but rather it is only one nature, which contains within itself the nature and properties of all the elements.

Furthermore, the whole **mastery** <term>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process or the "Great Work."</term> is this: to divide the elements from the metals, and to purify them, and to divide the **sulfur of nature** <term>sulphur naturæ; the active, masculine, or combustible principle believed to be hidden within matter.</term> from the metals. Sometimes, however, it is fixed in a greater or lesser time, according to the industry <note>meaning the skill or diligence</note> of the worker, and due to the greater or lesser quantity of the **coloring materials** <term>pigmentalium: substances used to provide the "tincture" or color change in the alchemical process.</term>.

...[decoc]tion, in which the body is fixed and turned into spirit. And so there are in total seven decoctions, namely four before the **vivification** <term>vivification: the stage where the "dead" matter is brought back to life, often identified with fermentation.</term> (that is, the fermentation) and afterwards three, which are designated by seven roastings, as the philosopher also says. Our **bronze** <note>original: *æs*; likely referring to the base metallic matter or "the subject" of the work.</note> has a dropsical body, just like Naaman the Syrian was a leper <note>Naaman was a biblical commander healed of leprosy by washing in the Jordan River seven times (2 Kings 5); alchemists used this as a metaphor for the seven stages of purifying base metal into gold.</note>, for which reason it seeks the bath of rebirth seven times in the Jordan, so that it may be cleansed from its innate passions and corruptions. Then you possess **sulphur** and **arsenic** that does not burn, which alchemists can use, and with it they create perfect silver.

Gratianus says: Therefore, whiten the **Laton** <term>Laton: a term for an impure, brass-like alloy that represents the matter in a transitional state; it must be "whitened" to become silver and "reddened" to become gold.</term>, that is, the bronze with **Mercury**, because Laton is an imperfect, yellow-colored body composed of the **sun** [gold] and the **moon** [silver]. When you have whitened this, and through long-lasting decoction brought it back to its original yellow color, you again have Laton that is malleable in the same way and in the quantity you desire; then you have entered through the gate, and you have the beginning of the art. And then calcine, dissolve, and **incerate** <term>incerate: to process a substance until it has a soft, wax-like consistency, making it ready for fusion.</term>, and so proceed through the middle stages; and if you make the resuscitated matter capable of penetration, then you have reached the end. 

For Rasis, Morienus, and Assiduus say: Because when the earth has been whitened and made bright, it becomes fixed due to the **fixation of the moon** [silver], but not yet fixed by the **fixation of the sun** [gold], and therefore it tints things into silver. And afterwards in the work there is the **leap of the moon** <note>original: *saltus lunae*; likely referring to a sudden sublimation or chemical transition.</note>, that is, the sublimation of the lunar moisture and the circle of the sun: Because after the extraction—

When you now have the dried earth, then work in glass, and place upon it a sixth or seventh part of Mercury, so that it may be dissolved: therefore, weigh it first, and seal the glass with the **Seal of Hermes** <term>sigillo Hermetis: an airtight seal made by melting the glass neck of a flask; the origin of the modern "hermetically sealed."</term> so that the **flower** <note>original: *flos*; refers to the volatile spirit or the most subtle part of the substance that rises when heated.</note> does not escape. Dry it over a slow heat in ashes and congeal it, and repeat this dissolution and coagulation four times. When the dissolution and coagulation of this earth of ours has been completed for the fourth time, this earth will remain **fixed** <term>fixed: a substance that is no longer volatile and can endure the fire without evaporating.</term> and shining, black when broken; and when cast upon metallic bodies, it alters their color, but not that of Mercury. And however many more times this earth is dissolved and congealed, it will be the more penetrating and subtle in its nature, as was also said above, tending even more toward whiteness in those four dissolutions...

...[with purifications] and congealings. But when that decoction <term>decoction: a process of heating or boiling a substance in liquid to extract its essence or alter its state.</term> which is called the first is complete, you must turn to the others in this manner.

   Know the weight of the entire congealed material, just as you first determined by your own judgment, and place it in a glass vessel. Add over it a fourth part of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurij*</note> so that it may be dissolved, and seal the glass as described above with the **Seal of Hermes** <term>Seal of Hermes: a "hermetic" seal made by melting the glass neck of a flask shut to make it completely airtight.</term>. Dry and congeal it over heat, and it will become a single mass of a different color than the first, somewhat black and clear. This arrangement of **whitening** <term>dealbatio: also known as the *albedo*, this is the second major stage of the alchemical Great Work, following the blackness of the *nigredo*.</term> continues after the soaking <term>imbibition: the process of a solid "drinking" or absorbing a liquid.</term> of its water, drying, dissolution, and congealing, until it becomes a white mass of perfect whiteness. It must endure in the fire, melting, flowing, and congealing Mercury, perfectly retaining it, and transmuting any imperfect metallic body into a true, unified one.

   And if you wish to volatilize or soak your prepared **Elixir** <term>Elixir: the transmuting agent or Philosopher's Stone, often described as a medicine for metals.</term> a second, third, or fourth time, this should be done with a fourth part of the mercury of the elixir. However, if you place a greater weight of that water upon the body itself than a fourth part—provided it is not submerged—it will be better; it will whiten the body, and it will be more subtle, more penetrating, and will convert with greater weight.

   Likewise, when a thing is soaked in corruption, it cannot tolerate the fire, nor can the fire...

<margin>See.</margin>
Note that the beginning of the entire work is **whitening** <term>whitening: *dealbatio*, the stage where the matter is purified to a brilliant white state.</term>, which **redness** <term>redness: *rubor*, the final stage (rubedo) of the alchemical process signifying the perfection of the Stone.</term> follows, and then the perfection of the work. After this, however, through the "vinegar" <note>original: *acetum*, likely referring to the "philosophical vinegar" or the acidic solvent used to break down the matter</note> by the will of God, the entire perfection occurs, which is to **dissolve and to coagulate** <note>original: *soluere & coagulare*, the fundamental alchemical axiom of breaking down and rebuilding substance</note>. And concerning that whitened earth, **Morienus** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist known for his dialogue with King Khalid.</note> says: "Because you can do nothing with it if it is not fermented." And because without **leaven** <term>leaven: *fermentum*, a substance added to the alchemical "paste" to trigger a transformation, analogous to yeast in bread.</term> no **tincture** <term>tincture: the power of the Stone to change the color and nature of base metals into gold or silver.</term> becomes perfect, as the Philosophers say—just as good bread is not made from unfermented dough—so it is in our Stone. For the leaven is like the **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note>, which grants life to the imperfect, dead body by means of the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note>, that is, **Mercury**. For **Aristotle** <note>Alchemical texts often attributed works to Aristotle that were actually written by later medieval authors.</note> says, "Nothing is completed except with a thinned leaven, like a spirit." *Verse:* "For a good dough, use water, and also leaven;" in a similar way, do so in our Stone. These three you will find consistent with the sayings of the philosophers. And the leaven is nothing other than **Sol** <term>Sol: "the Sun," representing Philosophical Gold.</term> for both the white and the red **Elixir**, and **Luna** <term>Luna: "the Moon," representing Philosophical Silver.</term> only for the white Elixir; specifically, the gold or silver of the philosophers, and not the common gold or silver of nature. Wherefore the leaven of gold is nothing but its own **sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur*, here referring to the active, "combustible" principle within the metal</note> which turns the white into silver, because that which is not naturally fixed <note>original: *fixum*, meaning resistant to the fire</note>, and never was, never fixes anything else.

Thus says **Raymond**. <note>Refers to Raymond Lull, a famous 13th-century polymath and reputed alchemist.</note>

Note that the **white ferment** is made thus: Feed <insert>†</insert> one part of the purest **Moon** <term>Moon: *Luna*, the alchemical name for silver.</term>—either finely filed or beaten into thin leaves—with double its weight of very clean, white **Mercury** <term>Mercury: *Mercurius*, or quicksilver.</term>. Grind them together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury drinks up the filings and it becomes like **butter**, so that nothing of the filings can be found. Then wash this ferment vigorously with strong vinegar and well-prepared common salt until the vinegar comes out clear and quite pure; then wash away the salt with fresh water and dry it over a fire. After this, add one part of **white sulfur** to it, grinding the whole together until it all returns as if into one body. Then **wax** it <note>original: *incera*, a process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency, often by adding liquid.</note> with one part of water, and send it to be **sublimated** <term>sublimated: *sublimandum*, the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and solidifies again, used for purification.</term>, etc.

In the same way, the **red ferment** is made with the purest Sun, as described above, although **Pandolphus** says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various sages.</note> that no staining poison <note>original: *venenum tigens*, "staining poison," a common alchemical term for the potent Tincture or Elixir that transforms metals.</note> is generated without the Sun and its **shadow** <note>The "shadow of the sun" often refers to the Moon or the base metallic state of gold during the process.</note>, which many others also maintain. This is because no other ferment is made for either the white or the red tincture except the Sun. **Aristotle** says: White and red...

Likewise, the **Rosary** <note>original: *Rosarius*; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a seminal 16th-century alchemical florilegium.</note> and **Peter of Zalento** say: The **ferment** <term>ferment: *fermentum*, a substance (often likened to yeast) added to the alchemical base to trigger the final transformation or "ripening" of the metal.</term>, which is the joining medium, if it is added at the beginning or in the middle, the work is completed more quickly, nor does it require repetition. <margin>☛ However, they do not say these things by way of denial.</margin> **Arnold** <note>original: *Arnoldus*; referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says: *When you wish to ferment the aforementioned medicine, then dissolve it in the specified distilled liquid, as was said above, until it is watery like **Mercury**;* <term>Mercury: *Mercurius*, or quicksilver, used here to describe a liquid, metallic state.</term> then place it in a vessel over the fire throughout the whole regimen, until the colors appear, as in the first regimen, until you have the **Elixir** as before, *fusible and staining.* And then the effect of that elixir is doubled in its fermentation, quantity, and **projection** <term>projection: *proiectio*, the final act of alchemy where the "philosopher's stone" or elixir is cast upon molten base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</term>, etc. Since in every solution and fixation it gains for itself ten times in multiplication, therefore the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, stained, and melted, *the better and more powerfully it operates.*

Also, note this concerning the ferment: Nothing is made from the perfect, because it is already perfected, just as this matter or artifice completes it. We have an example: bread that is leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its final end, nor can you leaven it any further. So it is with **gold**: pure gold has been brought through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body,

Likewise **Barsen** <note>likely "Barsen," a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early Latin alchemical text.</note> says: I command them to whiten the **copper** <note>original: *æs*; in alchemical texts, this term often refers to the "base" or "prime" matter of the work rather than literal metallic copper.</note> with white water, with which they make the red copper, namely **our copper**. Therefore it is necessary that it first becomes white before it becomes red: because there is no transition from one extreme to another extreme, from one contrary to another contrary, except through a mediating middle ground; that is, there is no transition from blackness into yellow or red, unless whiteness is the intermediary, because yellowness is caused by the highest or most intense white, and a little clear red essentially. Wherefore nature shows that **yellowing** <term>citrinatio: the "yellowing" or *citrinitas* phase that traditionally occurs between the white (*albedo*) and red (*rubedo*) stages of the Great Work.</term> is perfect and complete digestion.

Nor conversely can there be a transition from yellow to white, until the compound is turned into black. Nor can gold be made into indivisible silver, unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can a better thing be made from a worse one, except through the corruption of itself, because the **generation of one is the corruption of the other** <note>A core Aristotelian principle: for a new form to emerge, the previous form must be broken down.</note>. And this is done with the addition of the tinting substance, which is known to nature, and is perfected. And then the **leaven** <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance added to the work to "catalyze" or stabilize the final transformation, similar to how yeast affects dough.</note> is applied.

The spirit dries out the body, and is itself dried by the body—namely, being perfectly purged of its **phlegm** <note>original: *flegmate*; refers to the watery, inactive, or "crude" moisture that must be removed from the matter.</note>.

### How white and red sulfur may be perfected into the perfect Elixir.

Therefore, take the aforementioned **white sulfur** and **fix** <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable in fire so that it no longer evaporates or escapes as a gas.</term> it upon its own white, fixed, and cleansed body—that is, upon **silver**. Therefore, you must work prudently and discreetly, because neither the **sun** <note>gold</note> nor the **moon** <note>silver</note> can exist without **leaven** <term>Fermentum (ferment or leaven): a substance, like yeast in bread, added to the alchemical mix to catalyze the transformation and "multiply" the noble qualities of the metal.</term>. And also for this reason, so that what you are composing may become the perfect **Elixir**. When, however, the sulfur has been joined to its purified body, it does not stop acting upon it, penetrating it totally until it converts the whole into its own nature. And therefore...

### Method of Fixing

Prepare the **ferment** <term>Fermentum: A substance that acts like yeast, spreading its specific qualities (like the color of gold) through a larger mass of material.</term>, which is to say, the body before fermentation, so that it is dissolved and **calcined** <term>Calcinatum: Reduced to a fine powder through high heat.</term>. Specifically, the body should be dissolved and calcined by means of **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; common mercury.</note>, so that the quicksilver is then separated and removed from it, leaving behind the purest powder or ash. If you do not prepare the ferment in this way, it will be of no value. 

Similarly, prepare **non-burning sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur non urens*; a specialized alchemical sulfur believed to provide color and stability without being consumed by fire.</note> from the ash through sublimation, so that it is "simple" and "living." If you do not mix this into the **Elixir**, the metal body upon which you "project" or cast the sulfur will not take on the desired color. Furthermore, if you do not cleanse the body you intend to mix into the Elixir, that body will neither be able to direct the spirit nor retain it. If you fail to sublimate this sulfur before adding it to the Elixir, the resulting gold and silver will be very dark and dull.

If you do not cleanse the **spirit** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or ammonia that can evaporate or "flee" the fire.</note>, it will not be able to endure the heat of the fire, because an impure spirit cannot be joined to a body **at the most fundamental level** <note>original: *per minima*; a philosophical term meaning down to the smallest possible particles.</note>. You must also be extremely careful to ensure the Elixir is of a consistency between hard and soft. Unless you master this, the resulting gold and silver will not be workable—that is, they will not be capable of being hammered into sheets or melted for casting. The "medicine" must be of a more subtle and liquid substance than the metals it is cast upon, yet it must possess greater **fixation** <term>Fixio: The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire.</term> and "retention" than quicksilver naturally possesses. For **Euclid** <note>Though famous for geometry, several medieval alchemical works were attributed to Euclid to lend them authority.</note> says:

# T H E  T R U M P E T  B L A S T <note>original: *CLANGOR*; referring to the title *Clangor Buccinae*, a famous alchemical treatise.</note>

Let all investigators of this art know that the **Elixir** <term>Elixir: In alchemy, the refined substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver.</term>, however much it may be prepared or refined, is entirely nothing unless, after its preparation, it is joined with the true **ferment** <term>Ferment: An agent, often compared to yeast in bread-making, that "leavens" the alchemical matter and gives it the power to transform other substances.</term>.

->*Note regarding the ferment.*<-

It should be noted that when the Elixir is joined with **bodies** <note>original: *corporibus*; referring to the physical metals being acted upon.</note>, it must be joined through the smallest parts <note>original: *per minima*; referring to the theory of "minima naturalia," where substances must be broken down to their most fundamental particles to truly bond.</note>, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and bishop recognized as one of the greatest medieval authorities on alchemy and natural philosophy.</note> says. A powerful and useful combination can never be achieved with solid things unless they are first dissolved into waters, and then mixed with one another; then, in warm places by the action of natural heat—or a heat proportional to it—they connect themselves vaporously over a suitable period of time. 

Because it is necessary first to dissolve the Elixir, and afterward to prepare and dissolve the body just like the Elixir; then indeed, one must take and join the solutions: specifically, **three parts of the Elixir, and one part of the bodies** mentioned above. Afterward, it is necessary to congeal this whole mixture and dissolve it again, and congeal it once more, and so repeat the process until the whole has become one, without any separation. All of this is completed through the benefit of our **Mercurial water** <term>Mercurial water: A specialized alchemical solvent, not common mercury, used to break down substances into their primary matter.</term>; for it is with this water that the Elixir is dissolved and prepared, and with it the bodies are dissolved and prepared. For this water is that which cleanses, joins, dissolves, whitens <note>original: *dealbans*; referring to the *Albedo* or white stage of the Great Work.</note>, and makes red <note>original: *rubeum faciens*; referring to the *Rubedo* or final red stage.</note>.

### On the multiplication or augmentation of the stone.

Note first what augmentation is. Therefore, augmentation is the addition of quantity to that which already exists. And augmentation in quality and goodness is to dissolve and congeal the **tincture** <term>Tincture: In alchemy, this is the refined "essence" or "medicine" capable of transforming base metals or healing the body.</term> itself; that is, to soak it with our **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio nostro*; alchemists used this term to distinguish their "philosophical" mercury from common quicksilver.</note> and dry it.

Or it may be done thus: Take one part of the prepared tincture and dissolve it in three parts of our Mercury; then put it in a vessel and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes, throughout, just as was expressed above, until it is dried out and becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and soak it again, and dry it as above; and the more times you do this, the more parts you will gain, and it will tint further <note>That is, its power to transform metal will reach a higher ratio.</note>, as Arnold <note>original: *Arnoldus*; referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note> says.

Augmentation in quantity is as follows: Take three parts of the **fixed** <term>Fixed: A substance that has been rendered stable and will no longer evaporate or change when exposed to high heat.</term> matter which tints—that is, of the prepared tincture—and one part of the **Mercury of the Philosophers**, and put it in a vessel, and seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes as above, and dry it until it becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and soak it again, and dry it, etc., as above. And the water—that is, the **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum viuum*</note> or Mercury—does not add or give more weight to the body, except for as much of the metallic moisture as remains.

After the medicine has been dissolved <note>original: *soluta*; in alchemy, "solution" often means turning a solid into a liquid or "water."</note>, remove it from the fire for cooling, fixing, and congealing, hardening, or drying; and let it be dissolved in this way many times. The more the medicine is re-dissolved, the more perfect it will be. Such a solution is the refinement of the medicine and its spiritual **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: In this context, it refers to the process of purifying a substance and "raising" its quality by transitioning it between states.</term>. The more this is repeated, the more abundantly it works and the more parts it tints.

Whence **Rhazes** <note>original: *Rafis*; referring to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi.</note> says: The goodness of this multiplication depends on nothing except the multiplication of the repetition, the sublimation, and the fixation of the perfect medicine. Because the more this order of fulfillment is repeated, the more its abundance works and increases. For every time you have **sublimated** the perfect medicine more than usual and dissolved it, you will gain every time a power of projection of one weight upon a thousand. If at first it falls upon a thousand, the second time it falls upon ten thousand, the third upon a hundred thousand, the fourth upon a million <note>original: *mille millia*; literally "a thousand thousands."</note>, and so on unto infinity. For **Morienus the philosopher** <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: Know for certain that the more our stone is dissolved and congealed, the more the spirit and soul are joined and retained by them, and each time the **tincture** <term>Tincture: The transformative essence of the Stone that "dyes" or changes the nature of base metals into gold.</term> is multiplied. In another way, the medicine is multiplied through fermentation, and

### *The philosopher's stone is multiplied in three ways.*

In the first way, it is done through the repetition of the known corruption [returning] to the beginning—that is, by corrupting the stone through dissolution and **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: The stage of decay or "blackness" where the substance is broken down into its primary components to be reborn.</term>, and through the union of the elements, and burial in the air or in the earth, and through the **decoctions** <note>original: *decoctiones*; a process of boiling or heating to extract or concentrate essences.</note> of air and of common fire. 

And this [pertains] to other specific works, by the union of the elements with the **foliated earth** <term>Foliated earth: Also known as "terra foliata," a stage in the process where the matter becomes white and flaky like leaves.</term>, and by the heating of common fire, in a burial of dung <note>original: *humatione fimi*; stable manure was often used by alchemists as a source of gentle, steady heat for "incubation."</note>. Likewise, both types of multiplication happen at once if you lead the medicine—multiplied in quantity—to the said two wheels <note>original: *dictas duas rotas*; likely referring to the circular cycles of distillation and circulation.</note>, and do as has been said. 

For however many times the medicine passes through those two wheels toward its final completion, so...

### *On the projection of the medicine multiplied in power.*

Take one part or ounce of the said medicine <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" is a common synonym for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> that has been multiplied in power, and project <note>term: projection - the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to achieve transmutation.</note> it upon one hundred parts of Mercury. Immediately upon doing so, the Mercury will begin to heat up in the crucible, and it will be promptly congealed, and quickly the whole mass will turn into a **fixed medicine** <note>A substance is "fixed" when it can endure the heat of fire without evaporating or changing.</note>, for the purpose of making a further projection upon other Mercury. Afterward, take one ounce of that second medicine, and perform a projection upon a hundred parts of other hot Mercury, and the whole will still be pure, and a true medicine. In this way, you have multiplied your first medicine in quantity—either the whole of it, or a part—which you can again multiply through dissolution, congealment, and **inhumation** <note>term: inhumation - the practice of burying a sealed vessel in warm dung or earth to provide a gentle, steady heat for digestion.</note>, etc.

Because the method which I have described for multiplication allows you to increase the power [of the medicine] infinitely, and afterward its quantity. Project one weight of the medicine last congealed onto a hundred parts of Mercury that has been washed with salt and vinegar, and heat it over the fire immediately; when you see it smoking, it will be congealed into **gold**, etc.

### On the virtue, effect, and nobility of this praiseworthy science, or philosophical tincture.

<margin>On the virtues and the reasoning</margin>
It must be known that the ancient sages discovered four principal effects or virtues in this glorious chest of treasure—this science which provides comfort and aid.

<margin>On the nobility of the preceding [science]</margin>
First, it is said to heal the human body of many infirmities. Second, to restore imperfect metallic bodies <note>In alchemical theory, base metals like lead or copper were considered "diseased" or "imperfect" versions of gold; the Stone "heals" them into perfection.</note>. Third, to transmute common stones into certain precious gems. Fourth, to make all glass ductile, or malleable.

<margin>Malleable by anointing</margin>
